claim: Meta creative volume rule of thumb: about one new ad per $1,000 of monthly spend, so $100k a month needs about 100 new ads; returns diminish past $1M a month.
body: In the agency's creative pillar, the bottleneck is one of three things at a time: volume, diversity or quality. To test volume quickly, use about $1,000 of monthly ad spend per new ad launched: an account spending $100,000 a month should add about 100 new ads a month. If you are far below that, volume is probably the bottleneck. The ratio stops holding at large scale; an account at $1M to $3M a month does not need 1,000 to 3,000 new assets. Beyond the rule of thumb they use two models: a churn model (the monthly rate at which winning ads stop working, the hit rate of new ads, and therefore how many new ads you need to replace lost winners) and a winner-value model (average revenue a winning ad generates times your hit rate, worked back to a volume target). How to apply: count new ads launched last month against spend; if volume is fine, look at concept diversity next, then quality. Agency rule of thumb across its portfolio, not a published benchmark.
conditions: Meta ecommerce accounts from roughly $20k to $1M a month in spend; brands with a creative production capacity to match.
fails_when: Above about $1M to $3M a month (diminishing returns; use churn or winner-value models); very small accounts where 1 per $1k means too few ads to test concepts; when volume is met but concepts are all the same (diversity bottleneck).

claim: Under Andromeda, high-volume static ads can beat polished video: one large advertiser saw rough native statics outperform a sales video that took 2.5 months to make.
body: Meta's Andromeda delivery system tires out creative fast and rewards a steady flow of new ads. The speaker's argument for statics is volume and supply: even with a full creative team he struggles to produce enough video to keep the account fresh, while static images can be made in the thousands, quickly and cheaply. He also believes Meta favours statics because it can show more of them per person per session than videos, which suits Meta's revenue; that is his inference, not a stated Meta rule. His evidence is from his own account: about 17 long video sales letters running, and simple native-looking statics beating a polished one that took two and a half months of planning, shooting and editing. He pairs this with making ads that look like the content people already watch in the niche, found by following niche creators from a fresh account. How to apply: book one hour every week to make new statics around your current winning offer and product; keep video for proven angles; judge both formats on cost per purchase, not on production effort.

claim: Contested: a creator says spoken calls to action hurt TikTok retention, citing a no-CTA demo with 30M views and 7% CTR, yet also recommends micro-CTAs.
body: The tutorial's author shows his best ad: a 'underrated websites' demo for an AI video tool with a 2-second hook, no spoken call to action, about 30 million views, 2.3 million likes and a 7% click-through rate. His reasoning: a closing call to action lowers retention and rewatches, which TikTok weighs heavily when distributing both organic and paid videos, while paid placements already show a clickable button, so telling people to visit the site adds little. Other elements he credits: the hook promises something useful in the first 2 seconds, and the rhythm keeps changing (clips from half a second to 3 seconds, sound and silence alternating, zooms and speed-ups) so the video never feels flat. The contradiction: the same tutorial's general structure (hook 0-3s, promise 3-15s, proof 15-30s, call to action 30-35s, multiple micro-CTAs) includes CTAs. Treat it as a test variable: run the same video with and without the closing CTA and compare watch time, CTR and cost per purchase. One example, not a test.

claim: Treat a creative format as past its peak once it is widely promoted online; the operator saw native static ads decline across accounts after they went viral among marketers.
body: The operator's litmus test for saturation: by the time a format or tactic is being hyped on X or YouTube as 'the new meta', experienced advertisers have usually been using it for months or years. His example is native statics (image ads made to look like organic posts or editorial content rather than ads). Direct-response marketers had run that style on native ad networks for decades; when it became widely discussed among ecommerce marketers, he saw its performance decline across many accounts he had access to, as more advertisers flooded the feed with the same look and the novelty that made it stand out was lost. His underlying principle is contrast: study what competitors and creators in your niche are doing and make your ads look different, while still not looking like an ad (Gary Halbert's direct mail made to look like personal letters is his historical example). How to apply: 1) Keep the principle (content that does not look like a sales pitch) but vary the execution. 2) When a format is trending in marketer circles, check its recent CPA and hook rate in your own account rather than scaling into it. 3) Scan your category's ad library for the dominant look and test the opposite. No performance figures are given for the decline.
conditions: Paid social advertisers on Meta in crowded categories where competitors copy the same trending formats.
fails_when: Niches where the trending format has not yet been adopted by competitors; or formats that still work because they fit the platform natively; judge by your own account data, not by how talked-about a format is.

claim: Weight a video ad hook about 80% on the opening copy, 15% on the scroll-stopping visual and 5% on audio; test visuals for a 'what did I just watch' reaction.
body: The operator, who says he has spent tens of millions on paid ads, breaks the first 3 to 5 seconds of a video ad into three ingredients and ranks their influence: the copy of the first one or two sentences (about 80%), the scroll-stopping visual (about 15%) and the audio, whether voiceover or music (about 5%). He spends most creative effort on the opening line, aiming for it to 'punch in the gut' (a copywriting framework he credits to a known direct-response copywriter): vivid, emotional and clear rather than clever, written at roughly a 5th to 8th-grade reading level. For the visual, his test is to show the clip to someone and see whether their reaction is effectively 'what did I just watch?'; that reaction predicts his best scroll-stoppers. Practical sequence: 1) Write many first lines from customer research, ideally exact phrases from customer calls (one such phrase became one of his most profitable hooks). 2) Pair the strongest lines with several unusual visuals. 3) Use a simple voiceover. 4) Iterate on early winners quickly, within half a day once there is enough data. 5) Do not optimise for polish: his highest-spending profitable ads look 'ugly' but are clear. The weights are his rule of thumb, not measured.

fails_when: Sound-on, music-led formats (TikTok trends, Reels built around audio) where audio carries far more than 5%; purely visual products (fashion, home decor) where the image is the message; brand awareness objectives judged on recall rather than conversion.

claim: Alo Yoga's Meta account harvests demand made elsewhere: 0% of ads mention price or discounts, 15% name a celebrity, 96% target product-aware buyers; most brands cannot copy this.
body: An agency's scrape of Alo Yoga's Meta ad library found: about 21% dynamic catalogue ads; 99.6% use 'Shop now'; 98% send traffic to collection pages, the home page or product pages, none to a cold-audience landing page the site has built; 0% mention price, discounts, free shipping or returns, loyalty, the app or the 150+ stores; 15% carry a celebrity's name (for example Bella Hadid, Kylie, Kendall); and about 96% of ads sit in the product-aware and most-aware stages. The demand engine is celebrity seeding and cultural attention outside the ad account; Meta works as a distribution vehicle. The agency's verdict: this is right for Alo's scale and pricing power, but it fails for the roughly 95% of brands using Meta as their main new-customer channel, since without outside demand these assets would barely return their spend. The risk even for Alo: if cultural attention fades, there is no cold-prospecting creative to fall back on. What transfers: refusing to discount in ads, scarcity tied to real sell-outs, and creator content inside a catalogue style. Spend per ad is unknown from library data.

claim: Alo rotates ads fast (median live ad age 5 days, oldest 24); an agency for 15 to 20 nine-figure fashion brands advises keeping winners longer and reordering a winning SKU.

The agency calls this the fashion trade-off: balancing newness against squeezing winners, and says most fashion teams over-weight newness. Alo can afford it because its ad account distributes existing demand rather than creating it. For brands where paid social is the growth engine, their advice is the opposite: when an ad holds big spend at a strong return, keep it running; when a product wins, reorder it (if replenishment takes 3 to 4 weeks, do it) and push spend behind it. They use this to enter new countries: find one or two hero SKUs that sell, scale them hard (they cite selling at 15 to 20% net margin up to $1M a month), build a customer list, then broaden the range and keep winning ads live. Brand teams may object to being known for one product; the agency accepts that trade.

The strongest opened on a need ('I spend a lot of time in the gym so I need an outfit that's reliable') and named a fabric property that solves it. Their takeaways: 1) one named mechanism (a specific fabric technology) carries more weight than a string of adjectives like soft, buttery, cozy; 2) when the product is expensive, open on the need rather than the product; 3) add at least one missing beat that fits the brand, such as a call to action or a real sell-out fact. claim: Stores lift online sales: one client's Canadian online revenue rose about 20% after store openings; run store content in ads where shoppers don't know your stores.
body: The agency argues that retail stores raise online conversion, especially in fashion. Two mechanisms: trust (a shopper who learns a brand has 150+ stores sees a large retailer, not a small online shop) and direct spillover (people try on in store then buy online, find their size out of stock in store and order online, or come back after payday or to buy a gift). They report a client whose online revenue in Canada rose about 20% almost immediately after it began opening stores there. Alo Yoga, despite 150+ stores, never mentions them in ads or on landing pages; the agency's author, based in Australia where Alo has no stores, did not know they existed until researching. Recommendation: in markets without your stores, run store content as an authority signal, such as try-on hauls, new-collection walkthroughs or staff picks filmed in a flagship store. It is cheap to make because store staff can shoot it. True Classic's founder separately describes mall stores as top-of-funnel that should be judged on near break-even four-wall profit plus halo.

claim: Black Friday results corrupt creative analysis: judge ads at ad-set level and lean on CTR and CPC, since ad ROAS mostly reflects which product was discounted.
body: The period that generates the most data is also the least reliable for learning which creative works. An ad can show high ROAS because it featured a best-seller at 50% off, while a better ad that stopped the scroll and drew a strong click-through rate shows poor ROAS because its product was not discounted. Blue Sense Digital's rule for Black Friday: judge creative at the ad set level rather than the individual ad, because Meta optimises across multiple touches while reporting last click, and the breakdown effect makes ad-level ROAS especially misleading. In this window only, lean more on creative metrics such as CTR and CPC. Outside the sale they say the opposite: across large data sets CPC shows no meaningful correlation with ROAS (very low R-squared), so it should not be used to judge ads year-round. How to apply: tag Black Friday ads by product and discount level, read creative quality from engagement metrics, and avoid copying 'winners' into January without checking whether the offer did the work.
conditions: Meta accounts during heavy discount periods with mixed discount depth across products.
fails_when: Site-wide uniform discount on a single hero product, where ROAS differences do reflect creative; evergreen periods (use ROAS and incremental measures, not CPC).

claim: Keep evergreen Meta campaigns running through Black Friday (about 50 to 60% of spend) and add offer-badged copies; offer creative absorbs 4 to 5x more spend at similar 1-day ROAS.
body: Blue Sense Digital calls switching off evergreen campaigns the biggest Black Friday mistake: those campaigns carry campaign-level conversion history, and turning them off and on resets learning. In their 2025 portfolio evergreen campaigns held about 50 to 60% of budget and performed better than usual. Rather than editing them, duplicate the best evergreen ads, even fatigued past winners, badge them with the offer, and leave the originals running. Motion's creative data, which they cite, found offer creative delivered the same 1-day ROAS as evergreen creative but absorbed four to five times more spend; the reason to make offer ads is to hold more budget, not to convert bottom-funnel traffic. Their recommended spend mix: offer statics about 19%, offer-overlaid evergreen and catalog about 18%, with the rest in creator and founder content, product videos and early-access ads. Offer statics: discount and end date legible at thumbnail size, offer clear of 9:16 crop zones, offer or deadline in the first line of copy. Also write the offer into catalog (DPA) copy: in their scrape, 74% of brands' catalog ads had no written messaging and only 3% had sale messaging.

claim: Size Black Friday creative from per-ad spend ceilings: winners hold about $8k to $13k AUD a day, so a $150k peak day needs 12 to 18 such ads.
body: Creative is often the constraint at Black Friday spend levels. Blue Sense Digital's method: look at last November's peak daily spend per ad. In their AUD accounts the highest single ad reached about $12,500 a day; most evergreen ads spent about $4,000 to $8,500; a realistic working ceiling for a winner is about $8,000 to $13,000, so plan around $10,000 to $12,000 for winners and about $5,000 for an average evergreen ad. A $150,000 peak day therefore needs about 12 to 18 ads able to hold around $10,000 each, which is 12 to 18 winners, not 12 to 18 ads. Plan for a long tail too: Pareto did not hold. The top ad averaged about 7% of spend, top 3 17%, top 5 23%, top 10 33%, top 20 46%, so the bottom 80% of ads held about 54%. Concentration falls with size: top 20% of ads held about 53% of spend in accounts under $250k in November, 44% and 33% in larger bands. So you need many ads beyond your winners.
conditions: Meta accounts planning a Black Friday spend peak; figures in AUD from a large-brand agency portfolio, 2025.
fails_when: Small accounts where one or two ads can carry the whole budget; accounts in other currencies or markets with different CPMs (rescale the ceilings); dynamic catalog-heavy accounts.

claim: At about $100k a day on Meta, Ridge launches hundreds of ads a week and tests thumb-stops as named units, reading 3-second view rate per thumb-stop across all ads.
body: Ridge spends around $100,000 a day directly on Meta. Frank's reasoning: the best ad in an account probably tops out around $100,000 a day, so at that scale you need a strong new ad very often, and to get one you may need about 50 attempts, hence hundreds of new ads a week from an in-house studio, about four agency partners at any time, and UGC creators. Ads are broken into units. A test might run 10 concepts with three hooks each, and the thumb-stop (the first image or frame) is written into the naming convention, so in their attribution tool (Northbeam) they can compare one thumb-stop against another across every ad that uses it, for example finding one works 30% better. Metrics include the share of viewers reaching the 3-second mark (they cite 80% as a win). A counter-intuitive signal: if many viewers watch all the way to the end card, the middle message and call to action are not converting them. He says the thumb-stop matters most, then the hook; the middle and end matter less, and visuals must be radically different, not small edits, to reach new people.

fails_when: Small accounts that cannot fund hundreds of ads a week; high-AOV products with too little purchase signal (he suggests optimising to a higher-funnel event there); teams without a naming discipline.

claim: Comfrt's founder says three brands he advised each hit $500,000 in their third month and all had put about 200 new creatives into their ad account that month.
body: Hudson of Comfrt (which he says did $43M in one January about 2.5 years in) argues creative volume is the main growth lever: quality and quantity together, because the ads the team expects to win often flop and vice versa. Early Comfrt got around 200 creatives a month from about 20 influencers posting at least 10 times each, tested them on Meta, saw a 4 to 5 ROAS and doubled down on what worked. In mentoring calls, three brands that each reached $500,000 in their third month shared one trait: about 200 new creatives introduced that month. At scale Comfrt reports over 10,000 creatives a week across channels and asks each TikTok Shop creator for 5 to 7 posts a day. Ways to reach volume: many formats (street interviews, family first reactions, podcasts, voiceovers for creators who film well but dislike talking on camera, shock hooks); using an AI assistant to generate 100 hook ideas to bring to creator meetings. The three-brand pattern is a correlation from a tiny sample, so treat 200 a month as an ambition level, not a threshold.

claim: Scale a single multi-benefit SKU by running separate angle pillars for different buyer groups, each with its own landing page, since every angle hits a spend ceiling.
body: The speaker's read of Grüns' Meta Ad Library: about 660 live ads for one gummy product, grouped into pillars (gut health, GLP-1 support, daily multivitamin, fiber, hair health, energy, immunity, cognition), many run as partnership ads. Mechanism: each angle reaches a limited pool of people who have that specific problem, so spend on any one angle tops out; adding pillars adds separate pools, letting one SKU absorb far more spend. The alternative most brands take, launching new SKUs to reach new buyers, ties cash up in inventory, risks discounting failed launches, and adds 3PL and operating complexity; one SKU keeps cash flow lean. Two rules make it work. First, each angle should target a genuinely different person (social drinkers, people noticing first grey hairs, gamers, entrepreneurs), not ten hooks aimed at the same group. Second, the click must land on a page built for that angle: Grüns sends GLP-1 ads to a page about GLP-1 support benefits, because a hyper-specific ad that lands on a generic 20-benefit product page makes buyers wonder whether they need the whole product. The speaker uses a reasoning-mode LLM prompt to generate 10 to 15 angles, each with audience, hook and reason it works, then builds pages for the one or two that win.
conditions: Single-SKU or few-SKU brands whose product genuinely serves several jobs (multi-ingredient supplements, versatile consumables); Meta spend large enough to hit angle ceilings; ability to build angle-specific landing pages or advertorials.
fails_when: Single-benefit products where new angles stretch credibility; health angles (GLP-1, fertility, 'natural Adderall') that cross into disease or drug claims prohibited by FTC/FDA rules or Meta policy; wide-catalogue brands (fashion, furniture) that can scale by pushing other SKUs instead.

claim: IM8 scales one winning 'clock' script (day 1, 9, 21: ingredient, dose, scene) by swapping only the persona, and plans volume at about $2,500 spend per ad.
body: After transcribing every active IM8 video ad, the speaker found one dominant long-form structure. It opens with a symptom hook for a single persona, reframes the cause, then walks a timeline (on day one you notice this, by day 9 this, after 21 days this), naming a specific ingredient and dose at each checkpoint, describing outcomes as scenes rather than claims (playing with grandkids instead of fixes arthritis), and ending with proof, then offer, guarantee and scarcity. The timeline works as a retention device, like teasing what is coming in a YouTube video. The angle and offer stay fixed while the persona changes: joints, menopause, GLP-1 users, regular drinkers, gut and bloating, each with near-identical script lines adapted in language, and each driven to a matching persona landing page. Creative volume tracks spend almost linearly; the speaker estimates each ad holds about $2,500 of spend, so doubling budget means doubling ad count. In a 40-ad sample, most sat at problem and solution aware, with few unaware ads and one most-aware and three product-aware. Claims got more aggressive in unaware ads (kidney symptoms, antidepressant comparisons), where regulatory exposure concentrates. How to apply: once a script wins, list your top personas and remake it per persona before inventing new concepts.

claim: Smoke-test angles with one product-on-white image and a bold text bar, changing only the value prop; expand the winning angle into video, then test who appears.
body: The guest's first test with a small budget, which he calls a smoke test: take the easiest asset to make, the product on a white background with a white bar of bold call-out text, and run near-identical versions where only the text changes, one per value proposition (his fidget spinner example: reduce anxiety, increase focus, relieve stress). Whichever gets the most clicks and engagement at acceptable cost wins the angle. The next step is a longer explanatory video on that angle, then variations on who is shown: a man, a woman, both, or only hands and arms, which he uses so viewers can picture themselves without rejecting a face that does not look like them. The system repeats as winners emerge, getting more granular by creator, colour or region; he notes ads featuring people who look local to a state perform better there. Read the funnel in order: if CPM and click costs are normal for the niche (he cites $15 to $30 CPMs depending on audience) but people abandon at cart, the price or offer is wrong, so test price before more creative.
conditions: New products or new angles; small test budgets on Meta; product benefits that can be stated in a few words.
fails_when: Products whose value cannot be grasped from a still image and one line; when clicks are judged without checking cart and purchase behaviour, since cheap clicks can come from curiosity.

claim: True Classic cuts every ad with 4 to 5 different openers (6 for a comedy parody) because the first 3 seconds decide thumb-stop rate and taste is unreliable.
body: Bartlett says the opener is the whole game: if viewers are not hooked in the first 3 seconds, they never reach the message. So every True Classic ad ships with 4 to 5 alternative openers, and their recent movie-parody comedy ad had six, because what the team finds funny may not land with customers. The approach is iteration within existing content: one body, many first-3-second variants, then find the winner and build on it. Their creative mix pairs comedy parodies for brand reach with direct-response side-by-side comparisons that prove the fit claim (their fitted shirt next to a baggy generic one), which they also put on the home page instead of lifestyle images. He insists creative must reach an internal 8 out of 10 before release and says agencies often deliver a 6. How to apply: for each new concept, film or cut 4 to 6 openers (different first line, visual or pattern interrupt) on the same body; launch them together; judge on hook rate (3-second views over impressions) and then cost per purchase; carry the winning opener style into the next brief.
conditions: Video ads on Meta, YouTube and similar feeds; brands with enough spend to give each opener variant data.
fails_when: Very small budgets where 5 variants split spend too thin; static image ads; judging openers on hook rate alone when they attract the wrong viewers.

claim: Fix a video ad's first half first: only about 15% of viewers reach the second half, so reveal the product late and state benefits before features.
body: Across six Meta ads, the presenter's pattern was that winners delay the product and losers lead with it. A weak ad opened with 'these are my vital packs': no problem, no reason to care, and the value proposition arrived 7 to 10 seconds in. Because retention only falls over the length of an ad, he estimates only about 15% of viewers see the second half, so a strong ending cannot rescue a weak opening, while a strong opening can carry an average ending. Structure he credits in the winners: a high-stakes or curiosity hook aimed at the right buyer, a bridge that says a solution exists without naming the product, objection handling, category-level authority (for example a hat design centuries old), then a soft call to action. Cuts happen at least every three seconds. When features appear, state the lifestyle benefit first and the feature as the reason ('I can nap for 30 minutes mid-day because the armrests drop and the fabric is soft'), so more of the shrinking audience hears the benefit. Two failure modes: a hook that grabs attention through confusion attracts the wrong viewers, and a founder-authority ad with no on-screen proof only converts people who already trust the founder.
conditions: Paid social video ads (Meta, Instagram, TikTok) aimed at cold audiences; UGC, partnership and founder ads.
fails_when: Retargeting or warm audiences who already know the product, where an early product reveal and offer can work; partnership ads on a creator's page where the creator's credibility is the hook.

claim: Near-duplicate ads get grouped under one Meta entity ID and serve to the same users: 200 similar ads might count as about 20 unique ads, adding no new reach.
body: Meta's retrieval stage (Andromeda), extended by GEM to read video, audio and format, scans every ad and groups creatives it judges to be the same. Grouped ads share one entity ID, so in the presenter's example 200 ads uploaded as small variations might register as only about 20 unique ads, and every ad inside a group serves to the same pool of people. Extra variations then add cost and noise but no unique reach, which defeats the purpose of creative volume: reaching new people or giving existing viewers a genuinely new reason to buy. How to apply: plan creative by concept, defined as the intersection of angle, offer and persona, and treat format as a fourth axis because a big enough format change (static versus UGC video versus founder talking head) can register as a different ad even with the same message. Iterations (new hooks, colours, edits) still have a place for optimising a winning concept, but count your new-reach pipeline in concepts, not ad count. When reach stalls and frequency climbs, check how many distinct concepts are actually live before adding more variants. Broad targeting makes this matter more, because the creative itself now decides which user clusters see the ad.
conditions: Meta Advantage+ or broad-targeted accounts on the current Andromeda-era delivery system; any spend level running many creatives.
fails_when: Small accounts with only a few ads, where the bottleneck is spend or offer, not uniqueness; the 200-to-20 figure is illustrative, not a measured ratio.

claim: After Andromeda, still test hook variations: launch each net-new concept as its own ad set with about 3 variations, because a variation often wins where the original loses.
body: A popular reading of the Andromeda update is that advertisers should only launch net-new concepts and stop making variations. This media buyer disagrees. His launch structure: each ad set holds one net-new concept, and the ads inside it are the original plus variations of that concept, typically different hooks (for example one concept with three hooks). The variations are extra attempts at the same idea; in his experience one of them is often the winner while the original concept ad loses, so killing variations would have wrongly written off a concept that works. What rarely works is making variations of the account's existing top ad in the hope of beating it: they tend to perform decently but not better. Combine this with the entity-ID point that very similar ads collapse together: the variation should change something the viewer notices first (the hook, opening visual or framing), not just colours or end cards. How to apply: count tests at the concept level, give each concept a few hook variations, judge the concept by its best variation, and then build new concepts rather than endlessly re-cutting the current winner.
conditions: Meta accounts launching new creative weekly on broad or Advantage+ delivery; ecommerce creative testing.
fails_when: Very low budgets where splitting spend across several variations per concept leaves each with too little delivery to judge; variations so similar they share an entity ID.

claim: Test 4 or 5 angles by changing only the ad headline to one product page, then rewrite the page top around the winner; one brand reportedly tripled in a month.
body: The founder's sequence for a product that is not selling well: before rebuilding the site or changing the product, write four or five distinct angles. For a shaker bottle drink mix the examples were 'never drink out of a shaker cup again' and 'tastes like lemonade'. Run the same ad with only the headline or hook changed for each angle, all pointing to the same existing product page, so the angle is the only variable. Within about a day the click-through rates usually show a clear winner (he describes gaps like 12% against 1%). Then change the landing page to match: the top-of-page imagery, headline and copy are rebuilt around the winning angle so the ad's promise continues on the page. He says one brand tripled its revenue in a month from this alone, then the team made many more creatives on that angle. He treats this as the step most founders skip in favour of small conversion tweaks, and uses it to diagnose product-market fit: if several angles and demographics all still struggle to sell, the issue is probably the product or positioning, not the ads.

claim: IM8 grew from about 50 to 1,500 live Meta ads in 13 months, now about 75% statics (AI-assisted), with roughly 85% of spend on Meta and 15% on Google.

claim: In the US, comparison ads may name a competitor and may be unflattering to it, as long as the basis of comparison is clear and the ad is truthful and not deceptive.
body: The FTC's 1979 policy statement encourages advertisers to name or refer to competitors, because truthful comparisons give shoppers useful information. It asks for clarity, and a disclosure where needed, so buyers are not misled about what is being compared. Disparaging a rival is allowed if it is truthful and not deceptive. Comparative ads are judged by the same test as any ad: does it tend to deceive. How to apply: write the exact attribute compared (price per use, material, warranty length) on the ad, keep proof for each side of the comparison, and compare like with like (same size, same date, same market).
conditions: US advertising of physical products where the attribute compared is objectively measurable or a price.
fails_when: Claims about a competitor that cannot be checked, comparisons to a different size or an old price, or using a competitor's trademark in a way that suggests endorsement (a separate trademark question).

claim: The US rule on fake reviews (in force 21 October 2024) bans writing, buying or using fake or false reviews and testimonials, and allows civil penalties for knowing violations.
body: AI avatars are not banned, but a testimonial they give must not be fake. The FTC's Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule covers anyone who writes, creates or sells a fake or false consumer review or testimonial, and makes a business liable when it knew or should have known that a hired creator misrepresented using the product. There is no blanket ban on AI-generated avatars; the avatar's testimonial is illegal when the experience it describes is fake. A celebrity likeness used without permission breaks the rule if viewers would think the celebrity gave the testimonial. How to apply: every quote in an ad must come from a real customer record you can show; an AI presenter may read a real customer's words only when it is labelled as a dramatisation and does not claim to be that customer.
conditions: US marketing using reviews, testimonials, creator content or AI presenters.

claim: US advertisers need a reasonable basis for every objective claim before the ad runs, and a claim like 'tests prove' or 'doctors recommend' needs at least that level of proof.
body: The FTC's 1984 substantiation policy says making objective claims without a reasonable basis is an unfair or deceptive practice under Section 5 of the FTC Act. When an ad states its level of support (tests prove, studies show, doctors recommend), the advertiser must hold at least that support, and must also hold whatever proof the ad as a whole communicates to buyers. How to apply: build a claims sheet before production with each objective claim, the evidence file, its date and who checked it; cut or narrow any claim whose evidence is weaker than the wording.
conditions: Objective claims in US advertising: performance, comparisons, results, test and expert claims.
fails_when: Pure opinion or puffery that no buyer would read as measurable; health, drug and children's claims, which carry stricter rules on top.

claim: Meta ads must not assert or imply a viewer's personal attributes (health, age, finances, religion, race and others).
body: Meta ads must not assert or imply a viewer's personal attributes (health, age, finances, religion, race and others), so a line asking the viewer if they have a condition gets rejected while a line describing the product for that condition can pass. Meta's advertising standard on personal attributes bans ad content that asserts or implies personal attributes, directly or indirectly, including physical or mental health, age, financial vulnerability, religion, race or ethnicity, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, criminal record, voting status, union membership and name. Allowed examples describe a product or a group; banned examples address the viewer with the attribute, such as asking whether the viewer is bankrupt or 18 years old. claim: In India, the ASCI Code allows comparison ads only when what is compared is clear, the comparison is factual, accurate and capable of substantiation, it is not picked for an artificial advantage, and it does not unfairly denigrate a rival.
body: Chapter IV of the ASCI Code (fair in competition) permits comparisons in the interest of competition and public enlightenment, on conditions: the aspects compared must be clear; the comparison must be factual, accurate and capable of substantiation; it must not be chosen to give the advertiser an artificial advantage; there must be no likelihood of misleading the consumer; and the ad must not unfairly denigrate, attack or discredit other products directly or by implication. Chapter I requires claims of objectively ascertainable fact to be capable of substantiation, with proof supplied when ASCI asks. How to apply: in India, prefer comparisons against a category or the old way over a named brand, keep the tone factual, and keep the test file ready.
conditions: Advertising seen in India, including digital and influencer ads.
fails_when: ASCI is self-regulatory; statutory consumer protection rules and trademark law also apply and may be stricter in a given case.

body: The FTC's Endorsement Guides (revised 2023) say an endorsement must reflect the honest opinion of the endorser, and nobody may describe experience with a product they have not tried. If an endorser's result is not what people generally get, the advertiser must either prove it is typical or make clear what results people can generally expect. A connection a significant minority of viewers would not expect (employee, relative, payment, free product given to promote) must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. How to apply: label founder, staff and family appearances as such, keep each creator's real use on file, and pair any standout result with the typical one.

claim: The FTC's 2024 rule (16 CFR Part 465) bans fake reviews and testimonials, including AI-generated ones, undisclosed insider reviews, paying for positive or negative sentiment, and suppressing negative reviews.
body: On 14 August 2024 the US Federal Trade Commission announced its final Trade Regulation Rule on the Use of Consumer Reviews and Testimonials, 16 CFR Part 465, effective 60 days after Federal Register publication. It bans creating, buying, selling or spreading fake or false reviews and testimonials, including AI-generated ones and fake celebrity testimonials, when the business knew or should have known; offering compensation or incentives conditioned on the review being positive or negative; reviews by officers, managers, employees or their relatives without clear disclosure of the connection; presenting a company-controlled review site as independent; suppressing reviews through baseless legal threats, intimidation or false accusations, or claiming a filtered review section shows all or most reviews; and buying or selling fake followers or views. The FTC can seek civil penalties against knowing violators. For ads, every review shown must be a real review by a real buyer, unchanged in meaning, with any incentive disclosed and never tied to the star rating.
conditions: Businesses advertising to US consumers; a useful floor everywhere.

claim: In a video endorsement, the FTC wants the disclosure both on screen and spoken, early rather than only at the end, and inside the video, not just in the description.
body: The FTC's endorsement FAQ says that when an endorsement is both visual and audible, the disclosure should be made both visually and audibly. Viewers are more likely to miss a disclosure at the end of a video, so the beginning is better and repeating it during the video is better still. A disclosure placed only in the video description can easily be missed, and one covered by other elements is not clear and conspicuous. An audio-only disclosure fails viewers who watch with the sound off. How to apply in ecommerce video ads: when a creator or customer was paid, gifted product or told they might be featured, put a short on-screen line in the first seconds inside the placement's safe zone and say it once in the voice track; never rely on the caption field alone.

claim: India's E-Commerce Rules bar posing as buyers to post reviews, ads that misstate a product, pre-ticked consent boxes, manipulating prices for unfair profit, and treating buyers of the same class differently.
body: IndiaLaw's summary of the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 lists conduct rules that reach ads, reviews and checkout. All e-commerce entities must avoid unfair trade practices, record a buyer's consent to a purchase only when it is clearly given and not through pre-checked boxes, must not manipulate prices to make unfair profits, and must not discriminate between consumers of the same class. Sellers on marketplaces and inventory entities must not pose as consumers to post reviews, must not misrepresent the quality or features of a product, and must make sure their advertisements match the product's actual characteristics and conditions of use. An inventory entity that claims its goods are authentic is responsible for that claim. How to apply: never seed reviews from staff, agencies or friends posing as buyers; untick every add-on, insurance, donation and marketing box at checkout; check each ad claim against the product as shipped; and keep a written reason for any price difference between buyer groups, such as a published member price.
conditions: Online selling to consumers in India, including ads that lead to an Indian store or listing.
fails_when: The summary does not define unfair profit or the same class of consumer; the Consumer Protection Act and ASCI's code also apply to ads. Check the rule text for borderline pricing cases.

claim: From 1 January 2027, India's E-Commerce Rules require every e-commerce entity to follow the 2023 dark patterns guidelines, run a yearly self-audit, and prominently display a certificate that its platform is free of dark patterns.
body: Poovayya & Co. write that new Rule 4(15) of the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) (Amendment) Rules, 2026 gives statutory force to the Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 Guidelines for Prevention and Regulation of Dark Patterns. Every e-commerce entity must complete a yearly self-audit confirming its platform is free of such patterns and must prominently display a certificate saying so. The rules were notified on 9 September 2026 and take effect on 1 January 2027. The guidelines specify 13 patterns, including false urgency, basket sneaking, confirm shaming, forced action, subscription traps, interface interference, bait and switch, drip pricing, disguised ads, nagging, trick questions, SaaS billing and rogue malware. How to apply: before January 2027, walk every flow a buyer sees (ads, product page, cart, checkout, pop-ups, emails, subscription and cancellation) against all 13 patterns; screenshot each step as evidence; fix what fails; then publish the certificate where buyers can find it, such as the footer, and repeat the audit every year and after major checkout changes.

claim: Indian ad disclaimers must not contradict or correct the main claim, must be in the claim's language and font, visible on one normal reading, and keep pace with any voice-over.
body: Clause 11 of the CCPA's Guidelines for Prevention of Misleading Advertisements and Endorsements, 2022 says a disclaimer may explain or qualify a claim but must not contradict the main claim or message, change the ordinary meaning of the words, hide material information or correct a claim that would otherwise mislead. It must be in the same language as the claim and the same font, placed prominently (ideally on the same panel for packaging), clearly visible to a normally-sighted person reading it once from a reasonable distance at a reasonable speed, and, where there is a voice-over, in sync with it at the same speed. Clause 12 adds that guarantees must state a fixed period, and research cited in an ad needs its source and date. How to apply: if a claim only works with an asterisk ('huge savings*', 'visible results fast*'), rewrite the headline so it is true without the asterisk; set disclaimers in the same typeface as the headline at a readable size and hold them on screen long enough to read.
conditions: Print, packaging, video and digital ads seen in India.

claim: IM8's top script uses a timeline: a symptom hook for one persona, a reframed cause, then day 1, day 9 and day 21 checkpoints that each name an ingredient, dose and outcome, ending on offer, guarantee and scarcity.
body: Step by step: 1) Hook on one symptom for one persona, never everyone. 2) Reframe the cause to something the viewer has not considered. 3) Walk through checkpoints over time, and at each one name a specific compound, its dose and what it does. 4) Express each outcome as a scene from the viewer's life. 5) Put proof last. 6) Close with the offer, the guarantee and scarcity. Why the clock works: like a YouTube video that promises what comes later, each upcoming checkpoint gives a reason to keep watching, so the timeline acts as a retention device. One example targets men who drink regularly: what would change after three weeks of one sachet each morning, then repeating clock, mechanism, payoff. Versions aimed lower in the funnel lean less on mechanisms. How to apply: map your product's effects onto a realistic timeline using sourced ingredient facts, write one version for one persona, and keep every checkpoint claim within what you can back up.
conditions: Supplements, skincare and other products whose effects build over time.
fails_when: Instant-benefit or purely aesthetic products; regulated claims that cannot be substantiated.

claim: In supplements, claim strength trades CAC against survival: dark-hat brands at $50M to $100M beat IM8's CAC with outrageous claims but face constant ad account bans and are likely unsellable.
body: Blue Sense describes a hard middle ground. Supplements that are not aggressive often do not convert; brands that go too far risk legal trouble. Some rule-breaking supplement brands making $50 million to $100 million run wild claims, often in native-style statics, across TikTok, Shopify, affiliates and Meta. They get lower CAC and more profit than IM8, but their ad accounts are banned constantly and they probably cannot sell the business. IM8 pushes some lines hard, such as comparing a mood result to leading antidepressants, and Blue Sense thinks it sits about where a public company would want to be, testing where the line is because competitors are far past it. How to apply: choose your lane on purpose. If you plan to sell the brand or build for the long term, write a claims policy, keep substantiation for every claim, have someone review new ads before launch, and accept a higher CAC than the rule breakers.

claim: Write outcomes as scenes, not claims: show what the buyer can now do (play with grandkids, hike, dance) instead of naming a health result; it converts better and carries less compliance risk.
body: IM8 seems to have an internal rule against lines like improves mobility. Instead each outcome is a moment from the viewer's life, such as joining in with the grandkids instead of sitting and watching. Blue Sense gives two reasons this works. A scene plays on emotion and story and speaks to a specific problem the person has, so it outperforms a flat claim. And because it paints a picture rather than promising a medical result, it is safer from a compliance view. A related rule: lead with the mechanism before the benefit. Almost no IM8 ad opens with have more energy; it opens with why you lack energy, then names the compound that addresses it and why IM8's form is better. How to apply: go through your scripts and replace each benefit claim with a concrete scene for your persona; put the cause and the named ingredient or feature before the payoff; keep a file of what you can substantiate.

claim: Blue Sense's DTC script order is hook, problem, promise, mechanism, objection, proof, offer, risk reversal, then CTA, with the promise always before the mechanism.
body: This is the lens Blue Sense uses to review and write paid social scripts. Hook: earn the next line by being relevant. Problem: agitate what the viewer struggles with. Promise: what they will get. Mechanism: why this works when other things did not. Objection: answer the main reason they would not buy. Proof: reviews, tests, credentials. Offer: what to buy and the deal. Risk reversal: the guarantee, placed just before the ask. CTA: the action. Short ads can drop or merge parts, and longer ads can loop between promise, mechanism and objection more than once. In Gorilla Mind's best scoop-comparison ad, Blue Sense's notes were to move the promise above the mechanism, push the offer lower, and give a stronger mechanism, such as explaining why most brands underdose. How to apply: paste a script into a table with these nine rows, mark which parts are present, and check the order. Missing problem, mechanism or risk reversal sections are the most common gaps in creator scripts.
conditions: Direct response video and long-copy ads for DTC products, especially for cold or solution-aware audiences.
fails_when: Very short bottom-funnel ads for warm audiences, where hook, offer and CTA are enough; or pure brand films not built to drive purchase.
numbers: 9 parts: hook, problem, promise, mechanism, objection, proof, offer, risk reversal, CTA

claim: Build creative around concepts (persona, angle and offer) and give creators written scripts per concept; Gorilla Mind ran 143 unique, largely unscripted scripts but only about 35 real concepts.
body: Blue Sense found three main concepts behind Gorilla Mind's ads: night or caffeine-sensitive lifters who want a pump without losing sleep; energy drink fans, mostly around flavours; and label readers who want properly dosed formulas, the founder's original audience. There were 143 unique scripts, which shows creators had freedom to write their own, likely through a seeding platform or a TikTok Shop style agency, rather than following briefs. The result was many scripts with the same weak structure. Blue Sense's biggest strategic fix: run a concept-based system. A concept is a persona plus an angle plus an offer. For each concept, write the script (or a tight brief with hook, problem, mechanism and objection points), then hand it to creators to perform in their own style. The number to track over the next 12 months is total concepts live; they counted about 35 spoken concepts, generously. How to apply: list your live ads by persona, angle and offer; count distinct combinations; and brief new ones where gaps exist rather than asking creators to just make an ad.
conditions: Brands using many creators or a UGC agency, at a spend level where concept diversity limits scale.
fails_when: The creators are expert direct response writers whose own scripts already beat the brand's briefs, or the brand is too small to run more than a couple of concepts.

claim: Carry the site's offer into the ads: tie the CTA to how long the product takes to work, so buyers choose subscription or a 90-day supply, and put the guarantee right before the ask.
body: Blue Sense cross-checked Gorilla Mind's ad scripts against the offers on its landing pages. None of the ads they reviewed pushed subscribe and save or buying more, and none used the 30-day money-back guarantee, even though the site offers both. Their fix links offer to mechanism. Creatine only works when taken every day for long enough to saturate the muscles, and testosterone boosters take about a month. So the ad can say that results need consistent use, which is why the 90-day supply or subscription is the sensible choice. That raises order value and subscription take rate without sounding like an upsell. Then add risk reversal just before the CTA: you do not need to trust it, test it with the guarantee. Not every offer belongs in ads: Blue Sense would keep the military discount off ads to avoid abuse, and thinks a 20% welcome code is aggressive for new customers when the subscription is the better hook. How to apply: list every offer on your product page and check which appear in your top ten ads by spend.
conditions: Consumable products with a usage period before results and a subscription or bundle offer and guarantee on site.
fails_when: The product works in a single use, or the guarantee has terms too narrow to promote honestly in ads.

claim: Do not launch an unproven ad in eight near-identical text hook versions; Meta may group them as one ad or split budget across tiny differences, so test about three very different hooks on proven winners.
body: Gorilla Mind ran one creator, one script and one video as eight ads that differed only in the on-screen text hook: stim-free pre-workout, non-stim pre-workout, pre-workout without caffeine and similar lines. Blue Sense sees two likely outcomes, both bad. Meta may treat them as the same ad and serve them to the same people, so the variations mean nothing. Or Meta tests them all, splitting budget and learning across changes too small to matter. Their rule: hook variants are a way to squeeze more spend from a proven winner, not a way to launch something new. When you do run them, consolidate to around three and make each one materially different (a different promise, a different problem, a different emotion), so any gap in results can be traced to the hook and taught to future briefs. How to apply: before making variants, check the base ad has already held meaningful spend at a good cost per purchase. Write hooks that a viewer would read as different ideas, not synonyms.
conditions: Meta accounts testing hook or headline variants on video ads.
fails_when: The ad is already a proven winner, where several hook swaps can add spend; or the variants change the visual and audio, not just text, making them genuinely different ads.

claim: Fix creative in this order: ad quality first, then concept and format diversity, and only then raise ad volume; more ads of the same weak type will not scale the account.
body: Gorilla Mind's Meta account has high creative velocity, enough new ads to be a bare minimum for the eight and nine figure brands Blue Sense works with. Blue Sense's verdict is that velocity is not the problem: nearly all of it is one format (creators talking to camera) with mediocre scripts. Their order of fixes: 1) Ad quality. Better scripts, built on a clear structure, written for the persona and stage of awareness. 2) Diversity. Different concepts and formats, so ads reach different groups of people rather than the same pool. 3) Velocity. Only once the first two are fixed, raise the number of new ads per week, ideally on a steady schedule. Their ad library view showed new ads arriving in irregular batches, not a consistent weekly cadence, which suggests content agencies delivering in lumps. How to apply: before asking for more ads, check in Ads Manager how many distinct concepts and formats hold spend. If one format and a handful of scripts take most spend, brief new concepts and formats before increasing volume.
conditions: Accounts already producing creative in volume but concentrated in one format or one style of script.
fails_when: The account has very few ads live at all, where raising volume is the first bottleneck; or one format is genuinely the only one that works for the category after real tests.

claim: For buyers who already tried rival products, handle the objection by explaining why those failed (for example, root strength varies so 400 mg can act like 10 mg) and how long the product takes to work.
body: In Gorilla Mind's ad, the objection was handled with a line about being sceptical until reading the reviews. Blue Sense thinks that misses why these buyers hold back. People who tried a booster before and felt nothing are not doubting reviews; they think boosters do not work. Blue Sense's rewrite answers that directly. Problem: tongkat ali is a root, and strength changes from root to root, so a milligram number tells you how much powder is in the capsule, not how strong it is; a 400 mg dose of a weak extract may act like 10 mg. Mechanism: Gorilla Mind sources a standardised extract, tests it in a lab and shows results on the page or label, and uses a patented ashwagandha extract. Timeline objection: it is not a pre-workout, so feeling nothing in week one is normal; it needs about a month. Proof: third-party testing and a 4.8 star rating on about 1,300 reviews. Offer: three bottles on subscription for $104.97, about $35 a bottle, free shipping, cancel any time. How to apply: interview or survey people who bought a competitor and stopped, and build the objection section around their reason.
conditions: Solution-aware buyers who have tried competitor products and were disappointed, common in supplements and skincare.
fails_when: You cannot back the claim about your sourcing or testing with real evidence on the page, or the ad platform's health claim rules block the comparison.

claim: In a category most buyers already understand, like creatine, you can scale on solution-aware ads; Gorilla Mind's split of 14 unaware, 49 problem, 49 solution and 31 product-aware ads is healthy.
body: Blue Sense tagged Gorilla Mind's ads by stage of awareness: 14 unaware, 49 problem aware, 49 solution aware and 31 product or most aware. Most brands are heavily weighted to bottom-of-funnel product ads, so this spread is good. The tempting conclusion is that a brand needs many more unaware ads to scale on cold traffic. Blue Sense disagrees in this case: unaware ads are hard to make and rarely win, although winners do scale, and you do not need them where the market already knows the solution. Nearly everyone in Gorilla Mind's audience knows what creatine is and roughly how it works. The better use of effort is to give solution-aware buyers a reason to switch: why gummies beat powder, and why these gummies beat other gummies. Keep some education ads, but focus there. How to apply: tag your live ads by stage, and ask how well your target buyer already knows the category. If awareness of the solution is high, put most new briefs into solution-aware angles that explain why your version is better.
conditions: Established categories where most target buyers already know the solution type (creatine, protein, retinol, running shoes).
fails_when: The product creates a new category or solves a problem buyers do not know they have, where unaware and problem-aware ads must do the teaching.
numbers: awareness split: 14 unaware, 49 problem aware, 49 solution aware, 31 product or most aware

claim: Of Gorilla Mind's 188 video ads, 148 were creators talking to camera; Blue Sense calls one format at volume the account's biggest risk.
body: Blue Sense scraped and transcribed every Gorilla Mind ad in the Meta Ad Library. Of 188 video assets, 148 were creators talking to camera, 15 were lifestyle brand films or memes, 12 were plain product shots (very bottom of funnel), 10 were brand demos or motion graphics, and 3 were Joe Rogan clips. A small group of creators held much of the volume. Because Meta now decides who sees an ad largely from the ad itself, many ads in the same format and style tend to reach the same people, raising frequency and capping reach. Users also have format preferences, so missing formats means missing audiences. How to apply: export your active ads, tag each by format (talking head, street interview, demo, static, meme, founder, podcast clip, motion graphic, and so on) and by concept, then calculate the share of spend per format. If one format holds most of the spend and ad-level frequency on cold campaigns is above about 2, brief new formats for your proven concepts first. You can run the same audit on a competitor through the Ad Library.
conditions: Meta accounts at meaningful spend where creative mostly comes from one source, such as a UGC creator agency.
fails_when: The account is small enough that one format is not yet saturating its audience; or ad library counts mislead, since survivors only show what is still live.
numbers: 188 video ads: 148 creator talking head, 15 lifestyle or memes, 12 product shots, 10 demos or motion graphics, 3 Joe Rogan clips

claim: On-brand comedy static ads are worth keeping in the account: they build brand recall and teach lightly while reaching colder buyers than product shots.
body: Blue Sense did not break down Gorilla Mind's static ads in detail, but they noted a batch of comedy-led statics and liked them. Their reasons: humour fits the brand's voice, it signals a brand that makes content people enjoy, and the jokes often carry an indirect lesson, which makes them a little more top of funnel than plain product images. That adds format and concept diversity cheaply, since statics are fast to produce. How to apply: brief a small set of statics that make a joke your buyers would share, built on a real insight about the category (such as underdosed pre-workouts or caffeine crashes), with the product present but not the whole point. Judge them by spend share, cost per purchase and new-customer reach over a few weeks, rather than by click-through rate alone. Keep them only if the humour matches how your brand already speaks; forced jokes from a serious brand can feel off.
conditions: Brands with a playful or bold voice and an audience that shares memes, such as fitness, food, pets and youth fashion.
fails_when: The brand's positioning is clinical, premium or serious, or the jokes could be read as mocking the buyer's problem.

claim: Replace persona callouts with a hook in the buyer's own expert language; Blue Sense rewrote a booster hook to tell buyers to flip their bottle and check whether the tongkat ali shows a percentage.
body: The original hook spoke to anyone who had tried a testosterone booster before, which is just a persona callout. Blue Sense's rewrite asks the viewer to turn over their current booster and look at the tongkat ali line: if there is no percentage next to it, they are guessing. This works because it uses the exact words and habits of the target buyer. People who have bought natural boosters know tongkat ali is a core ingredient, many have read labels, and the hook gives them a concrete action and a reason to doubt what they own. Speaking their language makes the creator credible faster than claiming the product is good. How to apply: 1) Collect the specific terms your experienced buyers use: ingredient names, specs, standards, rituals. 2) Write hooks that make the viewer check or do something with what they already own or know. 3) Avoid opening with who the ad is for; open with something only that person would recognise. Source the language from reviews, Reddit threads and support tickets.
conditions: Categories with informed, solution-aware buyers who compare specs or ingredients (supplements, skincare actives, coffee, tech accessories).
fails_when: Buyers are new to the category and would not recognise the technical term, where plainer problem-led hooks work better; claims must also stay within supplement ad rules.

claim: Show the claim on screen, as in Gorilla Mind's best ad comparing an underdosed scoop with a full one, and cut or overlay any shot that runs as long as 12 seconds with no change.
body: The ad Blue Sense rated among Gorilla Mind's best opens by showing what an underdosed pre-workout scoop looks like next to a much bigger Gorilla Mode scoop. The persona (gym-goers who care about proper doses) and the angle (this one is properly dosed, and here is proof) are clear in seconds because the viewer sees the difference instead of being told. It also follows a structure: hook, demonstration, problem, offer, mechanism. Blue Sense's fixes: put the promise before the mechanism, move the offer later, and strengthen the mechanism, for example why most brands underdose. Contrast that with a creatine gummy ad that held interest only because the creator had a snake around his neck; without that pattern interrupt, it was a 12-second single shot of him standing still, and its story section simply repeated the hook in first person. How to apply: for each script, ask what the viewer can see that proves the main claim. In editing, look for any shot longer than a few seconds with no cut, overlay or change, and fix it; match the pace of content your buyer watches.
conditions: Short-form video ads on Meta and TikTok where the product benefit can be shown physically (dose, size, texture, before and after within platform rules).
fails_when: The benefit cannot be shown honestly on camera, or slow long-form formats like podcast cutdowns are the point, where longer shots are normal.

claim: Use earned authority inside proven ads rather than leaving it idle: Gorilla Mind used a Joe Rogan clip in only 3 ads and had zero paid usage of a 5 million follower creator.
body: Blue Sense found Gorilla Mind's strongest earned assets barely used in paid. The founder's Joe Rogan appearance shows up in only three ads; maybe it was already worn out, or the founder does not want the brand built on it, both fair. A middle path: drop the clip in at the proof point of a strong long-form script for the product discussed, so the authority supports the ad without becoming the brand's front end. Likewise Lean Beef Patty, a creator with about 5 million followers who has promoted the brand organically, has no paid use on Meta. Blue Sense says partnership ads are badly underused here. Running an ad through a creator's profile brings that profile's audience signal into delivery and can reach people the brand's own page does not, which helps when a scaling account runs into high frequency, likely here given how bottom-funnel the ads are. How to apply: list your podcast mentions, press and creator posts; get usage rights; test each one as a partnership ad or as proof inside a winning script.
conditions: Brands with real earned media or creator relationships and the rights to use that content in ads.

claim: When you change the hook to reach a new persona or awareness stage, rewrite the body to match; two Gorilla Mind ads had different hooks but nearly word-for-word the same product-dump body.
body: Blue Sense compared two testosterone booster ads from different creators. One opened with a line about your wife thanking you later, a persona aimed at men wanting to please a partner. The other opened by promising a booster that actually works, which speaks to someone who has already tried boosters and was let down. After the hook, both said almost the same thing: product name, all-natural ingredients backed by science, look at the reviews, buy now before it sells out. Blue Sense's point: a hook selects a person and a stage of awareness, so the rest of the script must answer that person's doubts. A man who tried boosters before needs to hear why those failed and why this one is different; vague words like all natural or backed by science make him trust it less. These ads are product aware and fine for retargeting, but they will not hold large spend, perhaps not $100,000, on cold traffic. How to apply: for each new hook, write down who it speaks to and what they already believe, then rewrite problem, mechanism and objection sections for that person.
conditions: Video ads scripted by creators or in-house, where hooks are varied to reach different personas.
fails_when: The hook change is only a small wording test on a proven ad aimed at the same person, where keeping the body is fine.
numbers: bottom-funnel product-dump ads unlikely to hold $100,000 in spend

claim: Size the in-house creative team for the quiet months and flex up with agencies or three-month contractors for the June EOFY and Black Friday peaks, booking the flexible part in marketing and the fixed team in opex.
body: Creative output needs to follow revenue through the year: flat in the first quarter, a June spike for end of financial year sales in Australia, a build through spring, then a big November and December. A fixed in-house team cannot match that curve; a team of four is overworked in the peaks and only right-sized in the quiet stretch. Blue Sense's approach: keep a steady in-house base for ongoing content, and send the extra volume to agencies or short-term hires taken on for about three months. Classify the in-house base as opex, a fixed cost you carry indefinitely, and the flexing agency and contractor spend as marketing, so MER rises and falls with the content that drives sales. Some brands put all content in marketing because all of it drives revenue; either is fine if you stay consistent. How to apply: map last year's revenue by month, set monthly content targets in proportion to it, and book the extra capacity two to three months before each peak.
conditions: Brands with clear seasonal peaks and an in-house creative function; the June EOFY peak applies to Australian brands.
fails_when: Demand is flat across the year, or creative is already fully outsourced.

claim: Campaign shoot imagery that earns ROAS at home is often propped up by years of brand awareness; in the US you are unknown, so lead with creative that builds trust from zero.
body: Being category leader at home counts for nothing on day one in the US: your reviews, recognition and reputation do not carry over. Blue Sense sees large, long-standing retailers make this mistake most. Their ad accounts lean on campaign shoots, which still show decent ROAS at home, so they look like good performance assets. They are not. A photo of a shoe on a model works because the brand has been a household name for decades. Launch the same asset in the US and it does almost nothing, which shows the brand was doing the work. How to apply: before a US launch, sort your best ads into those that explain or prove something (a problem, a demo, a creator testimonial, a clear offer) and those that only look good. Launch with the first group, and add trust builders such as reviews from US customers, creators and product demos. Treat polished brand imagery as support, not as your acquisition engine.
conditions: Established brands, especially legacy retailers, launching into a market where they are unknown.
fails_when: Brands already well known in the US through retail, press or social reach.

Go back through every winner from the last five years in your home market and translate the strongest into US accents and references before writing brand-new concepts.

claim: A tightly targeted creative (for example a call-out to owners of $10M businesses) saturates its cluster quickly, perhaps after $10,000 in spend, and then Meta either raises frequency or drifts to worse audiences.
body: The vector model also explains fatigue. A very specific ad leads Meta straight to a small cluster of matching people. Once they have all seen it, which for a narrow call-out might take only around $10,000 of spend, Meta has two options. It can keep serving the same people, so frequency climbs and response drops. Or it can push outward into neighbouring clusters that are further from your ideal customer, where the ad converts worse, so ROAS tapers. Meta prefers to stay near the centre, so frequency rising alongside falling ROAS is the usual sign. The cure is not a new background or a tweak; it is a new concept that leads Meta to a different cluster of buyers. How to apply: when a winner fades, check whether frequency on new audiences is rising; if so, brief ads that speak to a different persona, angle or offer rather than variations of the same ad.
conditions: Meta accounts running narrow persona-led creative at meaningful spend.
fails_when: Broad-appeal products where the creative already reaches a very large pool; fatigue there comes later and more slowly.
numbers: narrow call-out may saturate after about $10,000 in spend

claim: Andromeda groups near-identical ads under one entity ID: 200 similar ads may count as only 20 unique ads, each group serving the same people with no extra reach.
body: When an account loads many ads that look and sound alike, Andromeda reads them, decides they are the same, and groups them under one entity ID. Blue Sense's example: 200 ads in the account but only 20 entities, so in effect 20 ads. Ads inside one entity serve to the same pool of people and gain no unique reach. That defeats the purpose of volume, which is to reach new people or give existing prospects a genuinely different reason to buy; repeating near-copies to the same people does neither. The fix is to plan creative as concepts, where a concept is the intersection of angle, offer and persona. Format can count too: change the format enough (static versus founder video versus animation) and Meta will treat it as a different ad even with the same angle, offer and persona. Iterations within a concept are still useful, but net new audiences need new concepts. How to apply: before launch, tag each new ad with its angle, offer, persona and format and count how many truly distinct combinations you have.
conditions: Meta accounts loading high creative volume, especially AI-generated or templated variants.
fails_when: Small accounts launching only a few ads, where grouping matters less than finding one working concept.
numbers: example: 200 ads grouped into about 20 entity IDs

claim: A bottom-funnel ad that gets attributed sales may only be catching buyers who would have bought anyway; rewrite familiar-feeling ads with generic claims into retention or win-back ads for subscribers.
body: Two weak Lovevery ads show the pattern. One (screen-free fun for expecting parents) has no clear message about what the product is or why to buy. Another, a child happily unboxing a kit, has a lovely reaction but no problem, and a mechanism line any toy brand could say (designed to challenge growing skills). Blue Sense would not keep the first even with attributed sales, because those sales come from people already on their way to buy who clicked the nearest ad. For the unboxing ad, since its feel assumes the viewer already subscribes, the better move is to aim it at subscribers: a hook like about to cancel because the playroom is overflowing, watch this first, then problem, promise, mechanism and what is coming in the next kits. How to apply: list ads with low hook and hold rates but decent attributed ROAS; check if their sales skew to returning customers. Cut generic lines and replace them with a specific claim. Turn ads that only make sense to existing customers into retention or win-back ads targeted at current or lapsed subscriber audiences.
conditions: Subscription or repeat brands running mixed warm and cold delivery, with customer lists available for audiences.
fails_when: You have holdout or lift data showing the ad drives incremental sales; small customer lists too small to target.

claim: A slow, product-led first 8 to 9 seconds pushes an ad to warm buyers only; cutting straight to the first interesting line can turn the same footage into a cold prospecting ad.
body: Blue Sense reviewed a Lovevery how it is made ad (research with child development experts, 17 prototype versions, play testing, stress testing, a free return promise). The middle and end were strong, especially as quality and price reassurance for people already considering the brand. But the opening spent about nine seconds on a slow, product-heavy setup, which means only people who already care keep watching, so Meta delivers it mainly to warm audiences. Their fix costs nothing: trim the opening and start on the first line that creates interest (here, the hidden development happening in every child's brain). How to apply: review your long-running ads' hook rate (3-second views divided by impressions) and hold rate. For any ad where the first lines are a brand or product intro, make a cut that starts at the first surprising claim or problem, keep the rest, and launch it as a new ad beside the original. Use the original as middle-funnel reinforcement; give the trimmed one a chance at cold reach.

claim: Audit an ad library by sorting every ad into pillars and counting unique ideas once variants are removed; Lovevery's 86 ads held only 39 ideas in 7 pillars, which shows where to add volume.
body: Ad count flatters an account, because many ads are cuts of the same idea. Blue Sense pulled Lovevery's library and sorted it into seven pillars: newborns playing, beyond babies (4 to 6 year olds), the ladybug toy (an eye-catching item that became its own pillar), built for this stage (what the baby is developing now and why each item exists), gifting, expecting parents (only three statics and three videos), and worth it (price anchoring). Under 86 ads sat 39 unique ideas. The value is in seeing which pillars are thin and which carry the strongest ideas. Blue Sense's favourite was built for this stage, because it explains a unique mechanism, such as young babies seeing high-contrast shapes and red first, which suits performance ads. How to apply: export or screenshot all live ads, group variants, and tag each idea with a pillar, persona and awareness stage. Count ideas per pillar. Feed more new ideas into pillars with strong mechanism or results, and into thin pillars for valuable personas (such as expecting parents and gift buyers).

claim: Classify every ad by the awareness stage its hook speaks to, then check the spread to see which funnel stages you are over or under weighted on; Lovevery's 42 October ads had a good spread.
body: With broad targeting, the hook largely decides who an ad reaches: a hook that assumes product knowledge finds warm people, one that starts from a problem finds people earlier on. So the hooks across your account tell you how your creative covers cold, middle and bottom of funnel. Blue Sense tagged all 42 ads Lovevery launched in October and found unaware, problem aware, solution aware and product aware hooks, a spread they would recommend. How to apply: in a sheet, list each live ad and tag its hook as unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware or most aware. Count by stage and compare with your goal. If almost everything is product or most aware, you are mostly retargeting and will struggle to scale; brief problem and unaware hooks. If almost everything is cold, you may lack ads that close warm buyers. Redo this monthly for new launches, since teams drift toward the easiest stage to write.
conditions: Accounts using broad or Advantage+ targeting where creative decides who sees the ad.
fails_when: Accounts that still split audiences tightly by funnel stage and serve each stage its own ads by targeting.

claim: In a stage-based subscription, weight creative toward the earliest entry point because it has the most future orders; Lovevery aims 41 live ads at parents of 0 to 3 month olds versus 9 and 13 for later stages.
body: Lovevery sells quarterly play kits matched to a child's age, running up to age five, so a family that joins at birth can buy around 22 kits while a family joining at age three can buy far fewer. That makes the newborn buyer worth much more over time, and the ad mix reflects it: in the live library Blue Sense counted 41 ads to parents of 0 to 3 month olds, 9 to parents of 3 to 6 month olds and 13 to preschool parents. How to apply: for any subscription or replenishment product with a natural start point (a baby's birth, a new pet, a first skincare routine, a new home), estimate how many orders a customer joining at each stage can make. Allocate most of your new creative concepts to the stage with the longest runway, and judge those ads on expected lifetime gross profit, not first-order return. Still keep some volume on later entry points and on adjacent buyers such as expecting parents and gift givers, since the earliest stage can get crowded and expensive.
conditions: Subscription or repeat products whose number of possible orders depends on when in a life stage a customer joins.
fails_when: Churn is so high that early joiners do not actually stay longer; products with no natural life stage, where entry timing does not change lifetime orders.
