claim: Lovevery's best ad answers price with durability: a parent shows a cheap toy and a Lovevery toy after four kids, then a buy-it-once rule, cut with frequent scene changes.
body: Expensive subscription toys face an obvious objection: we will drown in costly toys. The strongest ad in the account handles it head on. A parent of four compares a broken cheap toy with a stained but fully working Lovevery toy, states a simple rule (buy it once), explains that most people pick short-term fixes, and notes that toys are not a line in their monthly budget because the kits bought six years ago served all four kids. The creator changes scenes often, which keeps a talking piece engaging and organic. Blue Sense's one improvement: many buyers will not have four children, so add reuse beyond siblings, such as passing kits to family or regifting, so the angle still lands for one-child families. How to apply: find your biggest price objection and script a side by side that shows long-term value (durability, cost per use, years of use). Use a real customer with history, a short rule they can repeat, and many scene changes. Add a variant for buyers whose situation does not match the main story.
conditions: Premium-priced products where durability or long life is true and can be shown.
fails_when: Products that wear out or are disposable; buyers with no experience of cheap alternatives failing.

claim: Opening a curiosity gap is fine, but leaving viewers unsure what an ad is about for 24 seconds loses most of them; give the why and the benefit early.
body: One Lovevery ad shows a creator introducing high-contrast cards in a sequence (black and white first, red elements at eight to ten weeks, colour at four months) without explaining why. Blue Sense likes that it is built on a unique mechanism, but notes that unless the viewer already knows about infant vision development, they are 24 seconds in and still lost. The ad also frames the benefit weakly (your baby loves to look at these) instead of saying what it does for the baby. How to apply: when an ad teases with a sequence or a reveal, add one line in the first five seconds or on-screen text that names what is going on and why it matters (for example, newborns can only see high contrast at close range, so these cards train focus). Then state the benefit, not only the behaviour. Look at the retention curve in Ads Manager video metrics: a steep drop between 3 and 15 seconds on a curiosity ad is the sign to add clarity sooner.
conditions: Educational or mechanism-led video ads, especially where the science is not common knowledge.
fails_when: Short, punchy curiosity hooks that resolve within a few seconds; categories where the benefit is obvious from the visual.

Keep the same core angles so you learn about format, not message. Choose formats that suit your brand look.

claim: A static made to look like an expert's tweet, run from that expert's own profile instead of as a branded partnership ad, can carry cold spend because it feels organic; IM8's version listed broad deficiency symptoms.
body: Blue Sense breaks down an IM8 multivitamin static with about 4,700 likes. Why it works: the format is a reposted tweet, which looks native to the feed. It runs only under the expert's name, not as a co-branded partnership post, so most viewers do not notice it is an ad until they reach the copy under the image. The image itself educates: a list of common complaints such as dry eyes, low energy, poor skin, cracked lips, bleeding gums, sore muscles and easy bruising, each linked to a vitamin shortfall. That symptom list is very broad, so the ad speaks to a huge market while still agitating a problem, then names the cause. The primary text then brings in the product and an offer, and the call to action button sends people to the site. It also borrows the expert's own audience. How to apply it: find an expert who already posts in your category, agree whitelisting (permission to run ads from their profile), design a tweet or post style image that teaches one wide problem to cause link, keep brand names off the image, and put the product and offer in the copy. Disclose the paid relationship as your market requires.
conditions: Categories with credible experts (health, supplements, skincare) and a problem that touches many people.
fails_when: No genuine expert relationship or no disclosure of the paid tie; health claims that breach advertising rules in your market.

claim: Ads fatigue for two reasons: they reach their lifetime spend or repeat other ads' visuals and audience, or the persona pool is too small; a narrow niche cannot hold $10,000 a day in a market the size of Australia.
body: First driver: the ad is stale. It has hit the end of its spend capacity, or it looks and speaks like other ads in the account, aimed at the same people with the same value proposition, so it wears out faster. Second driver: the audience is too small. Specific personas make better scripts, but they cap daily spend. Blue Sense's example: men training to run a marathon under four hours who want to cut minutes using creatine is a real group, but you will not spend $10,000 a day on it in Australia. In a B2B case, a call-out to Australian e-commerce finance chiefs at $100 million plus companies reaches maybe 1,000 to 2,000 people, so $10,000 a day would just show the same few people the ad hundreds of times; widening to e-commerce founders earning over $100,000 raises capacity. How to apply it: find each persona's spend ceiling, hold spend near it, and keep rotating new ads into it, since niche pools churn as people enter and leave (runners finish their race). Start with specific personas because they force better ads, then broaden as you scale. Broad call-outs need stronger creative to resonate with more people, and great unaware ads are hard, so Blue Sense suggests most brands under about $50 million should not lead with them.
conditions: Meta accounts running persona-specific concepts, especially in smaller markets like Australia.
fails_when: Very large markets where even a niche persona holds big spend; fatigue caused by an offer or landing page change rather than the ad.

B2B example: 1,000 to 2,000 people in the pool

claim: Advertorial statics, such as a ranked list of the best hair growth products and ones to avoid, convert cold traffic only when they lead to an education-led page or carry long teaching copy.
body: Blue Sense walks through a hair loss funnel. The static looks like an article headline promising the best products of the year and what big brands do not say, and it runs from a dermatologist's page for authority with short copy that does not sell. The click lands on a review style site owned by the brand: it introduces the doctor, ranks products, and explains each pick. Only the brand's own product links through, to a custom landing page and then a quiz that leads to purchase. Lower down, rival products get mostly negatives, and their links go to Amazon affiliate pages so even non-buyers earn something. Blue Sense calls it a very effective funnel. How to apply the useful part: pair an educational static with a landing page that teaches before it sells (comparison guide, buyer's guide, expert article), then hand off to a product page or quiz. If you cannot build that page, put the education in long primary text instead. Caution: a brand-owned site posing as an independent review can breach consumer law and Meta's rules in many markets; disclose ownership clearly and keep comparisons factual.
conditions: Considered purchases where buyers compare options (hair, skin, health, tech), with budget to build an education-led page.
fails_when: The page hides that the brand owns it or makes unfair claims about rivals, which risks regulator action and ad account bans; impulse products that need no comparison.

claim: At $30,000 to $100,000 a month on Meta, run 2 to 3 UGC creators, 5 to 6 concepts and 30 to 100 new ads; above $100,000, a full creative team, 8 to 10 concepts and 100+ new assets.
body: Blue Sense's closing summary sets a target for each tier. Under $30,000 a month: do the basics well, keep most spend on testing, and use Instagram trial reels to check ideas before they reach the account. From $30,000 to $100,000 a month: work with 2 to 3 UGC creators, put about 25% of spend into production, run 5 to 6 concepts so you are not dependent on one, use an ABO testing campaign plus likely a scaling campaign, launch 30 to 100 new ads a month (or use the revenue based volume method), and add partnership ads. Above $100,000 a month: build a full creative team (someone scripting, an editor, 4 to 6 creators and a designer; part-time is fine) so a production system runs every week instead of a scramble. Spend at least 10% of media on creative, keep 8 to 10 active concepts, launch at least 100 new assets a month by the one ad per $1,000 rule, and keep a financial model tracking cost per asset by source and profit contribution per ad, so you know which content sources earn their cost. For most brands, creative is the constraint on Meta growth.
conditions: DTC brands on Meta at the stated monthly spend, in Australian dollars.
fails_when: Brands whose main limit is offer, margin or stock rather than creative; tiers are guides, not exact cut-offs.

claim: Because roughly 80% of viewers leave during the hook, put video effort into openings: for the same hour, two solid bodies with 15 hooks usually beat two hooks with five bodies.
body: A video hook is a promise that what follows is about the viewer's own situation. Since most people drop off in the opening seconds, the opening decides whether the rest of the ad gets a chance at all. Blue Sense's rule for splitting production time is that, once the body script is good, a better opening moves results more than another body does. So in one hour of shooting, record two bodies and 15 different openings rather than two openings and five bodies, then pair each opening with each body in the edit to get many ads from one session. A hook has three layers you can change on their own: what is on screen, the audio, and the text overlay (the primary text above the ad also counts). How to apply it: in every brief, ask the creator to record several first lines and first shots; it adds minutes, not hours. Judge openings by hook rate (share of plays passing 3 seconds) against your account average. Two warnings. If the body scripts are weak, one body may win on its own and you will wrongly credit the hook, so fix scripting first. And do not chase hook rate with memes or bait: grabbing the wrong people raises views without raising purchases.
conditions: Video ads on Meta, Reels or TikTok where the body scripts already meet your quality bar.
fails_when: Body scripts are weak or untested, so the body limits results; static images, where the whole ad is effectively the hook.

claim: Blue Sense's worked concept: a 30 to 35 year old casual runner chasing a sub-4-hour marathon, sold creatine for long-run recovery promising about 5 minutes faster, with buy 2 get 1 free set by his $70k income.
body: An example of building one full concept and then multiplying it. Persona: a male casual runner aged 30 to 35, training for a sub-4-hour marathon, who follows particular running and science influencers and earns about $70,000 a year, which matters for framing value. Angle: science-backed, nodding to the kind of expert he follows (the presenter mentions Andrew Huberman), arguing that creatine improves recovery specifically for the long run, the session only marathon trainees do, linked to an expected outcome of about a 5-minute faster marathon. Every part of the angle ties back to the persona and a concrete result. Offer: creatine gummies on buy 2, get 1 free, chosen because gummies are expensive and this buyer's income means perceived value must be high. Formats to vary: UGC, founder talking head, a polished educational piece, a carousel; a video sales letter is parked because the age group is too young for that format. Then change one variable to make new concepts: the same angle for women training for a marathon, or a tweaked angle for new runners working up to their first 5k. How to apply: write your own concept sheet in this shape (persona with income and influences, outcome-linked angle, offer matched to value perception, list of formats) and spin variations from it.

fails_when: Claims you cannot support with evidence; health claims restricted by platform policy.

claim: Build 30 to 40 strong personas by hand before using an LLM; give it wide business context, ask for 20 more, keep the best 4 or 5, feed those back and repeat, or it will give you average ideas.
body: Language models produce the average of what they have seen. Give one three or four personas and your website, ask for more, and you get the same generic list every competitor gets, so your creative reverts to the market mean. Blue Sense's process: first do the manual work. Spend real time on who your avatars are, what problems you solve for each, and how their pain points, language and required proof differ. Aim for about 30 to 40 genuinely good personas. Then give Claude, ChatGPT or Gemini that whole list plus as much context as possible about the business and its buyers, and ask for another 20 to 30. Review them, cut to the best 4 or 5, give those back marked as good, and ask for another 10 to 20 in that direction. Repeat until you have roughly doubled your list. Specific personas are the point: broad ones such as 'women aged 25 to 45' are what weak AI output looks like. How to apply: keep the persona list in a shared sheet with problem, language and proof columns, so each AI round and each brief draws from it.
conditions: Brands using AI tools for creative ideation.
fails_when: Brands with no customer research to start from; the model cannot invent real insight from nothing.

claim: Build angles from six parts: problem agitation, a contrarian truth, domain-specific authority, a curiosity gap, comparison with what they tried before, and a before-and-after transformation, which works best but risks policy flags.
body: An angle is the specific argument you make to a persona; Blue Sense says most creative fails here because brands default to listing product features. Parts to choose from when writing a script. 1) Problem agitation: lead with the pain and make the viewer feel heard before showing the solution (not possible if they are not yet aware of the problem). 2) A contrarian truth that reframes a belief, such as 'everything you have been told about protein is wrong', leading into education. 3) Social proof and authority from the same domain: a marathon runner for a running product, not a doctor in a lab coat in every ad. 4) A curiosity gap: open a question early (what the top 1% know about saving money) and only answer it near the end, so viewers stay through the story. 5) Comparison and objection handling: 'I tried this and this, they did not work, then I tried this', common in UGC. 6) Transformation, a before and after: Blue Sense calls it the best performing and least compliant element, because Meta restricts it, so it must be shown carefully. How to apply: for each persona, pick the elements that fit, write the full script around them, and tie social proof to that persona's age, gender and situation.
conditions: Video and static ad scripts for problem-solution products.
fails_when: Categories where before and after or health claims breach platform or legal rules; check policies first.
numbers: six angle elements

claim: Compare production cost per ad with contribution margin per ad by format: if an average ad yields about $350 of margin but costs $400 to make, production is losing money.
body: Blue Sense calculates this in every audit. Step one: average revenue per ad, which is total revenue attributed to new ads divided by the number launched; Blue Sense says it is around $2,000 for most accounts. Step two: turn it into contribution margin per ad by subtracting cost of goods and the ad spend that ad used. Step three: compare with what each ad cost to produce. If margin per ad is $350 and an ad costs $400, every new ad loses money no matter how good the media buying is. Step four: split it by format and source. In their illustration images cost about $50 and return about $300 of margin while videos cost $500 and return $400, so even though videos perform better per ad, images earn far more per production dollar and deserve more of the budget. How to apply it: tag every ad by format and source (UGC creator, agency, in-house designer, AI), pull spend and 7 day click revenue per ad from Ads Manager, apply your gross margin, and set the result against invoices per asset. Rebalance toward the sources with the best margin per production dollar, and review quarterly as costs and hit rates change.
conditions: Accounts launching enough ads per month to give stable averages by format, with known gross margin and production costs.
fails_when: Too few ads launched to average (a handful a month); attribution so unreliable that revenue per ad is meaningless; formats with long lifespans judged too early.

claim: Define a concept as persona, angle and offer (plus format), and make personas specific problem archetypes, such as a consultant flying twice a week needing carry-on clothes for boardrooms and bars, not 'busy professionals'.
body: Blue Sense's concept architecture drives ideation, ad set structure and naming. A concept is a persona, an angle and an offer; change any one and the ad reaches different people. A new offer is a different value proposition or packaging. A new angle agitates a different problem: skincare about wrinkles versus acne. A new persona is both who you are talking to and who appears in the ad: a 60-year-old woman on screen reaches different people than a 20-year-old. Personas are not demographics; they are archetypes defined by problems, desires and buying triggers. Broad personas such as 'women aged 25 to 45' or 'busy professional' produce forgettable ads. Specific ones make the brief almost write itself: a consultant who flies twice a week and needs a carry-on wardrobe for boardrooms and bars; a mum who has tried six supplements because her toddler will not eat vegetables; women aged 30 to 35 with hormonal acne versus women aged 20 to 25 with acne. You are better off making five ads for a specific persona than five for a broad one; broad, unaware ads that work for everyone are hard to make well and are mainly for mid eight-figure brands. How to apply: for each persona, write the problem, the language they use and the proof they need, then brief angles to it.
conditions: Any brand producing paid social creative; works in fashion as well as problem-solution products.
fails_when: Very large brands with skilled teams deliberately making broad mass-market ads.

claim: Do not switch off low-ROAS ads inside an ad set that is hitting KPI; Meta optimises on multi-touch sequences, but reports last click, so the opener can show 1.4x while the closer shows 6x.
body: Meta works out which sequence of creatives leads people to buy: ad 1 then 2 then 3, or 3 then 2 then 1, or another order. Its delivery is optimised on views and clicks across that sequence. But reporting credits the last click. So if the journey is usually 1, 2, 3 and people click and buy on ad 3, ad 3 shows perhaps 6x, ad 2 about 2x and ad 1 about 1.4x. With equal spend, the obvious move is to switch off 1 and 2, which breaks the sequence and hurts the whole ad set. Meta knows ads 1 and 2 played a part, which is why it keeps spending on them, but Ads Manager gives no view of this. Someone strong in creative strategy can often see the roles: an unaware, top of funnel opener, a product-aware middle ad and a most-aware closing ad. How to apply: judge ads in groups at the ad set level. If the ad set hits its target, leave its ads alone even if some look weak; only intervene when the ad set as a whole misses. When reviewing, label each ad's awareness stage so you can see whether it likely opens or closes the journey.
conditions: Meta ad sets with several ads under one concept that are meeting their KPI.
fails_when: Ad sets missing KPI, where weak ads should be replaced; ads that are clearly broken (wrong link, policy issue).

claim: For premium products where price is the main objection, open the ad by admitting it, for example stating that it costs $120, is pricey, and is still the best seller.
body: Blue Sense calls this a truth bomb hook and says it has worked very well for one specific client. The idea: when most cold viewers would balk at the price anyway, saying the price first, plainly and with some honesty, becomes the reason to keep watching. A stranger who has never seen the product hears that something is expensive yet sells best and wants to know why. The ad can then move into an educational body that justifies the price: what goes into it, how long it lasts, what it replaces, and what buyers say. How to apply it: use it only where your post-purchase surveys, reviews or abandoned cart feedback show price as the top objection and your average order value is high. Write the opening around the real price and your real ranking (best seller, most reordered). Follow with proof of value, and consider a cost per use frame in the body. Test it next to your usual problem-led opening on the same body so the hook is the only change. It also works on ingredients or industry truths, such as admitting what most products in the category leave out.
conditions: Higher priced or premium products where price is the main reason people do not buy, and the product really is a best seller.

claim: Hook swaps still work after Andromeda: each new hook gets its own creative ID, and Blue Sense has revived fatigued ads that spent $50,000 to $100,000 with 50 new hooks for another $100,000 at similar efficiency.
body: A common worry is that changing only the first 3 seconds of a 90 second ad cannot count as diversity under Meta's Andromeda retrieval system. Blue Sense's answer: Meta treats a new hook as a separate creative with its own ID, so it is not merged with the original and can reach new people. There is overlap, since the rest of the ad speaks to the same person with the same problem and offer, and in their concept framework it is still the same concept. It is still worth doing because it is almost free. How to apply it: when filming, record each opening several times (around six) in a few extra minutes. When a hero ad fatigues, shoot a batch of fresh openings in about an hour and attach them to the proven body; Blue Sense has had ads that had spent $50,000 to $100,000 run another $100,000 this way at the same efficiency. Also rescue ads that never got going: if an ad's hook rate is far below your average, a new hook can make the body work. Keep concept diversity as the main growth lever and use hook swaps to extend winners and fix weak openings, not as a substitute for new concepts.
conditions: Video ads with a proven body on Meta, where the account also keeps adding new concepts.
fails_when: The body or offer has worn out, not the opening; accounts that rely only on hook swaps and never add new concepts.

claim: If your buyers are 50 and over and you can serve Facebook feeds, static images with long story-led copy can perform very strongly on cold audiences, provided the copywriting is skilled.
body: For older audiences on Facebook feeds, Blue Sense says a simple image with a long story in the primary text works very well. The story starts with a reader who does not know they have a problem and walks them, paragraph by paragraph, to understanding the problem, then the type of solution, then the product, and finally to buying. Because the copy does the teaching, the image can be plain. The catch is skill: AI can help draft, but if the writer does not understand how to appeal emotionally to that specific group, the ad will not work. How to apply it: check your age breakdown in Ads Manager; if a large share of buyers are over 50, brief a long copy static. Open with a relatable scene or curiosity, name the hidden problem, explain why common fixes fail, introduce your mechanism, then the product, proof and offer. Keep paragraphs short. Test it against your best video on the same concept. Blue Sense recommends classic copywriting books (Schwartz, Hopkins, Ogilvy, Cialdini) as the way to build this skill.
conditions: Brands with a meaningful 50 plus buyer base and placements on Facebook feeds.
fails_when: Younger audiences mostly on Instagram Reels or Stories, where long text is rarely read; teams without a strong copywriter.

claim: In a cold video ad, introduce the product as late as possible, once viewers are problem and solution aware; an early reveal keeps more viewers but usually produces fewer total purchases.
body: Blue Sense names two bridges in every video: hook to body, and body to call to action. A common failure is a good hook followed straight away by the product name, such as asking about marathon recovery and then pitching a brand's creatine in the next sentence. The viewer jumps from learning to being sold and leaves, even when hook, body and call to action are each well written. Instead, raise awareness gently. A strong cold ad moves people through the stages in order: unaware (a curiosity hook), problem aware (why plain water may be missing electrolytes), solution aware (the right ratio of salts), product aware (a canned mineral water that solves it), then ready to buy, perhaps later on a retargeting ad. Video sales letters do this well because they have time to teach. Many teams reveal the product early because the retention curve shows most viewers gone by around 90 seconds. Blue Sense says that is the wrong lens: the people who stay to a late reveal are far more qualified, so conversion rate rises enough that total purchases are higher. How to check: if hold rate falls sharply where the product first appears, the bridge is too abrupt; re-edit that section before scrapping the ad.
conditions: Top of funnel video ads for products that need some explanation, aimed at unaware or problem aware viewers.
fails_when: Retargeting or product aware audiences who already know the problem and the brand; very simple impulse products.
numbers: retention curves often show about 80% gone by around 90 seconds

claim: Large retailers built on campaign shoots often run about 90% desire-led and 10% pain-led ads; shift performance creative toward 60% pain-led, and the best brands sit near 70%.
body: Blue Sense audits many nine figure Australian retailers and sees the same imbalance. Their creative comes from traditional campaign shoots with models and polished imagery, which build desire for the product but never speak to a problem the buyer has. The result is an ad account weighted heavily toward desire. Blue Sense's view is that the strongest performance marketing ads sit on pain points. How to apply it: tag every live ad as desire-led (aspiration, look, lifestyle) or pain-led (a problem, frustration or need the product solves). Work out the share of ads and of spend on each side. If pain-led content is around 10%, brief problem-led concepts: fit or comfort issues, durability, what the product fixes, the moment of frustration before buying. Target roughly 60% pain-led first, moving toward 70% over time. Think of the pain-led share as performance assets and the desire-led share as brand assets: keep some brand work, but do not let campaign shoot output fill the performance account. Keep running both through the same tests so the data shows which wins for each product.
conditions: Retail and fashion brands whose creative pipeline is mainly brand photo shoots.
fails_when: Pure luxury or fashion led brands where desire is the main buying reason and pain points are thin; categories where problem framing would breach claim rules.

best brands: about 70/30

claim: Match the hook type to awareness: problem agitation only reaches people already aware of the problem and stops scaling, a contrarian truth works at every awareness level, and wordless texture openings currently win in fashion.
body: Blue Sense lists nine opening types most brands can use seven of right away. Problem agitation names a pain the viewer already feels (back pain from desk work); strong results, but only among problem aware people, so it caps out. Contrarian truth challenges a common belief (what you were told about protein timing is wrong) and works across awareness levels on paid and organic. Specific proof leads with a measured result and time frame, like a weight loss over 90 days without giving up a favourite food. Curiosity gap opens a question only the video answers; the presenter's own organic videos using this average over 45 seconds of view time. Price truth admits an uncomfortable fact about price or ingredients (see the separate card). Confrontation sounds like a friend calling you out, such as the drawer of products you never use. Sensory or texture openers run 2 to 3 seconds with no words: fabric handled, a product squeezed, liquid poured, a pack opened; Blue Sense has many fashion ads winning with these now. Founder letter tells the origin story with real stakes, like remortgaging a house to fund a $300,000 first order; it must be true. Social proof leads with a result share, like 90% of customers seeing results in 30 days. Build a hook bank with each type for every concept.
conditions: Brands with a real story, real results data or a tactile product for the matching hook types.
fails_when: The claim behind the hook is not true or provable (founder stakes, result percentages), or the category bans the claim, such as health outcomes.

claim: Meta learns which formats each person responds to, so an account of only lo-fi UGC and DPAs never reaches people who ignore those formats; mix formats so every concept can reach more of the market.
body: Andromeda prioritises formats that a given person engages with. The presenter says he could scroll Instagram for hours and never see a lo-fi UGC ad, because he never clicks on them, so Meta has learned not to show them to him. He says the same about DPAs: he has almost never been served one. If an account runs only UGC and DPAs, people like him are effectively unreachable, however good the personas, angles and offers. That is why Blue Sense treats format as a fourth part of concept design alongside persona, angle and offer, a part it says did not matter much before Andromeda. It also means bundling different concepts in one ad set with one format compounds the problem, and leaves you unable to tell what worked. How to apply: for each winning concept, make versions across several formats (for example UGC, founder talking head, high-production educational video, static, carousel, and video sales letters for older buyers), launch them under that concept's ad set, and check delivery and results by format to see which formats open new reach.
conditions: Meta accounts with broad targeting and a narrow format mix.
fails_when: Very small accounts that cannot fund several formats; categories where one format clearly dominates.

claim: More ads is not a strategy: Blue Sense has seen accounts launching 2,000+ new ads a month while barely reaching $250k monthly spend and staying unprofitable, because they misdiagnosed the bottleneck.
body: Blue Sense describes two recent accounts each launching over 2,000 new ads a month on budgets barely reaching a quarter of a million dollars, and neither was profitable. Anyone running large accounts knows that volume is absurd for that spend. If the ads had good offers, personas and angles behind them, the account would not need anywhere near that number. The first mistake was confusing activity with strategy; the second was misdiagnosing the bottleneck. Creative has many possible bottlenecks: the quality of the work, the variety of formats, not enough assets at certain awareness stages (often too few top of funnel ads to scale), not using partnership ads or other ways to unlock spend. Volume only helps if volume is the real constraint. A founder asking whether launching 40 more ads a month will double the business is asking the wrong question. How to apply: before raising output, review what share of new ads ever get meaningful spend, which concepts hold spend, and which funnel stages and formats are missing. Fix the gap you find (quality, format, stage, offer) and raise volume only once the concept strategy behind it is clear.
conditions: Accounts with high creative output but flat spend or poor profit.
fails_when: Accounts that genuinely lack volume, for example launching only a handful of ads a month at six-figure spend.

under about $250k monthly spend

claim: Most Meta ads hold little spend: Blue Sense puts mean lifetime spend per ad at about $700 to $1,500 depending on the account, so you need a steady stream of new ads, with strategy, to keep spend up.
body: Because each ad's audience is chosen from its content and repeated impressions of the same ad lose power, most ads can only absorb a limited amount of money before they stop delivering efficiently. Blue Sense's figure: the average spend per ad across an account typically sits around $700 to $1,500, depending on the account. A few winners hold far more, but they are the exception. So to hold or grow total spend you need enough new ads entering the account each month to replace the spend that fading ads give up. Volume alone is not the answer, though: Blue Sense stresses that many teams pump in volume with no strategy behind it and it does not work. How to apply: divide your target monthly spend by your account's own average spend per ad to estimate how many new ads you need each month, then plan those ads across distinct concepts (persona, angle, offer and format) so they reach new people. Check your number in Ads Manager by exporting ads with lifetime spend and taking the average.
conditions: Meta accounts with broad targeting and a mix of winners and ordinary ads.
fails_when: Accounts dominated by a few evergreen ads that genuinely hold large spend for long periods, though Blue Sense warns this is risky.
numbers: mean spend per ad about $700 to $1,500

claim: Moving $10,000 of a $350,000 monthly Meta budget into production could buy about 40 assets and double live ads; a 5% efficiency gain on that spend is worth $17,500 a month, more than the money moved.
body: This was Blue Sense's proposal to the brand in the 15 live ads case. Take $10,000 a month out of media and give it to a creative agency for about 40 assets, a mix of new ads, hook swaps and statics. That would roughly double the number of active ads, which Blue Sense expected to improve efficiency by at least 5%. A 5% gain on $350,000 is $17,500 a month. Two ways to take it: cut spend by the $17,500 equivalent and keep results flat, which after the $10,000 already moved leaves about $7,500 a month saved; or keep spend where it was and, at the brand's then return of about 3x, earn roughly $40,000 to $50,000 more revenue a month. Either way, revenue rises with the same total outlay. How to apply it: count your active ads against spend, estimate a conservative efficiency gain from more ads (start with 5%), and compare its value with the production cost. Present it to the founder as moving money between two revenue drivers, much like shifting budget between channels, rather than adding a cost.
conditions: Large accounts where too few active ads, not offer or tracking, are holding efficiency back.
fails_when: Accounts that already have plenty of fresh ads, where more volume adds little; the 5% gain is an estimate, not a measured result.

claim: No one can reliably pick which good ad will win, so define what a 7 out of 10 ad looks like and launch as many ads as possible above that bar; volume outranks concept, hook, editing, talent and storytelling.
body: Blue Sense ranks creative drivers in this order: volume, then concept quality, hook strength, editing quality, creator talent, and storytelling last. The reason is that hit rates are limited and nobody predicts winners well. Show five objectively good ads to ten top creative strategists and ask which spent the most, and the answers are guesses with reasons attached afterwards. Teams lose when they try to win that guessing game. Instead, get good at knowing the minimum standard, make sure every ad clears it, and then push volume. The failure mode is junk volume: Blue Sense has seen accounts launching thousands of ads a month on about a quarter of a million dollars of monthly spend while losing money, because the ads had no clear concept, no real hook and formats that did not match the awareness stage. How to apply it: write a one page quality bar (defined persona, angle and offer; hook passing the five trait check; format suited to the stage; clean edit and captions). Review each ad against it before launch. If it passes, launch it without debating which will win; if it fails, fix it or drop it.
conditions: Teams producing many ads a month for Meta or TikTok.
fails_when: Teams with no shared standard, where more volume just adds junk; very small budgets where each extra ad gets too little spend to learn.

claim: Pick the ad format last, after persona, angle and offer, by asking: does the concept need education, can the value fit one frame, does the product need a demo, and what awareness stage is it for?
body: Blue Sense starts with the concept and only then chooses format, never the other way round. Five questions guide it. What is the concept: settle persona, angle and offer first. Does it need education: if yes, you likely need a longer video or a long copy static that can teach. Can the value be shown in a single frame: if yes, lean to images or carousels, which are cheap and fast, so make statics whenever the idea allows. Does the product need a demo: some products only make sense in motion, which limits plain images unless a skilled designer can show it. Which awareness stage: unaware or problem aware buyers usually need longer formats; product aware buyers can be served with catalogue ads and simple images. Two ways to use statics: as a fast, cheap test of new angles and concepts, then rebuild the winners as videos that can go deeper and scale further; or as a main format in their own right because production cost per ad is so low. Blue Sense rejects the idea that images are only for the bottom of the funnel and says it knows brands doing hundreds of thousands of dollars a day in revenue mainly on statics. Age matters too: a video sales letter may suit older buyers better than buyers in their early 30s.
conditions: Planning a creative batch for Meta or other paid social with concepts already defined.
fails_when: Products that cannot be understood without seeing them in use, where video is required regardless of cost.

claim: Plan about one new ad per $1,000 of monthly Meta spend, or better, divide your new customer revenue target by expected revenue per ad: $300,000 at $3,000 per ad means 100 new ads a month.
body: The quick rule: one new ad for every $1,000 of monthly spend, so $30,000 a month means about 30 new ads and $50,000 about 50. It was set in Australian dollars but is close enough in US dollars. The better method works backwards from targets. Step one: average spend per ad. If you launched 500 ads last year and spent $500,000, each ad averaged $1,000. Step two: expected revenue per ad, using 7 day click ROAS or acquisition MER (new customer revenue divided by ad spend). At a 3 ROAS, each ad is worth about $3,000. Step three: divide the monthly new customer revenue target by that figure; $300,000 divided by $3,000 is 100 new ads. Step four: flex creative volume month by month with the revenue forecast, so peak months get more ads. Two limits of the simple model: ads take time to spend, so an ad worth $3,000 may take four months to earn it and you need more volume up front; and winners and losers differ hugely, so forecast them separately using your hit rate. Blue Sense offers a free model for this.
conditions: Accounts with a year or so of ad history to compute average spend and return per ad, and a monthly new customer revenue target.
fails_when: New accounts with no history; accounts whose spend per ad is dominated by one or two outliers, which skews the average.

example: $300,000 target / $3,000 = 100 ads a month

claim: Pre-test draft ads as Instagram trial reels with the call to action cut off: compare reach and retention graphs, then put only the best 5 of about 20 hook variations into Ads Manager.
body: Blue Sense does this with all its own ads as of April 2026 and notes it may change as the platform changes. Trial reels are shown to non-followers, so they give a quick read on fresh viewers. How to apply it: take a version one of the ad, cut the closing call to action so it reads as content, and post it as a trial reel from the business or personal page the ad will run from. Two outputs matter. Reach: how far did it travel compared with your other trial reels? Retention graph: where did viewers leave? A drop in the first seconds points to the hook, a drop where the product appears points to the bridge, and a slow fade points to the body. You can do this before the edit is final; post the first cut while round two is being edited, and pass notes to the editor within 24 hours. It is especially useful for hooks: post about 20 openings, see which hold viewers, and launch only the best five or so, instead of spending ad money to learn the same thing. Founders at small spend can use daily organic posting the same way, watching retention, shares and saves.
conditions: Brands making short video ads that also have an Instagram presence; works best for hook and structure checks.
fails_when: Organic reach is not a perfect proxy for paid conversion, so treat it as a filter, not a verdict; formats that need the offer or call to action to work.

claim: Proven hook formulas can carry a brand to eight figures, but an ad that holds about $500,000 in spend usually needs a novel opening that sits beside proven demand, not in an untested market.
body: Blue Sense frames positioning with blue and red oceans. A red ocean is selling the same as everyone and being priced down; a true blue ocean is something never sold before, which is risky because there is no proven demand and a lot of education is needed. The target is in between: something adjacent to what already sells, presented in a way no competitor is doing. In hooks this means novelty without gimmicks. How to apply it: keep running proven hook types for steady volume, and reserve part of each shoot for openings borrowed from other industries, other creators or new formats that nobody in your category uses yet. Check each one by asking whether the market has seen it a million times. When one of these breaks out, expect competitors to copy it within weeks, so plan the next novel opening before the first fades. The scripting still matters most; novelty sits on top of a good script, it does not replace one. Blue Sense points to its own long YouTube masterclass as an example of using a format few others offer in its space.
conditions: Brands already running solid hook formulas and wanting a few ads that can hold very large spend.
fails_when: Accounts still lacking basic hook and script quality, where novelty experiments distract from fundamentals; categories with strict claim rules that limit unusual openings.

claim: Purchase chance falls sharply after someone sees the identical ad twice, so cold ads should rarely show ad-level frequency above 2; above that, you lack creative volume and variety.
body: Blue Sense cites an older Meta article (it describes it as four or five years old) showing that after two impressions of an identical creative the likelihood of purchase drops steeply, while showing a different ad as the third and fourth impression keeps the likelihood high. The first and second views can both work, the second sometimes better because the person is warmer, but after that the same ad adds little. People generally need to see several ads before buying, so the answer is new ads, not more repeats. Blue Sense uses this as an account health check: on cold campaigns, look at frequency at the ad level for the last 30 to 60 days. In accounts it runs, a cold ad above 2 basically does not happen; if it does, it is treated as a red flag for creative fatigue and a sign the account needs more diversity and more volume. How to apply: in Ads Manager, filter to prospecting campaigns, go to the ad level, add the Frequency column, set 30 or 60 days, and sort. Any cold ad above 2 should trigger new concepts for that ad set, not a budget increase.

fails_when: Retargeting and existing customer ads, which run higher frequencies by design; very small audiences.

claim: Put about 25% of Meta media budget into creative production at $30,000 to $100,000 a month, falling to about 10% above $100,000; below $30,000, founder-made videos and statics are enough.
body: Blue Sense ties production spend to media spend. From about $4,000 to $30,000 a month, content should be founder-led and the production budget is the founder's time, not cash; statics and simple founder videos can carry most businesses to $30,000 a month. Blue Sense also urges founders at this size to make content themselves, since creative is the biggest lever and knowing what good looks like lets them hire and train for it later. At this level most of the budget, about 60 to 80%, goes to testing because there is not enough spend to scale winners. From $30,000 to $100,000 a month, allocate about 25% of media budget to production, so $25,000 at $100,000. That feels uncomfortably high, and Blue Sense says most brands spend far less, which is a key reason they stall. Above $100,000 a month the share falls to about 10% of media budget. At a 25% marketing cost ratio (ad spend at 25% of revenue), that is about 2.5% of total revenue. That level funds UGC, partnership ads, a full-time offshore or part-time in-house static designer and perhaps a low cost agency for formats like video sales letters.

fails_when: Brands whose ads are cheap to make in-house at high volume (for example AI statics), where a smaller share can deliver the same asset count; brands whose limit is the offer or product, not creative.

claim: Score each hook on five traits: clear to a stranger within 3 seconds, relevant to a real problem, novel, specific with numbers or names, and visually credible; two or three done well is enough.
body: Blue Sense grades openings with a simple checklist. Clarity: would someone who has never heard of you understand the topic in the first 3 seconds, or are you confusing them on purpose? Relevance: this is not the same as calling out the persona. Openers like 'if you are a mum aged 30 to 35 with this problem, listen up' are overrated because people do not want to hear themselves labelled; they respond to the problem they are living with. Agitating the problem beats a persona call-out almost every time. Novelty: ask whether this opening has been done a million times; if it has, change it. It is optional but creates white space. Specificity: a number (a share of customers who got a result), a famous name that genuinely relates to the product, or a concrete outcome builds authority fast. Credibility: usually carried by the visual, not the words, such as a doctor appearing for a supplement or a runner for a running product. How to use it: score every scripted hook from 1 to 10 on each trait before shooting, cut those that score well on none, and push the best ones to score high on at least two. You do not need full marks everywhere.
conditions: Scripting or reviewing hooks for paid social video and organic content.
fails_when: Very bottom funnel retargeting ads to people who already know the brand, where a plain offer can outperform any crafted opening.

claim: Similar creatives get bundled by Andromeda and shown to the same people, raising frequency, cutting reach and lowering ROAS; ask your Meta rep for your creative similarity score, where higher is worse.
body: Meta has begun producing a creative similarity score. Most accounts cannot see it yet in Ads Manager, but Blue Sense says a dedicated Meta rep can provide it; the higher the score, the more alike your creatives are, which is bad. The reason it matters: Andromeda groups similar creatives and serves them to the same pool of people. Similar means more than identical. It includes ads from the same shoot with the model in a slightly different pose, UGC with a small script change halfway, or even quite different formats that all speak to the same audience. When grouped ads keep hitting the same people, frequency climbs, reach stops growing into new users, and over time ROAS declines, which looks like diminishing returns from spend. The better position is three creatives that each talk to different people, so each finds its own audience with little overlap; frequency falls and each can scale into colder audiences. How to apply: ask your rep for the score; audit your recent launches by persona and angle rather than by format; and if most new ads share one persona and angle, change the brief to vary persona, angle or offer, not just the edit.

fails_when: Score access depends on Meta and may change; very small accounts may not get it.

claim: Split creative effort about 50 to 60% on replicating winners, 20 to 30% on iterating near-misses and 20 to 30% on net new concepts; never drop new concepts to zero, but most teams over-weight them.
body: Blue Sense ranks three content types by leverage. Replicating winners: taking ads, concepts and organic posts that already worked and redoing them with new hooks, new formats or simply reposting, which reaches new people each time. This is the highest impact work on paid and organic. Iterating: fixing underperformers through hook or format changes, and tangential ideas such as moving a working concept to a new persona or a new offer. Net new: completely new formats, angles and concepts. You must keep some net new work, because everything at the top will fatigue and you need a pipeline of future winners; zero is a terrible idea. But most teams spend too much here. The presenter admits his own organic output is 80 to 90% net new, while the 10 to 20% he repeats wins about 80% of views. Recommended starting mix: 50 to 60% replication, 20 to 30% iteration, 20 to 30% net new, adjusted for how well current winners are holding and how much risk you can take. How to apply it: label every brief by type and review the monthly split against these bands, together with which type produced your top spending ads.
conditions: Brands with some proven ads or posts to replicate.
fails_when: Brand new accounts with no winners yet, which must lean on net new until something works; accounts whose winners have all fatigued at once.

claim: Spread spend across many ads: three ads holding $1,000 a day at 4x beat one ad holding it at 4x; Blue Sense has seen 8 to 10 brands arrive 40% down in new customers after their few winners fatigued.
body: Every creative on Meta has a maximum spend it can hold and every creative eventually fatigues. Blue Sense's portfolio model: suppose $1,000 a day at a blended 4x ROAS. In one scenario a single ad holds all of it; in the other, three ads share it. The returns are equal today, but the second is far safer, because when one ad fatigues the other two carry the spend while replacements are found. In the first, fatigue means the business drops. Over about six years Blue Sense has met roughly 8 to 10 brands that came to it about 40% down year on year in new customer acquisition, having built eight-figure businesses on about three creatives that held around a million dollars of spend. When those fatigued, variations could not replace them. The usual cause is cutting creative production after finding winners, on the logic that production is wasted money. Blue Sense now declines some of these accounts as too late to fix, saying it needed action six to eight months earlier. How to apply: track the share of spend held by your top one and top three ads each week; if one or two ads carry most of the budget, raise production now and build backups across different concepts.
conditions: Meta accounts where a few ads carry most spend; growing brands that might cut creative budgets.
fails_when: Short-lived campaigns or drops where longevity does not matter.

claim: Test creative as concept ad sets (persona, angle, offer, ad type), then build around winners: a teeth whitening 'brides' concept could get a 14-day wedding bundle, its own landing page and a post-wedding retention flow.
body: Blue Sense's teeth whitening matrix shows how concepts become ad sets. Persona coffee drinkers, angle whitening without sensitivity, offer the plain product, ad type UGC, with many ad types rotated under that concept. Persona brides, angle 'ready for your wedding in 14 days', offer a bundle built for a fast 14-day result, ad type a testimonial from a real bride documenting the process. Persona smokers, angle stain removal, offer a subscription because the staining continues, ad type founder talking head if the founder is a smoker. When a concept wins, double down beyond ads: make much more creative for it, give it a custom landing page with matching testimonials, spin the bundle into a named product such as a 14-day wedding bundle, and build the whole funnel around it, which can scale that concept two to three times. It also tells the business who its customers are (for example 40% smokers, 40% brides), which can guide retention: a post-wedding flow with a congratulations gift and an offer into a product line for their next life stage. Keeping concepts broad hides these insights. How to apply: name ad sets by concept, review spend share by persona monthly, and route winning concepts into landing page, offer and email work.

claim: Test each new concept with at least 10 ads and size the batch from your hit rate: at the typical rate of about 5%, you need around 20 ads to expect one winner.
body: A frequent mistake is building a strong concept and launching only one to three ads for it, then judging the whole idea on that. Blue Sense's testing cycle: write a hypothesis (which variable of the concept you are changing: persona, angle, offer or format), build many ads under it, launch, then compare results with what you expected (spend, conversions and return), scale what worked and iterate. Most accounts have a hit rate around 5%, meaning one in twenty ads becomes a winner, so a fair test of a concept needs about 20 ads, and never fewer than about 10. How to apply it: work out your own hit rate from the last 6 to 12 months (ads that reached your winner threshold divided by ads launched). Ads needed per concept is roughly one divided by that rate. Plan shoots so each concept gets that many variations through hooks, formats and creators. Write down before launch how much spend and how many purchases you expect, so the read is against a plan. The cycle speeds up as spend grows, since bigger budgets give answers faster.
conditions: Accounts with enough budget to spend meaningfully on 10 to 20 ads per concept.
fails_when: Very small budgets that cannot give 10 or more ads any real spend; accounts whose hit rate is much higher, which need fewer ads per concept.

claim: Treat retargeting ads as objection handling: with a 5% conversion rate, 95% of visitors did not buy, so split them by reason (price, trust, quality doubt, not ready) and give each reason its own ad.
body: The main job of a product aware ad is to answer why people did not buy. Blue Sense's worked example assumes the non-buyers split evenly: about 20% think the price is too high, 20% do not trust the brand yet, 20% doubt the quality, and 20% simply are not ready because it was the first ad they saw. Each group needs a different message. Price: show discounts, anchor the value, or use a cost per use angle, such as a supplement costing half a coffee for the same caffeine; Blue Sense says cost per use ads do very well at the bottom of the funnel. Trust: social proof such as customer numbers, count of five star reviews and testimonial videos. Quality: footage of the product in use, before and after shots and demos. Not ready: keep showing up with educational or lifestyle content. How to apply it: estimate your own split from exit or post-purchase surveys, chat logs, reviews and abandoned cart replies. Brief retargeting ads in that ratio and check that your retargeting campaign has at least one ad for each objection.
conditions: Stores with enough site traffic to retarget and some insight into why visitors leave.
fails_when: Very low traffic stores where retargeting pools are tiny; the 20% split is an illustration, so use your own survey data where you have it.

claim: Under Meta's Andromeda system the creative is the targeting: Meta reads each ad's transcript, copy and visuals to choose who sees it, so a hook that names the wrong persona, or 'hey everyone', steers delivery badly.
body: Before, advertisers picked an audience (an interest) and loaded creatives into it. Now you load creatives with broad targeting and Meta looks at each ad, including the words spoken (it auto-transcribes every video), the copy and its own conversion history, to decide who to show it to. This captures more nuance than interest labels, which treat everyone 'interested in pets' alike when the real buyers share age, life stage and other traits. Blue Sense notes Meta had largely worked this way for a while and it had dropped interest targeting in most accounts about two years earlier; the Andromeda update made the approach mainstream. The practical result is that each ad's content decides its audience. Load many ads that say the same thing and you reach the same people. Use a vague hook such as 'hey everyone, look at this' and Meta has no idea who to find. Call out a persona your product does not suit, for example 'business owners doing over $5M a year' on an unrelated product, and Meta goes looking for those people. Mixing ads aimed at different people in one ad set also confuses delivery. How to apply: make each ad clearly speak to one persona early in the hook and keep each ad set to one persona.
conditions: Meta accounts using broad targeting and Advantage+ delivery, as of 2026.
fails_when: Accounts still using tight interest or custom audiences, where the targeting is set elsewhere.

claim: Use AI heavily for briefs, scripts and production, up to about 90% of video sales letter and static work, but not for ideation or final analysis, where models give average ideas and miss account context.
body: Blue Sense splits the creative process into ideation, briefing, production, then publishing and analysis that feeds the next round. Ideation: many teams build AI tools here, but at the time of recording models produce the average, however much context or Reddit scraping you add, so ideas do not stand out from competitors; a human strategist still has to do and validate the concepting. Briefing and scripting: the best place for AI. Build a brand-specific skill that walks you through about 20 questions (persona, concept, offer, long or short form, awareness stage) and produces a script or brief that is nearly final with small edits. Production: also strong leverage; it speeds up editing and can handle about 90% of the work for video sales letters and static images. Analysis: use it, but carefully. Models do not weight the metric hierarchy correctly (spend before ROAS before click metrics), ignore account structure, and do not link creative to commercial goals, so they often point decisions the wrong way. How to apply it: keep humans at both ends, idea generation and the final read, and push throughput with AI in the middle.
conditions: Teams using AI tools in their creative workflow, as of 2026 model quality.
fails_when: Future models may change the ideation picture; teams with no human strategist to check AI output.

claim: Use creators native to the market you target: Australian accents for Australia and US accents for the US; UK creators carry over to Australia fairly well, but local voices always perform best.
body: Blue Sense finds that an Australian accent run in the US market does not perform as well as a native US voice, even with the same script. UK creators used in Australia translate decently, but native accents still win. The script can stay identical; what must change is the creator delivering it. How to apply it: when launching in a new country, budget to recast your best performing scripts with local creators rather than running home market UGC abroad. Keep a roster of creators per market. When you review results by country, compare home creator ads with local creator ads on the same script to measure the gap in your own account. This matters most for talking head, UGC and founder style ads where the voice is front and centre; product only or music led ads are less affected.

claim: When ads are not working, test the angle first, then the offer, which matters most but runs out of options, then new personas for breadth, with format as the fourth lever.
body: Blue Sense's testing order. First, angles: if a persona has bought from you before, a failed ad for that persona is usually an angle or offer problem, not a persona problem, so rotate and sharpen the angle first, provided the persona is specific rather than broad. Second, the offer. It may be the single most important variable, but you have little room to move it. The product itself is mostly fixed unless you have a large range and are launching something new. The value proposition can be tested through bundles, gift with purchase, tiers and subscriptions, but after maybe seven variations of spinning two or three products you get stuck, and the only remaining lever is deep discounting, which Blue Sense avoids. Once the best offer is found you mostly stay on it. Third, personas: they give the breadth and volume needed to keep scaling once angle and offer are settled. Fourth, format, which Andromeda made important because different people see different formats. Keep one concept per ad set while testing, because if three concepts share an ad set and it hits 3x, you cannot tell which concept earned it. How to apply: diagnose a failing concept in this order and change one variable per test.
conditions: Accounts testing concepts with a proven product and buyer base.
fails_when: New products with no proven buyers, where the persona itself is unproven; large catalogues where the product can change.

claim: When hiring a creator, ask for past examples and the brief behind each one; it shows whether they need a detailed brief or can turn loose direction into strong work.
body: Blue Sense's view is that a creator's output follows the quality of the brief. Checking a portfolio is obvious; the extra step is asking for the brief that produced each sample. That gives a like for like test of how the creator works against a brief. If the brief was very detailed, you know you must match that depth. If they made something great from a thin brief, you can give broad direction and trust them. Blue Sense's default is still the most detailed brief possible. If a creator does not want to stick to a script, let them shoot two takes: one on script and one in their own words, then pick the better one or run both. How to apply it: add the request for briefs to your creator outreach, score samples against their briefs, and keep a standard brief template covering persona, angle, offer, hook options, awareness stage, must-say claims and format. claim: A 5-minute ad takes about two days to script while ten 30-second ads take the same time, so it only pays if longer ads win more often or carry much more spend.
body: Ads of every length have spent millions, from 30 seconds to 20 minutes, so there is no single best length. Cost of production, including scripting, rises with length. Blue Sense's maths: if both long and short ads have a 10% hit rate, ten short ads give you about one winner while one long ad likely gives none. The upside of length is scale: a longer ad has to start further up the awareness ladder, so it reaches colder, larger audiences and can hold more spend, and longer exposure builds trust. Blue Sense, which spends about $1M a day across clients, recommends testing a spread: many 30 and 60 second ads, plus some 3, 5 and 6 minute ads. Judge longer ads on how much spend they can hold, not only their hit rate.

fails_when: Small budgets or limited writing time, where short ads give more learning per dollar.

claim: A call to action needs four parts: name the action, say what happens next, price the effort, and give a reason to act now; shop now at the link below does only the first.
body: Learn more by clicking below names the action and nothing else. Blue Sense's stronger version for an apparel brand driving to a quiz: take the 60-second quiz and get your size plus two cuts that suit your shape. It names the action, prices the effort (60 seconds) and says what you get next. It still lacks a reason for now, so add an honest one, such as the top sellers being close to selling out. Honest urgency with a real number and date (our next batch ships on a named date and this month is full) is far stronger than limited time only. How to apply it: rewrite every CTA line with these four slots filled, and only use scarcity that is true.

claim: A competitor ad that has run for a long time proves it works for that brand at that spend with its built-up belief; copied into your account it will usually not.
body: Teams often skip copywriting and clone the longest running ads in a rival's Meta Ad Library, assuming age means a winner. Blue Sense's point is that the ad is carried by things you do not get when you copy it: the rival's brand recognition, proof assets and the trust their buyers already have. That is why nine-figure accounts can hold huge spend on average looking ads. How to apply it: use rival libraries to learn angles, formats and offers, not as scripts to paste. For any ad you want to borrow, list what belief the viewer must already hold for it to work (they know the brand, trust the founder, have seen the product). If your buyers do not hold that belief, your version needs the extra beats (problem, mechanism, proof) that the big brand can skip.

claim: A contradiction like as much energy as coffee with no crash is not a mechanism; either explain why it happens right after, move it to the hook, or cut it.
body: Contradiction lines feel strong in review meetings because they open a curiosity gap. But in the mechanism slot they promise an answer they never give, so the viewer has no reason to believe it. Blue Sense's options: add the actual reason the contradiction is true (the ingredient, release method or process), use the line as the hook where open questions belong and answer it later, or rewrite. How to apply it: for any but without line in the middle of a script, ask whether the next sentence explains how. If not, the line is unfinished.

claim: A new brand with no reviews should lean on demonstration and seed detailed testimonials by giving the product to about 20 people in exchange for specific, honest reviews.

The opposite: demonstration, the strongest rung, is open to anyone with a product. Show it working. For testimony, give the product free to around 20 people and ask for a detailed review that says exactly how it helped, not just that it was good. Pull the specific phrases from those reviews into the ads and landing pages. How to apply it: plan a demo shot for each core claim, run a small seeding round, and brief reviewers with questions that draw out specifics (what changed, how long it took, what they tried before). Disclose that the product was gifted where rules require it.

claim: A story is not one beat added to the script but the vehicle for all nine beats; it moves the viewer from judging the ad to wanting to know what happened.
body: Blue Sense notes some of the best brands spending around a million dollars a day run story ads of seven to eight minutes. Most advice treats story as a 30-second add-on at the start or end. Instead, the whole ad is told as events happening to someone, while still carrying the problem, mechanism, objection, proof and offer. Why it works: when watching an ad, the buyer audits every sentence and decides whether to agree. Inside a story, her job is to find out what happens, so the argument arrives while she is busy following it. How to apply it: take a winning nine-beat script and retell it as one person's past experience, keeping each beat but turning them into scenes. claim: Agitate the consequence the buyer has quietly adjusted their life around, not the symptom: you plan outfits around bad days beats bloating is uncomfortable.
body: A symptom is what the body or day is doing, and the buyer already knows it, so naming it buys nothing. The consequence, called the accommodation, is what they have changed to cope, usually without saying it out loud. Naming it makes them feel seen and calls out the persona without a callout. In the hair script, hair in the shower drain is a symptom any competitor can claim and the category already uses; you have stopped parting it in the middle without deciding to is an accommodation the buyer has likely never heard in an ad. Shifting it to first person (I stopped parting my hair in the middle) gives another variant for UGC, EGC or VSL formats. How to apply it: take the problem section of your latest script and ask whether it names a symptom or an accommodation. If a symptom, go back to reviews and calls for what customers changed.

claim: Blue Sense's ten-step scripting process runs desire with evidence, research, awareness and sophistication, offer, unique adjectives, consequence, promise then mechanism, hook into line two, proof over claim, then format.
body: The order matters because most of the work is done before writing. 1) Find a real desire and evidence it in customer data; invent neither. 2) Run the five research hunts (accommodation, failed solution, nearly didn't buy, the word, the moment). 3) Place the buyer on awareness and sophistication. 4) Fix the offer before scripting. 5) Find descriptive words only you can own, or pair ones rarely seen together, instead of category language like makes hair soft. 6) Agitate the consequence, never the symptom. 7) Promise before mechanism. 8) Make each hook flow into line two; AI-made batches of ten hooks often do not. 9) Proof must exceed the claim. 10) Choose a format that meets the script's visual needs. Blue Sense's claim is that the rewritten hair ad, built this way, is about ten times more likely to work and scale than the original, an estimate rather than a test result.

claim: Brand teams that object to negative ads are really objecting to pity; name one accommodation as a neutral observation and frame against the accommodation, never the affliction.
body: Problem agitation and an aspirational brand are not in conflict. Saying you have stopped parting it in the middle is not an insult; it is a true observation nobody has said before, and the buyer recognises it in herself. Pity comes from stacking many symptoms and describing someone as a sufferer, which is what happens when agitation drags on for minutes. How to apply it when a brand team pushes back: show them a version with one accommodation, stated plainly, with no list of symptoms and no sufferer framing. This usually passes brand review while keeping the persuasion. Keep the line accurate to the research so it does not read as a judgement.

claim: Cut any line the product next to yours on the shelf could also say; claims like vegan, cruelty free and locally made can burn 7 to 8 words and about 4.5 seconds.
body: In the sample hair supplement script, the line listing vegan, cruelty free and made in Australia was true and compliant, but most of the category can say the same, so it moved no one closer to buying. Teams often defend such lines as objection handling, yet they answer worries the buyer does not have. Nobody who has watched to the end of an ad about losing hair stops because they are unsure it is vegan. The edit: run each claim through two checks. Is it true? Could a competitor say it word for word? If the second answer is yes, delete it rather than polish it, and leave the space empty until research gives you a real differentiator or a real objection pulled from reviews and support tickets. Deletion is often the highest value edit in a draft.

claim: Design static ads with the same beat order as a script, mapped to where the eye goes; when objection, proof and offer will not fit, move them to the landing page.
body: A static follows the same path: the first place the eye lands is the hook, then the problem or accommodation (which can be carried by the image alone), the promise, the mechanism, then proof, offer and call to action. One static rarely has room for all of it, so keep hook, problem, promise and mechanism in the ad and let the landing page carry objections, proof and the offer. How to apply it: sketch the eye path on each static concept and label the beat at each stop. If the static only has a product shot and a tagline, it has skipped the beats that sell to cold buyers. Make sure the landing page opens where the static stops, so the argument continues rather than restarting.
conditions: Top of funnel static image ads on Meta that link to a product or pre-sell page.

claim: Do not name the product before the mechanism has landed; say we sell electrolytes early and you join a category of salt and magnesium where the cheapest wins.
body: Once a viewer files you as just another electrolyte, the comparison is on price. Introduce the mechanism that sets you apart first, and the product later, ideally at the offer or even the call to action. Even if your formula matches rivals, the supply chain or process can give a mechanism; Blue Sense's example is months spent in the factory to find a process that made the flavour much better. How to apply it: in the script, mark where the product or brand name is first spoken and first shown. Spoken naming should come after the mechanism. The product can appear in the visuals earlier without being named, which softens the reveal.
conditions: Commodity or crowded categories (electrolytes, protein, basics) selling to cold buyers.
fails_when: The brand name itself is the draw (a famous founder or known brand) or the ad targets product-aware retargeting audiences.

claim: Each awareness stage needs a different opening, and cost per result rises as you write for colder stages; mix stages across ads to widen who Meta can reach.
body: Commonly quoted shares put about 3% of a market ready to buy, about 9% product aware, roughly 30% problem or solution aware, and the rest unaware. Warm stages convert cheaply but are small; colder stages are larger but need more education, so return on spend falls and the writing skill needed rises sharply. Hair supplement examples by stage: unaware, a line about why you dislike photos taken from behind; problem aware, if you have started parting on the side this is for you; solution aware, most supplements use saw palmetto at a fifth of the studied dose; product and most aware, the 90-day pack is back at its last price. How to apply it: label each ad with one stage before writing. Run a spread of stages so the account is not limited to the small warm pool, and expect colder ads to need longer scripts.
conditions: Brands scaling past the warm, in-market pool on Meta.
fails_when: Small budgets where only the most aware buyers can be reached profitably; start low in the funnel and move colder as spend grows.

claim: Ease the product in: show it on screen before naming it, and name it at the offer or even the call to action, as organic speech goes thought, complaint, story, then maybe the product.
body: Nothing makes people scroll faster than a story-style video that suddenly becomes a TV ad five seconds in. Product awareness should not jump from zero to full in one line, such as that is why our brand is your best solution. People sharing something online usually start with a random thought, a small complaint, a personal story, and only then mention what helped. Blue Sense's rewrite of the hair script removed the early product line and bridged with the fix is not a better shampoo, it is getting the follicle to stop shrinking, then three things that do that. The product only arrives as: you can buy those separately, or take them in one capsule, here is what is in it. How to apply it: find the first line that names the product and try moving it later, letting visuals show it first.
conditions: Native-style video ads (UGC, story, talking head) for cold audiences.
fails_when: Short retargeting ads where the viewer already knows the product and needs the offer quickly.

claim: End the ad on an identity line tied to the mechanism, such as the women who keep their hair began before the loss showed, which also filters out buyers who will not stick with it.
body: Identity with no mechanism is a lifestyle brand with a product attached, and brand work stuck there rarely moves sales. Identity linked to a real mechanism is direct response. Blue Sense's practical rule: instead of ending on a bare buy now, close with the offer, a soft call to action, a nudge that each month waited is another cycle, then a final line aimed at who the buyer wants to be. The hair line does two jobs. It speaks to the person who acts early, and it quietly tells people who will not keep the habit that this is not for them, which protects refund and repeat rates since those buyers would quit anyway. How to apply it: write three closing identity lines, each grounded in a mechanism fact, and test them as variants.
conditions: Habit or long-term-use products where who sticks with it matters (supplements, skincare, fitness, haircare).
fails_when: The identity line is generic brand talk unconnected to anything the product does, or the filtering cuts volume more than it saves in refunds.

claim: Every physical product has a mechanism, even a t-shirt: merino's crimped fibre traps air so odour stays in the fibre, not on your skin.
body: Brands selling clothes or simple goods often say they have no mechanism. Blue Sense's definition: a mechanism is just the reason a feature produces the promise. Someone chose the fabric, the construction, the supplier, the wash testing and who cuts the garment, and each choice has a consequence you can name. Merino wool is a feature; the crimped fibre trapping air and holding odour away from skin during a workout is the mechanism, with no chemistry needed. How to apply it: list each production decision for your hero product, then write what each decision does for the wearer and why. Pick the one that best supports the promise your buyers care about.
conditions: Apparel, homewares and other non-technical physical products.
fails_when: The decision is standard in the category and stating it implies a unique benefit you do not have; check with the supplier first.
