claim: Find your market's sophistication stage from competitor ads, then write one stage higher: claims, bigger claims, mechanism, bigger mechanism, then identity, which beats plain claims even in young markets.
body: Schwartz's stages describe how tired the market is. Stage 1: the first claim works because it is new. Stage 2: rivals copy, so claims inflate (and compliance gets risky). Stage 3: buyers stop believing claims, so a unique mechanism revives hope. Stage 4: everyone has a mechanism, so mechanisms get bigger. Stage 5: mechanisms are exhausted, so ads sell who the buyer becomes. Hair supplement lines by stage: a supplement for your hair; the strongest on the market; it is the follicle, and DHT is shrinking it; saw palmetto at the dose the studies used, not what rivals use; the women who keep their hair started before they could see the loss. How to apply it: scan 20 to 30 competitor ads and tag their stage. Blue Sense's view is that higher-stage ads outperform even in an early market such as AI tools, so lead with a mechanism or identity rather than a bare claim.
conditions: Any category with visible competitor advertising to judge the stage from.
fails_when: A genuinely new category where buyers do not yet understand the basic claim; you may need plain education before a mechanism lands.

claim: Get new ads from one angle and persona by changing only the register: casual UGC, a flat third-person documentary voice, or a first-person diary entry written to nobody.
body: Blue Sense rewrote the same accommodation three ways. UGC: second person or casual first person, present tense, low reading level, many contractions (I stopped parting in the middle and did not even notice). Documentary: third person, older voice, no hype (she changed where she parted her hair a year before she admitted why). Diary: first person past tense written to no one (I stopped parting in the middle today, I did not decide to). Same persona, same angle, same research, very different feeling ads. How to apply it: once a concept has a working script, brief two more registers before inventing new angles. It is a fast way to add creative diversity without new research.
conditions: Concepts with a proven script that need more variants.
fails_when: The register clashes with the brand or the platform placement (a documentary voice in a fast Reels slot may lose the scroll).

claim: Handle six objections in this order: not for me, it won't work, it won't work for me, not worth it, what if I'm wrong, I'll do it later; each has a set fix.
body: Most brands' objections fall into the same six. Not for me: use persona-specific language, which is why speaking to one person beats a wide audience. It won't work: the mechanism plus proof. It might work but not for me: proof from people like this persona, not general proof. Not worth it: the offer and perceived value, or the cost of not buying; an acne cream ad can point out that the medical route means appointments and two to three years of prescription treatment costing thousands. What if I'm wrong: a guarantee. I'll do it later: urgency, which is why sale events like Black Friday spike sales. The order is the order the script should run; opening with guarantees and urgency before the buyer believes it is for them makes no sense. How to apply it: check your script answers all six, in sequence.
conditions: Direct response scripts and landing pages for cold buyers.
fails_when: Very short ads; prioritise the one or two objections your research shows matter most.

claim: Hunt research for five things, each feeding one beat: the accommodation (problem), the failed solution (objection), the nearly didn't buy (risk reversal), the word (hook) and the moment (urgency).
body: The accommodation is what the buyer changed about their life to work around the problem, often without admitting it; in the hair example, a review said she stopped parting her hair in the middle because that is where it showed. The failed solution is what they tried first, what it cost and why they quit (four months of rosemary oil, a smelly pillowcase, no change). The nearly didn't buy is the last barrier (everything in this category takes six months and I have been burned twice). The word is the noun they use (shedding, my part, never hair loss or alopecia). The moment is the trigger that made them search (seeing photos from a sister's wedding). On customer calls, always ask for the moment. Five of the nine script beats come straight from these finds, so the ad is mostly written before anyone writes a line. Save each quote with its source under the matching beat.
conditions: Problem-solving products where customers have a before state they can describe (health, beauty, home, pets, apparel fit).
fails_when: Pure impulse or fashion purchases with no problem to accommodate; then the moment and the word still apply but the problem beats are thin.

claim: If you cannot find the buyer's desire written down outside your own marketing (a review, support ticket, Reddit thread), you have a product description, not an ad concept.
body: Copy cannot create desire; it can only point a desire that already exists at your product. Most briefs start from the product and hunt for a reason to care, which produces the same flat ads competitors run every month. Blue Sense's rule is to require outside evidence of the desire before a concept goes to scripting. Their example: a shampoo client led with gentle shampoo for sensitive scalps. Reading reviews and email support tickets showed a repeated theme the brand never used: the fragrance did not set off histamine reactions. That is a narrower, more specific desire that almost nobody in the category was speaking to, and it allows a line like every fragrance-free shampoo I tried still triggered me, this scented one did not. How to apply it: for each concept, paste at least one real customer quote that shows the desire. No quote, no concept.
conditions: Brands with some customer history (reviews, tickets, calls) and a category where generic benefit claims are crowded.
fails_when: A brand new product with no customers yet; then use forums, Reddit and competitor reviews as the outside evidence instead of your own data.

claim: If you write only one story script, write it in first person past tense; then rewrite winners in other tenses and persons for cheap variants, and never resolve the story in the hook.
body: Blue Sense finds first person past tense the best performer for stories. Switching a winning script to present or future tense, or to second or third person, is one of the easiest ways to get more ads from one idea. Writers worried about retention often rush to resolve the story early; do not. They have seen strong ads spending heavily at nine minutes long. Stories must also be true: if it did not happen, it is fiction and should read that way, and claims inside invented stories create compliance risk. Source stories from customer calls and real events. How to apply it: draft the hero story in first person past tense from a real customer account, then brief variants that change only tense or person, and keep the resolution for the back half.
conditions: Story-based video scripts on Meta.
fails_when: No true story exists yet; do customer interviews before writing rather than inventing one.

claim: In the problem beat, argue at category level, speak to one person not two, and do not resolve the discomfort; one person is the single biggest predictor of whether agitation works.
body: Three guardrails for the problem section. First, talk about the category, not your product: buyers cannot dismiss a whole category such as preventing hair loss as hype, so starting there borrows its credibility, and you are not yet asking them to believe anything about you. Narrow to your product later in the script. Second, agitate one specific person. Trying to speak to two personas in one problem section blurs the language so neither feels it is about them. Third, leave the discomfort open. Resolving the problem right away removes the tension that carries the viewer into the promise and mechanism. How to apply it: check that the problem section names no product, describes one person's life, and ends on the unresolved consequence.
conditions: Problem-solution scripts for cold buyers.
fails_when: Product-aware retargeting ads, where the buyer already knows the category and wants the offer.

claim: Keep the problem beat to about 10 to 15 seconds in a standard script, and check it escalates: if you can swap any two lines without changing the argument, you wrote a list.
body: Longer agitation risks sounding like complaining, which happens when a writer stacks symptoms instead of building toward one consequence. The test is simple: reorder the lines. If nothing breaks, it is a list and the viewer is not being moved anywhere. Each line should raise the stakes on the last. Long formats are the exception: animated, claymation or AI VSL ads can agitate for two minutes, and Blue Sense has seen such ads hold half a million to a million dollars of spend. Treat those as separate variants rather than the default. How to apply it: time the problem section when read aloud; if it runs past 15 seconds in a 30 to 60 second ad, cut to the strongest consequence and one escalation step.
conditions: Standard 30 to 90 second video scripts.
fails_when: Long-form VSL or story ads built to agitate for minutes; there length is the strategy, though escalation still matters.

claim: Link every feature as feature, which means the promise, which is why the mechanism; for example 320 mg saw palmetto, which means you stop losing hair at the part, because it blocks the DHT enzyme.
body: Each part fails alone. A feature sells only to people already convinced, which on cold traffic is nobody. A promise alone is what every rival says. The mechanism makes the promise believable and sets you apart, but it needs the promise to give it meaning. Joined in one or two sentences, they do the job: the feature (what it is), the promise (what it means for you), the mechanism (why it works). How to apply it: for each feature on your product page, write the chain in that order. If a feature has no clear promise, it does not belong in the ad. If it has a promise but no mechanism, look in formulation and manufacturing for the reason it works, or back it with proof instead.
conditions: Products with ingredients, materials or processes that can be explained.
fails_when: The mechanism claim cannot be backed for your product, which raises compliance risk in health categories.

claim: Match the beat to format strengths: proof needs a believable face, invisible mechanisms need animation not a talking head, and long-form native statics read most like a person but give up sequence and sound.
body: Blue Sense scored three broad formats. Live action talking to camera (UGC, EGC, founder): has a face, cannot show the unseen, controls sequence, has sound, is middling at holding attention, and reads as a person only if the script and talent feel natural. Drawn, rendered or AI animation: no human face, can show the unseen (for example gut lining repairing), controls sequence, has sound, holds attention better because cuts are flexible, and can read as a person. Long-form native static (a plain image such as a garden photo with a long story in the copy): no face, no control of what the eye reads first, no sound, but holds attention and reads most like a real person. None wins overall; each has produced millions. Formats can also blend within one ad, such as talking head into AI animation and back.
conditions: Choosing formats for a written script on Meta.
fails_when: New formats (claymation AI ads are the current hot one) have different property mixes; score them fresh rather than assuming.

claim: Most scripts never state the promise in one sentence; avoid the four failures (no promise, five promises, a feature posing as a promise, a promise bigger than the proof), and keep claims smaller than your proof.
body: Without a single clear promise the buyer has to work out the outcome from the problem, mechanism and proof, and many will not. Technical brands and supplements often jump from problem to mechanism with no promise at all. Others list five benefits so none land (vegan, cruelty free, locally made). Others state an input as the promise, such as six clinically studied ingredients, which is a feature. The last failure is promising more than you can show. Bencivenga's rule: a smaller promise you can prove beats a bigger one you cannot. Since most markets are at sophistication stage 4 or 5, large claims now need even more proof. The hair script added a promise between problem and mechanism: this is about keeping the hair you have, not regrowing what is gone. That is honest for the category and believable. How to apply it: write the promise as one sentence in the buyer's terms and check you have proof that matches its size.
conditions: Direct response scripts in claim-heavy categories (supplements, skincare, fitness, tech).
fails_when: Very short ads with no room for a promise, or brand spots with no explicit outcome.
numbers: 4 promise failure modes

claim: Open the problem beat one of three ways: the accommodation, the moment they noticed, or a failed solution; the failed-solution opening locks the ad to solution-aware buyers.
body: The accommodation opening names the workaround (you stopped parting it in the middle). The moment opening names the trigger (seeing a photo from behind at a wedding). The failed solution opening names what they tried (four months of rosemary oil that only made the pillowcase smell). Teams often keep failed solutions for the objection beat, but they also work as a strong way into the problem. The tradeoff: anyone who has tried a solution is already solution aware, so that ad will reach a narrower group. That is fine, as long as it is a deliberate choice and other ads cover colder stages. How to apply it: write three versions of the problem opening from your research quotes, one per path, and run them as separate ads under the same concept.
conditions: Problem-led ads with research quotes for each path.
fails_when: The research has no clear moment or failed solution; do not invent one.

claim: Pick the format after the script: find the load-bearing beat (mechanism for invisible benefits, proof for visible ones, offer for unusual terms) and choose a format that can carry it.
body: Most teams decide on UGC first and write to fit. Blue Sense reverses that. The load-bearing beat is the part of the script doing most of the persuading, and it comes from the proposition, not the format. A multivitamin's edge is invisible, so the mechanism carries it and needs a format that can show the unseen. A gadget with a visible result is carried by demonstration and proof. A product whose terms are different is carried by the offer. Score candidate formats on six properties: can it carry a believable human face, can it show what a camera cannot, do you control the order the viewer takes things in, can you assume sound, can it hold attention long enough, does it read as a person rather than an ad. Their view is that most format failures are writing failures that look like production failures, which is why edits keep bouncing back.
conditions: Teams producing several formats (UGC, animation, statics) for Meta.
fails_when: You only have the means to make one format; then write to its limits from the start.

claim: Pre-empt objections through an experience buyers already had: instead of gentle for sensitive skin, say you will react in week one, everyone does, so the first tube is 0.05%.
body: Generic reassurance asks the buyer to trust you. Naming what has happened to them before shows you understand, then explains what you did about it. Research shows many skincare buyers bought products sold as gentle and still flared up on first use because their skin was not used to the active. The rewrite calls that out and ties it to the product decision: a low first dose, stepped up in the second tube. How to apply it: take the top objections from mid-star reviews and tickets, find the past experience behind each, and write a line that names the experience, then the product decision that answers it. Do not invent the experience; it must come from research.

claim: Put most testing into native-looking hooks (screenshots, notes, lo-fi talking camera) over polished hero shots; the hook should pre-qualify buyers, because Meta optimises toward whoever watches.
body: Blue Sense sorts openings into two buckets. A: polished hero shots, centred logo, tagline, clearly an ad. B: openings that look like organic posts, such as a screenshot, a note to self or lo-fi talking to camera. Performance usually comes from B, while A helps by lifting perceived value and brand image; fashion still needs its photo shoot ads. The hook's job is to attract the right people, not everyone, because even on a purchase objective Meta learns from who watches and serves more people like them. Example: introducing the new summer collection is weak; a creator saying she bought one dress in three sizes because she could not tell which was hers opens a gap and feels native. Follow it with the size guide so you do not encourage buying three and returning two.

claim: Put the promise before the mechanism; leading with jargon like lowers ghrelin and raises leptin loses viewers before they reach the point, a mistake in roughly 30 to 40% of feed ads.
body: Retention falls through every ad, so the clearest, most widely understood line should come first. A promise like you stop thinking about food at 11am holds everyone; then explain that ketones suppress ghrelin, the hunger hormone, and the jargon now makes sense because the viewer knows why it matters. When there is no mechanism for a promise, pick a different feature that has one. If none do, swap the mechanism for proof and run promise then proof, which is common in less mature markets and works, though not as well. How to apply it: in each draft, find the first technical term and check a plain outcome comes before it. Blue Sense says that once you notice this, you will see the reverse order in about a third of the ads in your feed.

claim: Rank proof from strongest to weakest: demonstration, third-party verification, volume of specific social proof, named individual testimony, mechanism explanation, then founder assertion.
body: Demonstration is the product visibly working on camera, including before and after. Third-party verification covers clinical results, lab tests, certifications and independent press; Blue Sense says real news-anchor style ads from actual coverage are among the best they have seen. Volume is how many reviews or customers. Named testimony can beat volume where the buyer needs someone like them; for an agency, one video from a $100 million beauty founder outweighs thousands of vague five-star reviews. Mechanism explanation is not proof as such, but it makes the claim feel logical. Founder assertion is weakest and only works when the founder has standing, such as a famous athlete or a leading neurosurgeon launching a brain health product; a young founder with no credentials should leave it out. How to apply it: list what proof you have at each level and use the highest ones, matching testimony to the persona.
conditions: Ads and landing pages that need to back a claim.
fails_when: Ranking differs by category; in high-trust B2B or premium services, named testimony can outrank volume.

claim: Replace adjectives with checkable specifics: numbers, a named third party, a physical detail, a timeframe or a proper noun, like dry in 40 seconds, we timed it, instead of fast absorbing.
body: Any competitor can use an adjective, so it carries no information and buyers forget it. Specifics read as evidence. Blue Sense's ladder, drawn from Hopkins: measured numbers first, then a named third party, then a precise physical detail, then a specific time, then proper nouns. Examples: a serum that leaves skin healthier becomes a 0.05% retinol with a first tube dosed low on purpose (which also opens a question the ad answers later). Luxury craftsmanship becomes one person stitches each pair start to finish, four hours each. How to apply it: highlight every adjective in a draft and replace each with a fact from the factory, formulation or testing. If compliance blocks a specific outcome claim, stay specific about inputs and time (a 90-day course, the dose, the process) rather than promising a result by a date.
conditions: Any product with real facts about its making, dose or testing.
fails_when: You lack verified data; an invented number is a compliance and trust risk worse than an adjective.

claim: Replace customers love it with counted specifics from your reviews, such as 360,000 customers and the word finally appearing over 6,000 times.
body: Customers love it is in many scripts and proves nothing. The stronger version combines two kinds of proof in one short line: the volume of buyers and a word that keeps repeating in reviews, which works as a testimonial said thousands of times. In the finished hair script it became about 4,800 reviews with finally as the most common word. How to apply it: export your reviews, count the most frequent meaningful words and phrases (ignoring product names and filler), and pick one that carries emotion and fits the promise. Pair it with your total reviews or customers. Check the counts are accurate before running, since they are factual claims.
conditions: Stores with hundreds or more reviews in an exportable app.
fails_when: Too few reviews for a meaningful count, or no word stands out; then use one strong named testimonial instead.

claim: Retention drops sharply at weak bridges, most often when 20 separately written hooks are stitched onto one body; each line's only job is to get the next line watched.
body: A normal retention curve declines smoothly. A broken bridge shows as a cliff right after the hook and again where proof turns into the offer. The usual cause is workflow: someone makes a batch of hooks that each look fine alone, an editor stitches them onto the same body, and several make no sense leading into the problem line. How to apply it: write hooks with the second line in view, and read each hook plus the first body line together before approving. In Ads Manager, compare hold rates across hook variants of the same body; a variant with a strong hook rate but a steep drop by the 5 to 10 second mark usually has a bridge problem, not a hook problem.
conditions: Video ads where hook variants are produced in batches.
fails_when: Each hook variant gets its own written transition, so the stitch is already handled.

claim: Run a so what test on every line: a correct, logical script can pass every review and still sell nothing, because believing is not the same as wanting.
body: Blue Sense says it taught for years as if a buyer who believes the mechanism will buy. They do not. Review meetings check whether a script is correct and follows the framework, not whether anyone wants the result. Nobody buys a supplement for its own sake; they buy a version of themselves who acted early. The fix is to ask so what of each line until the answer is about the person, not the product. Feature to identity examples: blocks DHT means someone who starts before loss shows; 12 g of collagen means someone who takes it seriously instead of dabbling; merino that does not smell means someone who travels with one bag; a 90-day guarantee speaks to someone burned before who does not trust the category; absorbs in 40 seconds means someone out the door at 6:30am; third-party tests mean someone who checks things. How to apply it: add this test to your script review checklist.
conditions: Mature markets at sophistication stage 4 or 5, where mechanisms alone no longer cut through.
fails_when: Simple, low-price practical buys where the function is the whole decision.

claim: Set six sentence choices on every script: person, tense, varied length (long, long, short), reading level under grade 7 for general buyers, contractions always, and a strong last word.
body: Person: first for stories, second for most scripts, third last; Blue Sense sees performance in that order. Tense: past for stories, present for mechanisms. Length: vary it; nonstop short punchy sentences and contrast negation (it is not X, it is Y) are clear signs of AI writing. A long, long, short rhythm sounds like real speech and can be given to a model as a rule. Reading level: keep it below grade 7 for most consumer products, raising it for expert buyers such as athletes who know muscle fibre types. Contractions: always (can't, don't); AI tends to avoid them, which sounds robotic. Last word: end sentences on an important word where possible. How to apply it: put these six rules in the instruction file you give any AI script tool, and use them as a checklist when editing.
conditions: Consumer ad scripts, especially those drafted with AI.
fails_when: Expert or professional audiences, where a higher reading level and technical terms build trust.

claim: Size beats to ad length: at 15 seconds only hook, a problem line and CTA fit; the mechanism needs 45 to 60 seconds; risk reversal needs over 60; ads over 4 minutes need several CTAs.
body: Blue Sense's guide by beat. Hook: always one line. Problem: one line at 15 to 45 seconds, several lines at 90 seconds plus, a full scene of 2 to 3 minutes in 6 to 10 minute ads. Promise: none at 15 seconds, one or two sentences from 30 seconds, rarely more. Mechanism: none at 15 seconds, one sentence at 45 to 60, two to four sentences at 1 to 3 minutes, and it can become the bulk of a long ad as edutainment that leaves older viewers feeling they learned something. Objection: none at 15 seconds, two or three sentences at 1 to 2 minutes, large blocks in 6 minute ads, often woven into agitation. Proof: one to three items at 1 to 2 minutes, five or six in long ads. Offer: always short. Risk reversal: only over 60 seconds, one line. CTA: in every ad, two or three lines in longer ads, and at around the 3, 5 and 7 minute marks in ads over 4 minutes.
conditions: Planning scripts for a target length on Meta video.
fails_when: Formats with different viewing habits (pre-roll, TV) where attention and skip points differ.

claim: State the awareness stage on the brief, because a problem-aware script, a product-aware static and solution-aware primary text in one ad will confuse buyers and delivery.
body: Awareness is a property of the whole ad, not of the script alone. A common failure: the copywriter writes the video as problem aware, the designer drops in a product shot that speaks to product-aware buyers, and someone else writes primary text for solution-aware buyers. Each person did their part well, but nobody said which stage the ad was for. The viewer gets three starting points, Meta cannot tell who the ad is for, and the message is muddled. How to apply it: add a required line to every creative brief with the awareness stage and sophistication stage, and check the first frame, spoken words, on-screen text, primary text, headline and landing page against it before launch. Treat a mismatch as a reason to send the ad back, not a style note.
conditions: Teams or agencies where scripts, designs and ad copy are made by different people.
fails_when: One person makes the whole ad end to end and already keeps it consistent.

claim: Story ads break three ways: the story ends and then the ad starts, the narrator is obviously acting, or nothing is at stake; I stopped going to the hairdresser beats I've been looking for something.
body: The bridge is the most common failure: a story runs, then an abrupt sell. Second is a narrator who is clearly reading a script, which can happen even with real customers who are poor on camera. Third is no stakes: nothing risked, lost or embarrassing. This usually comes from thin research, since the writer is rarely the customer and has no accommodation, failed solution or moment to build from, so they invent one that feels off. Compare I've been looking for something for my hair (no stakes) with I stopped going to the hairdresser because I thought she would say something (embarrassment, something to lose). If your category seems to have no stakes, you have not found the accommodation yet. Stories can also be told in third person by the brand (someone worked out why this happens) or around an old remedy. Only make claims as a customer if the speaker really is one.
conditions: Story-led video, advertorials and long-form statics.
fails_when: The story is true and high stakes but too long for the format chosen; then the bridge problem returns.
numbers: 3 failure modes

claim: Structure every direct response script in nine beats: hook, problem, promise, mechanism, objection, proof, offer, risk reversal, call to action.
body: Each beat has one job. The hook buys attention and filters for the right people; it sells nobody. The problem agitates the consequence the buyer already lives with. The promise says what they get in their terms. The mechanism gives a reason to believe the promise. The objection handles the other solutions they have tried. The proof backs the claims. The offer presents the product and what they get. The risk reversal makes the offer safe. The call to action says what to do. Blue Sense uses this order for videos and also for static ads, where the eye path replaces time. How to apply it: label each line of a draft with its beat. Missing beats (very often the promise) and beats in the wrong order (mechanism before promise, product named too early) are the first fixes. Longer ads loop the middle beats rather than adding new ones.
conditions: Direct response video, static and primary text ads selling to cold or lukewarm buyers.
fails_when: Very short formats (15 seconds) where only the hook, a problem line and a call to action fit, or pure brand films.
numbers: 9 beats

claim: The hook gathers roughly 80% of the audience but persuades almost nobody, so put most writing effort into the 57 seconds after the first 3 of a 60-second ad.
body: Blue Sense corrected its own earlier line that the hook drives 80% of performance. The better framing: the first three seconds decide who stays, but there is not enough script in that window to sell anyone. Selling happens in the problem, promise, mechanism, objection, proof and offer that follow. When preparing this masterclass they pulled 360 YouTube transcripts on writing ads and found that around 70 to 75% of the airtime was about hooks, which is why most teams over-invest there. How to apply it: when reviewing a script, spend a fixed hook budget (write three to five options) and then judge the draft on the body. A weak hook with a strong body still sells to the people who watch past it; a great hook on a product description loses the sale. The exception is a category where a strong unique mechanism can be stated in the opening line, so the hook itself starts persuading.
conditions: Video and long primary text ads on Meta meant to drive purchases from cold audiences.
fails_when: The goal is reach or recall rather than a sale, or the ad is a very short bumper where there is no body to write; then the hook is most of the ad.

claim: The most specific detail in an opening line can target, prove and cast at once, like John Carlton's one-legged golfer headline, which was proof that the method worked, not a niche callout.
body: The famous golf headline about a secret found by a one-legged golfer looks like it targets a tiny audience. It does not. The detail tells every golfer that this man had every reason to swing badly, so his success must come from the method, not from talent. That single detail carries proof, signals who the ad is for and makes the story memorable. How to apply it: when writing an opening, look for one concrete, odd detail from research (a constraint, a person, a number) that makes the result more believable because of who achieved it. Ask what the detail proves, not only who it calls out. On Meta this matters because the message is now the targeting: broad audiences are sorted by the words in the first line, and a word that does not match how the buyer would say it signals the ad is not for them.
conditions: Cold prospecting on broad targeting where the creative decides who sees and stays with the ad.
fails_when: The detail is invented or cannot be backed, or it is so odd that the main buyer reads it as not about them.

claim: To lengthen an ad, loop problem, promise, mechanism, objection and proof about three times, or walk a results timeline (7, 14, 30, 90, 180 days) as IM8 does.
body: Length mostly comes from going more unaware: long animation ads may open with an unrelated life story and not start agitating until ten seconds in, then agitate for minutes. A second method is looping the middle beats. In the hair example: agitate, promise, explain DHT, handle objections, then loop with DHT alone is not enough because you have tried DHT products, so add rosemary oil for blood flow to the root, then more objections and proof, then loop again. Blue Sense says IM8 extends ads by timelining the effect: by day 7 you feel one change, by day 14 another problem is solved, and so on to 30, 90 and 180 days, each step reopening a problem and promise. How to apply it: plan each loop around a different ingredient, problem or time milestone so it adds new information.
conditions: Long-form video (2 minutes and up) for products with several mechanisms or staged results.
fails_when: The product has only one mechanism and one result, so loops repeat and viewers drop.

claim: Turn a factory process every rival also uses into your mechanism if nobody says it; Hopkins took Schlitz from fifth to first in 1907 by naming steam-cleaned bottles.
body: Every brewer sterilised bottles with live steam, but nobody had advertised it, so the first to say it owned it. Blue Sense gives three questions to find your version: what does your factory do that you think is boring, what did you reject during formulation, and what constraint did the product force on you that you have never mentioned? Their magnesium example: most magnesium is the oxide form, which is cheap to make and largely passes through the body, while glycinate is absorbed but harder to produce, so the brand had to clear hurdle after hurdle in the factory. A process becomes a reason to believe. How to apply it: interview your manufacturer or product lead with the three questions, write down each answer as feature, then what it means for the buyer, then why it works, and test the strongest as a mechanism beat.
conditions: Physical products with real choices in sourcing, formulation or production.
fails_when: The claim implies your product is uniquely safe or effective when rivals do the same thing in a way buyers would see as misleading, or the fact is not true for your supplier.

claim: Two personas times three angles gives six concepts, and ten ads per concept gives 60 ads from one research pass, varied by script, hook swaps and format.
body: A concept is a persona (who), an angle (the value proposition and message) and an offer (what they get). Do one large, batched research pass, then file quotes under each persona and angle. Most brands can find two to three personas, larger brands more, and three to four core angles. Only pair angles with personas they fit. With a conservative two personas and three angles each, you have six concepts. Under each, make about ten ads by writing different scripts to the same person and angle, swapping hooks (worth doing because most of the audience sees only the hook) and switching formats such as animated VSL, claymation, UGC, EGC or founder story. Keeping persona, angle and research fixed while changing the script and format still produces ads Meta treats as diverse, reaching new people, without redoing research every week.
conditions: Brands that need high creative volume (tens of ads a week) on Meta.
fails_when: Spend is too low to test 60 ads properly; then fewer concepts with fewer ads each is better than spreading thin.

claim: Use support tickets and return reasons to find which claims the product fails on, and drop any angle with a high return rate (50% in their example) even if its ROAS looks great.
body: Unhappy customers tell you where the product does not deliver. A makeup brand might promise glow, acne cover and long wear, and nail all but one. If ads push the one claim the product misses, buyers return it. Blue Sense's rule: no matter how strong the return on ad spend looks in Ads Manager, an angle that drives something like a 50% return rate is not a winner, because the refunds, shipping and lost product wipe out the margin the ROAS figure shows. How to apply it: tag tickets and return reasons by the claim the customer expected, then join that to which ad or landing page they came from (UTM or post-purchase survey). Rank angles by net revenue after returns, not by platform ROAS, and stop scaling any angle whose buyers return far above your store average.
conditions: Products with several claimed benefits and measurable returns (beauty, apparel, gadgets, supplements with guarantees).
fails_when: Low return categories or one-claim products, or when returns cannot be linked back to the ad angle; then you are guessing.
numbers: 50% return rate on one angle as the example to kill

claim: What makes an ad look like an ad is marketing language, not production quality; lowering the resolution of a polished ad does not make it feel native.
body: Halbert described people sorting mail into two piles: obvious advertising, which goes in the bin, and what looks like a personal letter, which gets read. Video hooks get sorted the same way. Brand teams often reject native hooks because they think it means low-fi UGC they will not sign off. Blue Sense's answer is that fidelity is not the main signal. Lowering the quality of a polished ad still reads as an ad. The giveaway is the language: launch announcements, slogans and benefit lists. How to apply it: keep the brand's production standard if you must, but rewrite the opening words to sound like a person talking or writing to a friend. Native visuals help further when the brand allows them.
conditions: Brands whose guidelines restrict lo-fi or creator content.
fails_when: Placements where polished creative is the norm and expected, such as some catalogue or Advantage+ shopping slots driven by product images.

claim: Write each ad length as its own script; cutting a six-minute ad down to two minutes in the edit usually produces a weak ad because the bridges no longer fit.
body: Blue Sense reversed its own earlier advice to script one long ad and have an editor cut a five-minute and a one to two minute version. The bridges, beat sizes and pacing of a long script do not survive being snipped, so the short version feels broken. Sometimes it works, but usually not. How to apply it: if you want to test lengths, write the long script, then have the writer, not the editor, rewrite a separate two-minute script with its own transitions. AI is helpful here if you tell it exactly which beats to shorten or extend.
conditions: Brands testing multiple ad lengths from one concept.

claim: Write scripts to be spoken: one idea per sentence, verb up front, no complex words, then read it aloud standing at real pace and fix every stumble, breath or cringe.
body: What to say and how it sounds are different skills. Compare a textbook line about follicular miniaturisation from dihydrotestosterone with: a hormone binds to the follicle, each cycle the hair comes back finer, then one cycle it does not come back. The second wins because it has one idea per sentence, verbs early followed by what matters, no complex words and shorter sentences. The biggest tip is to say the script out loud, not in your head. Stand up, project, and read at the speed it would be recorded. Every trip means a cut, every time you run out of breath the sentence is too long, and every line you would be embarrassed to say should be rewritten. It takes about four minutes and no software.
conditions: Any spoken script: UGC, founder, voiceover, VSL.
fails_when: Text-only ads, where reading rhythm matters but the breath test does not apply.

claim: Write the problem in the buyer's words, not the label on the pack: hair thinning becomes I can see my scalp, bloating becomes looking four months pregnant by 4pm.
body: Marketer language makes the buyer translate a category term into their own feeling, and many will not bother. Research often shows buyers avoid the category word entirely. In the hair example customers never said hair thinning; they said they could see their scalp or found hair in the drain. Bloating is too broad and too clinical; a line about looking pregnant by late afternoon is the emotional version. Joint support becomes struggling to get up off the floor without help. Creatine for muscle support asks a 55-year-old with new leg pain at the gym to make a long mental jump; speak to the leg pain directly. How to apply it: before writing, list the five most common phrases customers use for the problem in reviews and tickets, and ban the packaging term from the hook and problem beats. One wrong word can tell the buyer the ad is not for them.
conditions: Cold audience ads for products that solve a felt problem.
fails_when: Expert or professional buyers who do use the technical term (athletes, clinicians, trade buyers); match their register instead.

claim: In mid 2025 Blue Sense used AI image generation only for parts of an ad, such as a person holding the product, because full AI ads still came out with typos and products that did not match.
body: Nathan said Blue Sense was barely using end to end AI image ads, not by choice but because outputs needed too much fixing. The usual pattern was to generate one element, such as a model holding the product or a new background, then add the text and product details by hand. Caden described a common cheap route: take a product photo, swap the background with AI and add text in Canva. The pipeline Nathan expects soon: the brand's guidelines, products and value propositions go into a language model that writes about 100 ad briefs; an image model makes the ads; a second model checks each one for typos and product accuracy and sends failures back to be regenerated; only passing ads reach the client, who approves or rejects each quickly, and approved ads go straight into the account. How to apply now: use AI for scenes, people and backgrounds, keep the real product image and the copy under human control, and run every AI ad through a written check before launch (spelling, price and offer, product shape, label, logo and colours). Caden adds that agencies with data from many accounts may turn it into better prompts. This is a dated snapshot: image tools have improved since, and another Blue Sense card shows a brand scaling almost entirely on AI ads.

claim: To grow at $50k to $250k a month, launch about 100 to 300 new ads a month; two campaigns of 10 ad sets each then carry a manageable 5 to 15 ads per ad set.
body: Concept testing matters most in the middle spend tier because each campaign now has enough purchases to support ad set splits, so you can judge each concept rather than the campaign as a whole. That lets the creative team aim refreshes: losing concepts get a rethink, winning concepts get more volume, and wins can direct work on landing pages, retention flows and new products. Volume is the other reason. If you want to grow in this tier, plan on roughly 100 to 300 new ads a month. With about two campaigns and 10 ad sets each, that is 20 ad sets, or roughly 5 to 15 new ads per ad set a month, which is easy to manage. If you do not plan to grow, you do not need that many. How to apply: set a monthly ad launch target from your tier, name each ad set by concept, and review concept results with the creative team before briefing the next batch.
conditions: Brands spending roughly $50k to $250k a month on Meta with growth targets.
fails_when: The brand is holding spend flat, or creative production cannot keep up, in which case fewer, stronger concepts beat volume.

claim: When a concept wins, build the whole funnel around it: a named bundle, its own landing page and a matched retention flow, which Blue Sense says can scale that concept 2x to 3x.
body: A concept is a persona, an angle and an offer combined, tested as one ad set. Teeth whitening example: coffee drinkers who want whitening without sensitivity; brides who want white teeth in 14 days for the wedding; smokers who need ongoing stain removal on a subscription, told through a founder who smokes. The payoff comes after a win. If the bride concept takes off, make much more creative for it, spin the offer into a named 14-day wedding bundle, give it a landing page full of bride testimonials, and keep continuity from ad to page. Then extend it into retention: a post-wedding flow with a thank-you gift and an offer that moves buyers into a product line suited to their new stage of life. Concept-level reads also tell you who your customers are, for example 40% smokers and 40% brides, which can steer product range and the wider business. Keep concepts too broad and you lose this persona insight.
conditions: Brands with enough spend to test several concepts at once and the ability to build pages and bundles quickly.

claim: Over BFCM 2025, Blue Sense's 8 and 9 figure clients grew 58% against 40% for the whole portfolio, and those clients were getting 300 to 400 new Meta ads a month.
body: Nathan linked the gap between big and small clients to creative volume. Since Meta's Andromeda change, the platform rewards a large, varied set of ads, and the biggest clients could fund 300 to 400 new ads a month. Smaller clients could not pay for that output, or even for the time to upload it: putting 400 ads into an account is a full time job on its own. Meta was the main growth channel for most of the portfolio over Black Friday, so the volume gap showed up in results. At the same time, most brands he talks to, including big spenders, have never launched more than about 10 ads a month, and Austin met brands spending $30,000 a month on Meta that did not know about the shift. Both see a short window where brands that move to high volume, diverse testing gain before everyone catches up. Another Blue Sense card gives a rule of about one new ad per $1,000 of monthly Meta spend; this video adds the top end of 300 to 400 a month at 8 and 9 figure brands. How to check yours: in Ads Manager, count ads created in the last 30 days and set that against monthly spend. If you spend $30,000 or more and launch under 10 a month, creative volume is your first lever, ahead of any change to campaign structure. Budget for production and for upload time. Count distinct ideas, not just variants of one ad.
conditions: Brands with Meta as a main growth channel, after the 2025 Andromeda change; the 300 to 400 figure applies to 8 and 9 figure revenue brands.
fails_when: It is a correlation in one portfolio, not a controlled test; volume made of near identical variants adds little; small brands cannot fund this output and should focus on fewer, better native ads.

claim: A hook's first job is to attract the right buyer, not just stop the scroll; Meta learns from who keeps watching, so meme or bait openers pull in the wrong people and wreck conversion.
body: Blue Sense believes Meta still leans on soft signals, such as who watches through half the video, even after an ad set passes about 50 conversions and should be learning from purchases. So whoever your hook attracts is who Meta goes looking for next. A meme opener or a random fact that cuts to a product trains delivery toward people who like memes. The host was served a viral snow removal video that opened like a science reel; he lives in Australia and has no snow to clear. On organic that can be fine, because reach is free and a few leads from millions of views still cost nothing. On paid, buying millions of views can cost around half a million dollars, so a hook that does not filter for buyers burns money. Rule: whoever is on screen and whatever is said in the first seconds must match your buyer and lead into what you sell. Gaming and a few niches are the exceptions.
conditions: Paid video on Meta and TikTok for most product categories.
fails_when: Gaming and some entertainment niches where meme openers match the buyer; organic posts where reach is free.

claim: Do not show or name the product in the first seconds of a cold video ad; an electrolyte ad opening on powder poured into a bottle, with the brand named in line one, fails every hook test.
body: The weak example: a creator says he just finished a workout and has to talk about the brand, while the visual is the powder going into a bottle. Viewers know at once it is an ad, the visual is dull, and there is no problem to care about. Blue Sense's rewrite turns the persona and problem template into a story: if your workouts keep getting shorter, you probably tried testosterone boosters or eating more and still lost drive; then the reveal that it was dehydration, with a short lesson on the sodium and magnesium balance and muscle force; then the other electrolyte powders he tried lacked enough sodium; only then the product, the result (back to long sessions three or four times a week) and a partner discount as the call to action. For the hook visual, skip the product shot: an iPhone talking head works, or B-roll of feeling flat in the gym.
conditions: Cold video ads for consumables and supplements.
fails_when: Retargeting, where naming the product early is right; products striking enough to be the hook themselves.

claim: Most good ads die at the bridges: move from hook into education, not a pitch, let product awareness rise slowly, and script the turn from body to call to action as carefully as the hook.
body: Picture product awareness, how clearly the viewer knows they are being sold to, plotted against time. It should sit near zero through the hook and creep up until the call to action. Most ads instead show steps: a jump at the bridge from hook to body when the product appears, and another jump into the call to action. Each jump is where viewers drop off. Blue Sense says the bridge is the most common mistake even among people who make good ads. A useful pattern from a hydration creator: mention the product briefly, then go straight back to teaching, then bring it in again, so awareness bumps up a little and settles and the viewer stays because they are still learning. The second bridge matters as much: an ad can have a strong hook and body and still flop because it lurches into buy now with no reason. Check the retention graph for drops at these two points and rewrite those first.
conditions: Video ads with a hook, body and call to action, especially for cold audiences.
fails_when: Very short ads under about 10 seconds and statics, which work differently; retargeting ads that should sell from the start.

claim: One spoken hook can become 20 to 30 hooks by changing visuals and overlays: cut from the talking creator to a supermarket haul of rival packs and back to a whiteboard, or an AI clip of jerky snapping like cardboard.
body: Copy is only one layer. If a jerky brand just has a creator say the taste-test line to camera, it will likely do worse than the same line with a cut at about one second to someone sweeping every jerky off a supermarket shelf and through the checkout, then back to the creator holding a whiteboard ready to list the two problems. The visual makes the line believable and keeps the eye busy. Other ideas Blue Sense floats: a one to two second AI clip of jerky cracking like dry cardboard, a slow pan across rival ingredient lists, or rival packs dropped in a bin. Keep the pace quick and the visual tied to the words. How to apply: for each hook line, plan three to five visuals and two to three overlays, then combine them. That turns one scripted line into a batch of 20 to 30 distinct hooks, and it is why a line that failed with one visual should not be written off.
conditions: Video ads with a fixed body where hooks can be swapped.
fails_when: Visuals that mock named competitors can breach comparative advertising rules; AI clips must not mislead about the product.

claim: Rewrite product hooks into a lesson the viewer wants, such as a quick label check to spot sugary protein snacks before buying jerky, so the ad opens as education and never feels like an ad.
body: Blue Sense rewrote the weak jerky hook three ways, each based on a hook type. A problem statement: most jerky is either dry like cardboard or full of junk ingredients, and this brand fixed both. A confrontation: if your protein snacks are basically sugar, stop, and learn the quick label check. A curiosity gap: the team tried the top-selling jerkies and kept finding the same pair of flaws. None of them sells the product or reveals that this is an ad. Each promises the viewer something useful, how to spot sugar in a snack or which flaws to look for, and earns the right to show the product later as the answer. The value points from the original ad (grass-fed beef, no processed ingredients, a few herbs) then become proof in the body rather than the opener. How to apply: for each product claim, ask what the buyer would want to learn that makes the claim matter, and open on that lesson.
conditions: Food, supplements, beauty and other categories where buyers compare labels or ingredients.
fails_when: Impulse or visual products where a demo is faster than a lesson; retargeting ads, where the product can lead.

claim: Score hooks out of 10 on clarity, relevance and novelty first, with specificity and credibility as second-tier bonuses; a wordless audio hook for jerky scored low because strangers could not tell what it was or who it was for.
body: Clarity: could a stranger say what this is about after three seconds? Relevance: is the pain obviously theirs? Novelty: is there a twist, a new angle or a format no one has used? Specificity: numbers, time frames, limits. Credibility: proof or a reason to believe. Blue Sense ranks them in that order. Specificity and credibility are hard to fit into three or four seconds, so treat them as extras; the easiest credibility is visual, such as a known influencer or expert delivering an otherwise normal hook. Example: a jerky ad opens with an unboxing sound and no words. It creates curiosity and has some novelty, but it fails clarity and relevance, so everyone watches, including vegetarians and people who dislike jerky, and most leave once they see the product. How to apply: score each draft hook on all five, and rewrite any that score low on clarity or relevance before worrying about the rest.
conditions: Reviewing hooks before production or diagnosing a weak hook rate.
fails_when: Pure brand awareness pieces where curiosity alone is the goal; very visual products where the product itself makes the hook clear.

claim: Start with the Persona, Problem, Pattern interrupt, Promise hook template, keep the speaker believable for that persona, then move beyond templates once you can write hooks from scratch.
body: The template: say who it is for, hit their problem within about two seconds, break the pattern so people do not swipe once they sense an ad, then promise what they get if they keep watching. A spoken version runs: if you are this person with this pain, you are probably doing the usual thing, which is why the result is poor, and here is the better way. It also suits YouTube openings. Two rules. Continuity: the person speaking must fit the persona; a 50-year-old mum addressing 20-year-old men breaks trust. And templates are a starting point only: everyone uses them, so your ads start to look like everyone else's. To scale, learn to write from scratch and find openings rivals are not using. If you are stuck, give an LLM the template line plus your site, product and buyer context to draft first versions, then edit hard.
conditions: Teams new to hook writing, or any brand needing fast first drafts.
fails_when: Saturated categories where template hooks all sound alike; problem-led openers often beat persona callouts, so test both.
numbers: problem within about 2 seconds

claim: Treat every hook as three layers, the visual, the audio or script, and the on-screen text; changing only the overlay to a bolder line like 'this transformed my life' can double hook rate and results.
body: Most people think of the hook as the opening image. It is three things that can each be changed: what is on screen (camera movement, a fast cut, a surprising action), what is heard (the spoken line and any sound), and the copy on the creative (a headline overlay or styled captions on video, the text on a static). A hook that is doing fine can jump when one layer improves. Blue Sense's example is adding an exaggerated overlay line over the same footage, which doubled hook rate and the ad's results. The overlay can also reframe the product toward a different pain for a different pool, for example an electrolyte ad framed around getting stronger, because the viewer stops feeling too tired to train. Check health and claims rules before going that far. How to apply: for each winning body, list options for each of the three layers and combine them, rather than only reshooting the opening line.
conditions: Video and static ads on Meta, TikTok and Reels.
fails_when: Overlays that make claims the product cannot support breach ad policy and consumer law, especially in health and supplements.

claim: Use a small, specific number in the hook (the same two problems in almost every rival); a vague 'problems' reads as a sales line, while 'two' signals a short, concrete payoff worth staying for.
body: In Blue Sense's rewrite, the word two does a lot of work. Saying a product category has a bunch of problems sounds like the setup for a pitch and gives no reason to stay. Saying there are exactly two tells the viewer the answer is short and specific, and that the speaker actually tested something. That makes people more willing to watch to the end, and the host expects a better hook rate from it. The same idea applies to time frames and outcomes: a three-second label check, a result in 90 days. Pair the number with a visual that proves the effort: a fast pan across 10 to 20 jerky packs on a shelf, then a whiteboard with one and two waiting to be filled in. How to apply: go through your current hooks and replace vague words like many, lots or some with the real, small count or time frame.
conditions: Hooks that promise information, comparisons or results.
fails_when: When the number is invented or cannot be backed up; large numbers that make the payoff sound long.

claim: As a simple creative volume rule, launch one new ad for every $1,000 of monthly Meta spend ($100,000 a month means about 100 new ads), until returns diminish in the $1M to $3M a month range.
body: Blue Sense reads creative as three possible bottlenecks: volume, diversity or quality, and only one is the real constraint at a time. Volume is checked first because it is easiest to measure. Their shortcut is one new ad per $1,000 of monthly spend. If you spend $100,000 a month and launch 20 new ads, volume is almost certainly your problem. The rule weakens at very large scale: at $1M to $3M a month you do not need 1,000 to 3,000 new ads, because extra volume gives diminishing returns. There they switch to two models. A churn model: how many winning ads stop working each month, your hit rate, and therefore how many launches you need to replace them. And an average winner model: if a typical winner returns, say, $20,000 and you know your hit rate, work back to the volume that hits your revenue target. If volume is on track, move on to whether the ads differ enough in concept, then to quality.
conditions: Meta accounts from roughly $20,000 to $1M a month in spend with a working creative pipeline.
fails_when: Very large accounts (multi-million a month) where the per-$1,000 rule overshoots, or tiny accounts where each new ad cannot get enough spend to be judged.

claim: Concepts needed by Meta spend: under $100k a month test one to three; $100k to $500k needs two winners with two to six in test; above $500k, three or more winners.
body: Diversity here means concepts, not formats. A concept is a distinct mix of angle, offer and persona. Example: a creatine brand spending $200,000 a month and launching 200 ads a month looks healthy on volume, but if every ad sells the same bundle to men 25 to 45 on gym performance, it keeps hitting the same people and fatigues. Their spend bands: below $100,000 a month, one working concept can carry you to $100,000, so you need one to three concepts, tested properly with enough volume each, until one wins. From $100,000 to $500,000 a month, you want two winning concepts live while testing two to six. Above $500,000 you usually need three or more winners and four to five core funnels working at once, unless you sell into the US or worldwide where two strong concepts can be pushed hard. In fashion, concepts are usually different products or categories; in CPG they are different reframes of the same product. Brands over-index on new formats and under-index on new concepts.
conditions: Meta-led DTC brands; the bands come from Blue Sense's portfolio of mostly Australian and US brands.
fails_when: Brands in huge markets (US, global) that can scale one or two concepts further, or brands below about $20,000 a month that should focus on finding one winner first.

$100k to $500k/month: 2 winning concepts, 2 to 6 in test
over $500k/month: 3+ winners, 4 to 5 core funnels

claim: A second ad library test is how often ads frame a problem: Alo Yoga 0%, Hostage Tape 33%, Resilia 18%, and Smooch almost every ad, which marks brands that win cold buyers on Meta.
body: Cold buyers on Meta do not know you, so an ad has to give them a reason to care before it shows the product, and naming a problem they feel is the most reliable reason. Aspirational brand ads skip this because their demand comes from elsewhere. Blue Sense tagged ads for whether they framed or agitated a problem: Alo Yoga had none, True Classic very few, Hostage Tape 33%, Resilia 18% and Smooch nearly all. Examples of problem framing that worked: a mouth tape ad opening on one in three couples sleeping apart because of snoring, which talks about sleep divorce long before the product appears; a shirt ad built on a fit worry (tight on the arms, loose on the middle). How to apply: score your live ads and a competitor's on two columns, needs brand knowledge (yes or no) and frames a problem (yes or no). A Meta-first brand should have many ads in the second column and few in the first. If yours is the reverse, brief new concepts that open on the buyer's problem, show it in the visual too, and delay the product reveal.
conditions: Products that solve a felt problem (sleep, skin, fit, health) sold mainly through Meta to cold audiences.
fails_when: Pure fashion or identity products with no real problem to name, where desire and status drive purchase and problem framing would feel forced.

claim: A strong cold UGC script runs persona callout hook, problem, product, promise, then mechanism, before and after, objections, identity payoff and offer; putting the promise before the mechanism keeps people watching.
body: Blue Sense broke down a Smooch eyebrow serum ad that had run for months. The hook names a shared past (people who over-plucked their brows in the 90s), which calls out an age group without saying an age, so the right buyer feels seen. The order that follows is the lesson: a short problem story (patchy brows, pencils and gels that did nothing), the product introduced, a clear promise, then the mechanism and ingredients, a dated before and after (week 4 baby hairs, week 8 fuller brows), objections handled (no irritation, no flaking, gentle for daily use), an identity payoff (brows that look like brows again), and finally the offer (buy one, get one free). How to apply: map your best ads to these beats and look for missing ones. Make the promise before you explain how it works, so viewers have a reason to stay for the mechanism. Use a cultural or generational detail in the hook to target an age group. Keep talking-head UGC moving with frequent cuts. End on a clear offer and call to action, not a vague line.
conditions: Problem-solving products (beauty, health, personal care) sold with UGC or creator video to cold Meta audiences.
fails_when: Impulse or visual products where a short demo outperforms a story; markets or categories where before and after claims break ad policy.

claim: All three fast scalers run alternative ads that name what the buyer uses now, show why it fails and offer the switch; these hit warm, category-aware buyers and perform very well.
body: A buyer who already uses a rival product has the problem, knows the category and has money in it, so you only need to win the switch. Every brand in the video does this. Hostage Tape opens on cheap surgical tape that will not stay on through the night and needs three strips. Smooch opens on rival colour-changing foundations that turn orange, and a negative hook (I stopped doing brow lamination). Resilia attacks weak, under-dosed oregano oil sold on marketplaces. Blue Sense notes these are often paired with negative or objection hooks, such as a man coughing to show what people fear mouth tape does, then answering it. How to apply: list the 3 to 5 things your buyer uses instead of you (a rival brand type, a cheap fix, a service, doing nothing). For each, write the specific way it lets them down in their words and a demo that shows yours does not. Avoid naming competitors in ways that break ad policy or comparative advertising law; a category description is usually enough.

fails_when: Brand new categories with no alternative to compare against; claims of superiority you cannot back up.

claim: At hundreds or thousands of live ads, claims start to contradict each other; scrape and transcribe your ads with AI and check the set for clashing statements.
body: When creative volume gets high, different writers and editors make claims that clash. Blue Sense found Hostage Tape running one ad saying it sold out after Joe Rogan mentioned it and another saying it over-ordered and the warehouse was full. A buyer who sees both stops trusting either. Short ads cannot carry enough context to reconcile two stories, so the fix is upstream. How to apply: on a regular cycle (monthly, or at each big launch), export or scrape your live ads, transcribe the videos and on-screen text with an AI tool, and ask it to list every factual claim: stock status, sales counts, prices, guarantees, results and timelines, ingredients. Flag pairs that conflict and claims that conflict with your site or terms. Keep a short approved claims list that scriptwriters must use, and retire ads that break it. This also helps with compliance on health or results claims.
conditions: Accounts with large creative volume, many creators or editors, or several pages and partner ads running at once.
fails_when: Small accounts with a handful of ads that one person writes and reviews.

claim: Before copying a brand's Meta ads, count the share whose hook only works if you already know the brand; Alo Yoga was 96%, while Meta-built brands ran 3% to 18%.
body: A brand whose hooks lean on brand recognition is using Meta to collect demand that other channels created, so its ads are a poor model for a store that needs Meta to find new buyers. Blue Sense counted live US ads one by one. Alo Yoga had 699 live ads; 96% only made sense to someone who already knew Alo, 696 used Shop Now, and none mentioned a price, a discount or a problem. True Classic, which says it puts most of its spend on Meta, sat at 38%. Fast-scaling Meta-first brands were far lower: Smooch 18%, Hostage Tape 7%, Resilia 3%. How to apply: open the Meta Ad Library for the brand you want to copy, pull 30 to 50 live ads, and tag each hook: does it need prior knowledge of the brand or product (brand or product aware), or does it start from a person, problem or desire? If more than about a third need the brand, treat that library as retargeting and look elsewhere for acquisition ideas. Run the same count on your own account; a high share means your ads are built for warm people and will struggle to scale cold.

fails_when: You already have strong demand from other channels (search, retail, creators, PR) and Meta's job really is retargeting; then brand-aware hooks are the right fit.

claim: Before launching a Meta-first brand, check how many distinct angles the category allows; mouth tape has a fixed few, which caps creative diversity, while supplements support endless angles and funnels.
body: Meta scaling now depends on a steady flow of genuinely different concepts. A product that can only be sold from a few angles runs out of new concepts and fatigues. Blue Sense says this is why it would not launch a mouth tape brand: Hostage Tape is limited to snoring, sleep quality, mouth breathing and a handful of others, so it leans on celebrities and persona variants to get variety. Resilia's supplements can be pitched against many problems (its own framing is one mechanism, five problems) and fed into different funnels. How to apply: when picking or adding a product, list every distinct problem, desire, persona and alternative it can be sold against. Aim for at least 10 to 15 angles a different person would care about; if you only find three or four, plan for higher creative cost per new concept or a channel other than Meta. For existing products with few angles, widen through personas, offers and formats.
conditions: Choosing a product or category for a brand that will rely mainly on Meta ads.
fails_when: Brands with strong non-Meta demand (retail, search, community) where creative range matters less; narrow products with huge single-angle demand.

claim: Keep product-led, organic-looking demos in the account even though they rarely scale, because viewers coming off polished or AI ads need proof the product is real and used by real people.
body: Not every ad has to be a big spender. Smooch runs short, product-focused UGC (a two-minute routine for busy mums, TikTok Shop style clips) that Blue Sense does not expect to carry large budgets, alongside its long story ads. Their role is funnel diversity: someone who watched an animated or AI ad needs to see a believable person using the real product before they buy. What makes these work is that they feel unscripted. One strong example is shot like an organic post, with on-screen text and no captions, filmed without edits to build trust, showing coverage of acne and redness in about 30 seconds and a neck match test, plus an us versus them jab at rival formulas that turn orange. How to apply: brief a steady stream of low-cost creator demos with real application, before and after in one take, and objection checks (does it crease, does it match). Coach creators to speak naturally rather than read lines; if it looks scripted, it loses the point. Judge these ads on blended results and assisted conversions, not on whether they win big budgets.
conditions: Accounts already running polished, animated or AI-made ads for prospecting, in categories where seeing the product work matters.
fails_when: Accounts with very few ads and tight budgets, where every slot must be a scaling candidate; categories where demos cannot show the benefit (supplements, long-term results).

claim: Match the proof to how risky your claims are: no risky claims, use creator demos; big claims, use experts; no claims but a borrowed-trust category, use celebrities or founders.
body: Each of the three brands picks its main form of proof to fit what it says about the product. Smooch makes few risky claims, so creator demos showing the product working are enough. Resilia makes strong health claims, so it puts them in the mouths of experts and storytelling authority. Hostage Tape makes almost no claims, so it borrows trust from celebrities and founders the same way another brand would use a doctor. The common thread is that proof has to answer the doubt your message creates: a visual promise needs seeing, a medical promise needs someone qualified, a lifestyle product needs someone admired. How to apply: write down the boldest thing your ads say. If a buyer could check it with their eyes, invest in demos and before and afters. If it needs knowledge, use a qualified expert (real and credentialed). If there is no claim, use admired people your persona follows. Avoid making claims you cannot prove just because experts would make them sound credible.

claim: Meta-first brands scaling to $10M to $30M a month keep one core persona and mechanism fixed and get diversity from sub-personas and angles, at thousands of live ads across many pages.

Smooch keeps the same buyer (women over 40) and the same mechanism (a colour-changing foundation) in every ad, then spreads across sub-personas: busy mums with two minutes, women burned by formulas that turn orange, women who think foundation stopped working for them at 52. It had 400+ ads on its main page, had hit the page cap, and was running more through other pages, partnership ads and third-party editorial funnels, likely 4,000 to 5,000 live ads in all. Resilia had about 3,000 live ads across 37 pages. The key is that the volume is real variety: different people, angles and personas, not small edits of one ad. How to apply: write the core persona and mechanism down and never change them in ads. List sub-personas and angles under it and brief new concepts against each. Only split into many sub-personas once your volume allows testing them; at low volume, stay on the core persona. When one page fills up, add pages, partnership ads or editorial funnels to keep volume flowing.

claim: To study a competitor's winners, pull only ads live for at least 60 days, and treat several versions of one angle as a sign it is scaling, but beware libraries where every start date looks recent.

Ads a brand keeps running for two months or more are almost certainly paying for themselves, because fast-moving Meta buyers switch off losers within days. When a brand runs two or more cuts of the same angle or talent, it usually means the first one worked and they are trying to scale it. How to apply: in the Ad Library, filter to active ads and sort or scan by start date; collect about 10 ads that have run 60+ days. Download the videos, transcribe them and break each into hook, persona callout, problem, mechanism, proof, offer and call to action. Mark angles that appear in several formats. When that happens, do not treat start date as a winner signal; lean on repeated angles instead.

claim: Write bottom-funnel offer ads that also carry value points and objection handling, so if a cold viewer gets past the hook the ad can still convert and scale beyond retargeting.
body: Pure offer ads (timer, percent off, ends today) are easy volume for warm buyers, but they cannot hold much spend because cold people have no reason to care about the discount. Smooch's fix is to start with the offer or a punchy negative hook, then back into the product's benefits and the common objections. Examples from the video: an apology to the thousands who bought yesterday because a bigger discount just dropped, followed by value points; a fake complaint hook (I have to return it) that turns into a list of ingredients and benefits, then the sale. Blue Sense notes a negative hook sometimes earns a good hook and hold rate with cold viewers; when it does not, the ad still lands on warm buyers and converts them because the reasoning is there. How to apply: for each offer ad, add 2 to 4 lines of mechanism or benefit and 1 to 2 objection answers after the opening. Keep the most simple offer-only cuts for retargeting volume, but do not expect them to hold large budgets. Trim duplicated lines (one Smooch ad repeated its hook by accident).

fails_when: Brands that avoid discounting for positioning reasons; fake apology or fake return framings can break consumer law or Meta policy in some markets if the claims are untrue.

claim: A founder ad needs no audience: one of the best founder ads Blue Sense has seen came from a founder with zero followers, used purely as paid distribution to cold audiences.
body: A common objection is that founder ads are a personal branding exercise, chasing followers and views apart from the brand itself. Blue Sense says that is the wrong frame. The founder in the ad is a vehicle for trust and authenticity while the script tells the brand's story to cold audiences through paid placement, not organic posting. One of the strongest founder ads they have seen from a client featured a founder with no following and a name few people knew. Buyers learn who the founder is only because they met them in the ad. The script should keep a clear line between the person and the product: people buy because of the problem, the mechanism and the proof, not because they are fans of the founder. How to apply: do not wait to build a following before running founder ads, and do not write scripts that depend on knowing who the founder is; brief them like any cold acquisition ad with the founder as narrator.

Blue Sense reframes the job: you are presenting the argument only the founder can make. A founder on camera does bring three advantages. Authenticity, because a real person stands behind the brand at a time when feeds are filling with AI creative. Authority, without celebrities or a pile of reviews, which grows with the founder's profile. Trust, because someone is putting their reputation on the line. But Blue Sense warns that stopping there produces ads that do not perform. The script still needs a hook, a problem the viewer recognises, a mechanism, proof and a call to action; the founder is the most credible messenger for parts of that script, not a replacement for it. How to apply: write the founder ad as a direct response script first, then mark which lines gain credibility because the founder says them.

claim: A strong founder-led pattern: a negative hook (a public apology for having lied), the product visibly working within 3 seconds, and an underdog story of small founders against big, chemical-heavy brands.
body: Blue Sense breaks down a dishwashing sheet ad from an Australian brand run by two brothers. The hook is negative and fast paced: an apology to past buyers for having lied, which grabs attention and does not feel like an ad. Within the first three seconds the product is shown cleaning well, so the hook is paid off with proof immediately. The brothers are the face of all the brand's marketing, which builds trust because they visibly put their own reputation on the line. And they lean into an underdog story: a couple of Queensland brothers taking on the giants who sell bleach and harsh chemicals. Nathan points out that almost any small business can use the underdog position; it only takes putting the founders' story and narrative into the brand positioning and creative. How to apply: test a negative or confessional hook that resolves into a benefit, show the product's result in the opening seconds for categories where results are visible, and frame the brand as the small challenger if it is true.
