claim: Build founder scripts on the three claims only a founder can credibly make: why the business started, why the mechanism works, and what was wrong with competitors' products they tested; product experience is better from customers.
body: Every guide says the founder's story is the moat, but Blue Sense breaks it into parts. Origin: why the business exists, a claim only the founder can make with full credibility, such as building it because an industry was misleading people. Mechanism: why this solution works, which carries weight from the founder (who spent time and money developing it) or a credentialed expert, much more than from a UGC creator. Adversarial: we bought and tested the competitors and they failed for these reasons. Founders of smaller brands are usually willing to take that swing, which gives an edge most brands avoid for legal and compliance reasons; keep it factual. The fourth common element, how the product feels to use, is not a moat. Anyone can say it, and from the founder it is less credible because they are biased. Viewers want to hear from people like themselves with their problem, which is where diverse customer and persona content belongs. How to apply: draft each founder script with an origin line, a mechanism line and an adversarial line, and move experience claims to testimonial ads.
conditions: Founder-led brands with a real origin story and a product difference they can explain.
fails_when: Adversarial claims that cannot be substantiated or that name competitors in ways that invite legal action; regulated categories where comparison claims need proof.

claim: Change the founder's role to diversify scripts: protagonist (I built this), witness (relaying a customer email), interviewer (asking the lab or team why) or reader (reading out and answering a one-star review).
body: Almost all founder ads cast the founder as the protagonist telling what they did. Blue Sense suggests three other roles, each a different script shape. Witness: the founder relays something that happened to someone else, such as a customer email. Interviewer: the founder asks a team member, a lab tester, someone in manufacturing, design or buying why a decision was made, and the answer carries the mechanism and proof. Reader: the founder reads out a review, even a one-star one, and responds, with the review and reply scripted (or a real review chosen) to walk the viewer through the stages of awareness. These roles give more concept and script diversity than another protagonist ad. They are most useful for six and seven figure brands that want to make most content themselves rather than pay creators. For eight to ten figure brands, where the founder's time is scarce, many of these formats work about as well with non-founders, so save the founder for the highest-leverage scripts.
conditions: Founder-led brands making their own content, especially from six to low eight figures.
fails_when: Large brands where founder time is the constraint; or fake reviews and emails presented as real, which is deceptive.

claim: Founder ads are cheap to make and let a commoditised product stand apart through the founder's own story, but a $200M brand does not need them to grow, and one ad holding big spend can complicate an exit.
body: From a business view, founder content costs only the founder's time, which matters for smaller brands that cannot fund agencies, freelancers or creators. It also creates differentiation that works almost like a unique mechanism. In a crowded category such as electrolytes, where anyone can launch and every brand argues the same ingredient story, a founder who was a professional marathon runner, suffered from dehydration, found every product lacking and made their own speaks to a precise persona and problem that rivals cannot copy. For large brands the advice is softer: a $200M fashion brand does not need the founder on camera to reach $300M because it is unlikely to be the bottleneck, yet good founder content will still lift performance. The one real downside Blue Sense names is exit risk: if a single founder-led ad carries much of the spend, buyers may flag the dependence in a term sheet. How to apply: use founder ads freely, but keep enough non-founder creative winning that the business does not rely on one face.

claim: Founder ads need not show the founder: work down a ladder of face, voice only, founder evidence, a proxy (employee, dietitian or supplier), then founder absent via animation, to vary format with the same script.
body: A camera-facing founder is the top of the pyramid, but Blue Sense uses the whole range. Voice: the founder narrates over B-roll, animation or UGC creators, useful for founders uneasy on camera. Evidence: photos or clips of the founder in the lab, with certificates, or walking through the factory facing away from the camera, so they stay private but still prove the mechanism. Proxy: an employee, a dietitian or other credible expert, or even the supplier tells the founder's story; less effective than the founder but workable. Absent: no face, voice, evidence or proxy at all, with the same story shown as an AI animation or claymation journey through the problem, the factory and the mechanism. Animation can show things a camera cannot, such as cells changing as the mechanism works. Each rung counts as a different format, so you get format diversity while keeping a concept that already works. How to apply: take your best founder script and brief it at three or four of these levels before writing anything new.
conditions: Brands with a working founder story and a founder with limited time or willingness to appear.
fails_when: Proxy or animated versions that drift from the facts of the real story, or animated health visuals that imply results the product cannot deliver.

claim: In founder ads, the offer is the easiest concept element to vary (a story per product), the angle is harder, and the persona hardest; reach new personas by retelling a true story through someone else in your life.
body: Concept diversity means changing the persona addressed, the angle (the core reason to buy) or the offer (what is being sold). With founders the offer is easiest: each product gets its own origin story, such as why a new product was made and what the factory visit revealed. The angle is harder if there is only one real reason the product beats rivals. Persona is hardest, because much of why a persona responds is who appears on screen; a 65-year-old male founder selling clothes to women aged 20 to 40 cannot easily wear them or speak to why. Blue Sense's way round it: re-angle a true story. A 30-year-old founder of creatine gummies started because he disliked chalky powder; another version tells how his mother would not take creatine powder but loved the gummies, which led to flavours she liked and a push to reach older women who rarely take creatine. Same founder, new persona and angle, still true. They are blunt that inventing a founder story is black hat: the point is a true story told through a proven script.

Story also helps; he says weaving a story into an ad has always made it perform better in his experience, founder story or not. His criticisms are worth applying to any story ad. First, the product appears in the opening two to three seconds, which tells the viewer instantly they are being sold to. Second, the edit keeps cutting from the speaker to product shots, so every few seconds the viewer is reminded it is an ad, and some B-roll even shows his mouth out of sync with the audio. claim: Low-fi footage does not damage a premium brand if the product is not in it; open low-fi on the problem (rivals' mouldy, porous brushes), then switch to high-end product shots to build contrast.

It then tells how the team bought every top-rated toothbrush, used them for months and found porous plastic and charging bases growing mould. For a long stretch the product is not shown; the ad only agitates the problem with rough, lower quality footage of competitors' brushes. Then it reveals the product in polished, high-end shots: aircraft-grade aluminium, 14 motor frequencies tested to land on 32,000 vibrations a minute, a wall mount and a 60-day battery. Nathan's point: people worry that low-fi content cheapens the brand, but that only happens if the product appears in the low-fi footage. Keeping the product out of it means you are not building a cheap association; you are building contrast, so the premium shots look better next to the grimy alternatives. How to apply: use scrappy, native-feeling footage for the hook and problem, and save brand-standard visuals for the product reveal.

claim: Nobody cares about the founder: a founder story converts only when told through the viewer's own problem (for example a lifetime of makeup-triggered acne), so they think 'this is me' and keep watching.
body: Nathan calls this the most important part of the masterclass. Everyone has a story, so a founder narrating theirs means little to a stranger. Some pure-story ads do work, but most do not. The ones that convert pick a story the target viewer has lived. If the founder says makeup has caused acne and flare-ups all their life, a large group of viewers has had exactly that, so they watch out of recognition, not interest in the founder. From there the script runs a familiar path: keep agitating the shared problem so the viewer stays, open a curiosity gap that a solution exists, walk through the mechanism, then close that gap at the end. That is how a founder ad speaks to an existing desire rather than asking for attention. Teardowns later in the video show the failure mode: an ad that reopens a curiosity gap and never closes it, or a CTA that hints at a reveal that never comes, leaves viewers confused. How to apply: rewrite the opening of each founder script from the viewer's experience, then check every question you open is answered before the end.
conditions: Story-led ads for problem-solving products where many buyers share the founder's experience.

claim: Place most ads in the unaware, problem aware and solution aware stages and only about 20% in product and most aware; an account made only of bottom-funnel or personal-brand ads will not scale.
body: Two teardowns make the point. A skincare founder ad opens with compliments, testimonials and the oils in the product. It introduces the product immediately with no problem or education, so it only works on people already product aware. That is fine as a bottom-of-funnel ad pushing near-buyers over the line, but it is wrong to put a quarter of a million dollars behind it in a cold campaign. The Bryan Johnson Blueprint ad library is worse as a whole: every ad leans on his personal brand and talks about taste, the dose of each ingredient and how much cheaper it is than buying the pills separately. Those are objection handlers for someone about to buy, not reasons for a cold viewer who does not know him or the product to care. Having a few ads like that is fine; an entire library of them only harvests his existing audience and will struggle to scale. Rule: map each ad to one of the five awareness stages and keep roughly 80% in stages one to three.

claim: Prepare 10 hooks and 3 distinct bodies to get 30 founder ads from about 5 minutes of recording; Blue Sense says one or two hours of founder time can yield hundreds of ads lasting 3 to 4 months.
body: Blue Sense treats founder content as a production line. Write 10 different hooks and 3 bodies that tell genuinely different stories; every hook can sit on every body, so you get 30 materially different ads. Adding two CTAs would double that to 60, though they rarely bother (see the CTA card). The camera time for one set is only about four to five minutes of reading from a teleprompter or a memorised script. Nearly all the real work, which Nathan puts at 99% of performance, is in ideation, scripting and copywriting before recording starts, plus editing after. For eight and nine figure brands the scripting and editing can sit with a dedicated in-house writer or agency so the founder just turns up: a one to two hour block can produce hundreds of ads, enough for three to four months. They have clients producing 200 to 400 ads a month with a content team of one or two people. How to apply: batch scripts in advance, shoot all hooks back to back, then record bodies, and let editors assemble the combinations.
conditions: Brands with a founder available for short shoots and someone who can script and edit at volume.
fails_when: Hooks or bodies that are only light rewordings of each other, which Meta will group as the same ad; the maths only helps if the pieces truly differ.

claim: Single founder ads with their hook swaps have driven $20M to $30M for DTC brands, but brands that ride one concept decline when it fatigues; keep VSLs, statics and animation ads live alongside.
body: Measured by lifetime revenue from a single ad, the biggest ads Blue Sense has seen fall into two buckets: VSL ads (now including animation and claymation styles with similar structure) and founder ads. Including variants and hook swaps, they have seen founder ads hold whole businesses together and generate $20M to $30M. The warning comes from brands that found Blue Sense afterwards: a year of growth riding one founder ad, then the concept fatigued because everyone in the target market had seen it. Their response was to make more variants of the same concept, which could not work, instead of building other formats, so the business kept declining. When Blue Sense has a founder ad take off for a client, they do lean in and make more, but apply portfolio thinking to the whole creative mix: do not overweight one concept, and keep VSLs, statics, animation and other formats winning so the account survives when the star ad stops. How to apply: track what share of spend sits on your top concept; if it is the majority, fund other formats now, not after it fades.
conditions: Brands with one dominant winning ad or concept carrying most spend.
fails_when: Brands still searching for a first winner, where focus on the one working concept is right until it scales.

claim: Skip testing different calls to action in video ads: watch time falls off so steeply that almost nobody reaches the CTA, so test hooks and bodies instead.
body: When building hook and body combinations it is tempting to add variant CTAs to multiply volume further. Blue Sense is not a fan. Average watch time on an ad drops sharply in the first seconds and keeps falling, so only a small share of viewers ever see the final line. A CTA test therefore changes an element almost no one sees, its effect is tiny and hard to measure, and it spends budget that could test something that matters. The places that move results are the hook, which every viewer sees, and the body, which decides whether interested viewers are convinced. If you must hit a volume target, a second CTA is a cheap way to do it, but do not expect to learn much from it. How to apply: check the average watch time and retention curve for your video ads in Ads Manager; put test budget into new hooks first, then new bodies, and keep one standard CTA unless the offer itself changes.
conditions: Video ads on Meta and TikTok with typical short watch times.
fails_when: Short ads under about 10 seconds or static ads, where most viewers do see the CTA; or when the CTA carries a different offer, which is really an offer test.

claim: The best-performing structure across Blue Sense's top 15 founder ads was: a bold adversarial claim, proof of the claim, the mechanism, proof of the mechanism, then CTA with offer, scarcity and social proof.
body: To find it, Blue Sense used Claude through the Meta MCP connection across their business manager (about $400M of yearly spend), pulled every founder ad with screenshots and scripts, ranked them by total spend and performance, and distilled the common structure of the top 15. Steps: (1) Claim, usually adversarial, such as supermarket products being full of plastic, which doubles as a strong hook. (2) Proof of the claim straight away; none of the ads that made a claim without backing it performed. Example: creatine gummy brands that contain a fraction of the creatine stated, with a study to show it. (3) Mechanism, tied to the founder story: I did not do what they do, I did this. (4) Proof of the mechanism, more founder story: label comparisons, visiting the factory, third-party testing, an ingredients panel showing only meat for a clean beef jerky. (5) CTA, the offer, scarcity and urgency, plus customer social proof. A colostrum gummy ad that Blue Sense credits with about $500,000 in revenue follows this pattern: a startling cost hook, a family origin, studies as proof, then a format no one else had.
conditions: Founder-led products with a genuine difference from competitors that can be shown with evidence.
fails_when: No credible proof exists for the claim, in which case the ad reads as an attack without substance and can breach ad policy or consumer law.

claim: The founder's face is the account's strongest sameness signal; reshooting a fatigued founder ad's identical script outside the gym instead of inside pushed about $40,000 more spend through it.
body: Once a few founder ads work, brands double down and the same face, in the same seat, telling a similar story, starts to look like one ad to Meta and to viewers. It then serves to the same people and fatigues fast, especially with talking heads. Blue Sense says this is avoidable with two things: true concept diversification (see the concept card) and varied formatting. Formatting alone has unlocked a lot of spend for them. Example: the same script and edit, same B-roll, filmed once inside a gym and once out the front of it. The outdoor version revived a fatigued ad and carried roughly another $40,000 of spend. Reusing a script is fine even under Andromeda, as long as the editing or the setting is clearly different. As founder volume grows, the changes must get bigger: a completely new location or set, or a new format altogether, such as a tier list video, or the founder walking a store aisle handling competitors' products instead of sitting at home with them.
conditions: Accounts running several founder ads at meaningful spend where frequency is rising.
fails_when: Very small changes (shirt colour, camera angle) that Meta still groups as the same ad; or when the concept itself is exhausted and a new setting only delays fatigue.
numbers: scene change unlocked about $40,000 more spend on a fatigued ad

claim: Build BFCM creative across five types: offer statics, the offer overlaid on evergreen winners, creator videos, product or VSL videos, and early access or VIP ads, while keeping evergreen ads live.
body: Blue Sense's list for the sale, each with a brand it showed: 1) the offer static, a clean image that states the offer (True Classic); 2) offer-overlaid evergreen, the sale offer added to proven winners, which adds capacity fast without new shoots (Ridge); 3) creator videos (True Classic); 4) product and VSL style videos that explain the product (HexClad); 5) early access and VIP ads that build a list before launch (Alo Yoga). Dynamic product ads are a bonus layer. There is no single right sale look; Australian brands such as Country Road and Seed Heritage run very different styles. The rules around the list: offer creative is what lets spend scale during the sale; do not switch off evergreen creative, since it still converts and keeps the mix varied; and lock the offer early, because most of this cannot be made until the offer is known. How to apply: map each type to dates in your sale calendar and assign who makes each one.
conditions: Brands running a sale offer through Meta with existing evergreen winners.
fails_when: Brands that never discount, who should use early access, gifts or bundles instead; very small budgets that can only carry one or two of these types.

claim: During BFCM, judge creative on creative metrics and at ad set level instead of ad level ROAS, because last-click reporting over multi-touch delivery makes ad level ROAS even less reliable in a sale.
body: Meta optimises delivery across many touches but reports purchases close to a last-click basis, and its breakdown effect means an ad holding lots of spend can look worse at ad level than a small ad that only picks up cheap conversions. In a sale, buyers see several ads and wait for the sale to open, so ad level ROAS gets noisier still. Blue Sense says it judges this way all year, and that it matters more in BFCM, and that it should shape the campaign structure. How to apply: make budget calls from ROAS at ad set or campaign level. Judge each ad on creative signals such as hook rate (3-second views over impressions), hold rate, click-through rate, cost per click and add to cart rate. Do not switch off an ad with poor ad level ROAS while its ad set performs well. Group ads into ad sets you are willing to judge together.
conditions: Meta accounts with several ads per ad set during sale periods.
fails_when: Ad sets with a single ad, where ad set and ad level are the same; very low spend ads whose creative metrics are too noisy.
numbers: 3-second views over impressions as hook rate

claim: Plan creative volume for the long tail: in Blue Sense's data about three quarters of spend runs through ads outside the top few, and larger accounts concentrate spend even less.
body: The common belief is that a few winners take most of the budget. Blue Sense's spend data across accounts showed the reverse: around three quarters of spend went through the long tail of ads, and the bigger the account, the less concentrated spend became. One ad can only hold so much spend, so at higher budgets the number of good live ads becomes the limit on growth. How to apply: look at spend per active ad in Ads Manager over the last 30 days to estimate how much daily spend a typical ad holds in your account. Divide your peak daily spend target by that figure to get the number of live ads you will need. Count distinct concepts, not variations. Build that inventory before the peak, not during it. Compare spend share and ROAS by format (statics, video, carousel, catalogue) in your own account before setting the mix.
conditions: Accounts at meaningful spend with many live ads.
fails_when: Small accounts with a handful of ads, where one or two winners can still take most of the spend.
numbers: about 75% of spend through the long tail of ads

claim: Treat creative volume and variety as a CPM lever in BFCM: Blue Sense found accounts with more, more varied and better creative saw less CPM inflation in an auction running 72% more expensive.
body: Reviewing last Black Friday's data, Blue Sense found a qualitative link between creative quality, diversity and volume and how much an account's CPMs rose. Their explanation: when the platform releases extra inventory, a larger set of distinct ads wins more auctions across more people and placements. So creative is not only a conversion lever. How to apply: work out from target spend how many live creatives you need before the period (Blue Sense models this per client; one example came out at 365 creatives). Count distinct concepts, not assets: ten sizes of one idea add little variety. Keep evergreen winners live alongside sale creative. If the volume needs it, add more Facebook pages to run ads from. Phase the creative: teasers and early access before launch, launch creative, a mid-sale refresh, then deadline messaging for the last 24 to 48 hours.
conditions: Accounts spending enough in BFCM to need many live ads; the link is qualitative, from Blue Sense's portfolio review.
fails_when: Small accounts where extra creative spreads too little budget per ad; there is no measured effect size behind the link.

claim: A concept is persona plus angle plus offer, and changing any one reaches different buyers: collagen for women over 40 can be pitched on menopause, on injury prevention, or as gummies versus powder.
body: Blue Sense builds creative strategy around concepts. The persona is who you speak to, the angle is the argument that cuts through for them, and the offer is what you sell them. Change any one and Meta tends to find a different group of people, because the ad reads differently. Their example: even with a broad persona such as women over 40 buying collagen, one angle about menopause and another about preventing injuries from falls as you age speak to different problems and fragment into different audiences. Keep persona and angle and switch the offer from collagen gummies to collagen powder for strength and connective tissue, and you reach yet another group. That is how a broad market gets more reach: several concepts, each with its own problem. How to apply: write a grid of your personas, the angles that matter to each, and your offers. Every live ad set should map to one cell. Count the cells you are running; gaps are new concepts to brief. Blue Sense recommends specific personas over broad ones like the example.
conditions: Brands with a product that serves more than one problem or buyer type, at a spend level where reach is limited.
fails_when: The product serves one narrow use for one buyer, leaving few real angles, or new angles stray into claims the product cannot back.

claim: As a rule of thumb, launch about one new ad per $1,000 of monthly Meta spend, so 100 new ads a month at $100,000.
body: For a quick target, Blue Sense uses one new ad per month for every $1,000 of monthly spend: $30,000 a month means about 30 new ads, $100,000 about 100. It follows from each ad having a limited lifetime spend: if the average ad spends about $1,000 before fatiguing, holding spend needs about that many new ads. Smaller brands should simply make more and better ads than they do now, using this ratio as a ballpark. How to apply: count the new ads you launched last month (in Ads Manager, filter by created date) and compare with spend divided by 1,000. If you fall short, that gap is the first thing to fix, ahead of buying changes. Count distinct ads, but remember volume only counts above your quality bar and should spread across concepts and formats, not be eight copies of one script. For a sharper number, back-calculate from your new-customer revenue target and expected value per ad, or from how many winners you lose each month.
conditions: Meta accounts where creative fatigue limits spend, at roughly $10,000 a month and up.
fails_when: Average spend per ad is far above or below $1,000 in your account, which changes the ratio; very small accounts may need fewer, stronger ads.

claim: At a typical 5% creative hit rate you need about 20 ads per winner, so test at least 10 ads per concept before you abandon it.
body: Blue Sense works backwards from hit rate. If about 5% of the ads you launch become winners, which they say is typical for most accounts, you need about 20 ads to find one. A concept tested with only three or five ads has not even reached the account's average odds, so a failure says almost nothing about the concept; it is noise. Their rule is at least 10 ads per concept before moving on, and they believe most concepts that brands abandoned were never tested properly. How to apply: work out your own hit rate from the last few months, as winners divided by ads launched, where a winner is an ad that held meaningful spend at or under target cost per purchase. Divide one by that rate to get ads needed per winner. Set the minimum ads per concept test at about half that number or more, and budget each concept ad set so those ads can actually spend. If you cannot afford that, test fewer concepts at a time rather than thinning each one.
conditions: Meta accounts that test new concepts regularly and can define what counts as a winner.
fails_when: Accounts with a much higher hit rate from strong briefs and proven formats, which need fewer ads per concept; or budgets too small for 10 ads to each get spend.

claim: At six-figure monthly Meta spend, move about 10% of media budget into pre-production (scripting, ideas, new talent); Blue Sense claims $90,000 media plus $10,000 production can beat $100,000 media by about 50%.
body: Blue Sense sees brands spending $100,000 to $300,000 a month on Meta while still shooting everything on a phone with no production budget. Owners treat production as a sunk cost and would rather give the money to Meta, which feels like it drives revenue. Blue Sense's claim is that taking $10,000 out of a $100,000 media budget and spending it on someone to help with scripting, someone to generate more ideas, and new talent on camera (for example a woman if a man usually fronts the ads, which adds diversity at once) can lift performance by about 50%. They frame it as a guarantee, but it is their opinion, not shown data. Production here means pre-production first, not expensive cameras. At $50,000 a month the same move is $45,000 media and $5,000 production, spent on whatever you are worst at: scripting, ideation, filming or a new format like AI animation. How to apply: add a production line to the P&L as a percentage of media spend, fund the weakest step first, and compare cost per new customer over the next two months.
conditions: Brands spending roughly $50,000 to $300,000 a month on Meta with little or no production budget and in-house or founder-shot creative.
fails_when: The brand already invests well in production and scripting, or the bottleneck is offer, product or tracking rather than creative; the 50% lift is an unshown claim.

claim: Avoid running many specific persona callout hooks: Meta cannot tell who fits each band, so the same viewer sees several callouts and none feels personal.
body: A persona callout hook names the viewer's group, such as owners doing over $100,000 a month, listen up. Blue Sense thinks these are overrated. First, a callout does not agitate a problem or sell anything; it only says who the ad is for. Second, brands often run a series of narrow callouts for different bands or types. Meta's targeting cannot tell which band a given person is in, so it shows several of them to the same person. The viewer sees one for a group they are not in, then another, then one that fits, and by then they know the brand is cycling through callouts, so the one meant for them feels generic. The callout loses its whole point. How to apply: when a hook names a group, rewrite it to name the group's problem or use language only that group would recognise. If you do test callouts, run one or two broad, distinct ones rather than a ladder of narrow variants, and check frequency to see whether they overlap.
conditions: Meta video and static ads where hooks are written to address specific segments.
fails_when: Segments are defined by something Meta can target or that the creative itself filters well, such as clearly different products, ages or life stages that read differently on screen.

claim: Build the angle as an argument: lead with the pain until the viewer feels heard, reframe with a contrarian truth, and open a curiosity gap early that only closes late.
body: Blue Sense treats the angle as the argument the ad makes, with a reliable pattern. 1) Problem first. Lead with the pain and make the viewer feel understood before you introduce anything you sell. 2) Contrarian truth. Say something that reframes what they already believe, such as the real reason their current fix is not working. 3) Curiosity gap. Raise a question near the start that you only answer near the end, so they keep watching through the selling part. 4) Transformation, where you can keep it compliant, showing the before and after state; Blue Sense says this is the strongest element in B2B and info and it applies to many consumer products too. They also say most accounts lean too much on desire content (aspirational, pretty, lifestyle) and too little on pain. Big brands like Alo Yoga run mostly desire content and get away with it because of brand strength built outside the ad account; a smaller brand copying that usually fails. How to apply: in each script, mark the pain line, the reframe line, the open question and where it closes. If any is missing, rewrite before filming.
conditions: Direct response creative for brands without a famous brand name doing the selling for them.
fails_when: Very strong brands where desire and lifestyle imagery already convert, or categories where pain framing would breach ad rules, such as some health and weight topics.

claim: By monthly Meta spend: under $30,000 shoot on iPhone with about 3 concepts live; $30,000 to $100,000 run 5 to 6 concepts with 10% of spend on production; over $100,000 run 8 to 10 concepts and 100+ ads.
body: Blue Sense's playbook by spend level. Under $30,000 a month: shoot everything on an iPhone, the budget is your time, keep about three concepts live, script as many ads as you can script well, and focus on learning what looks good. $30,000 to $100,000 a month: mix phone footage with some higher production, set aside about 10% of media spend for production (mostly pre-production: scripting, ideation and talent), and keep five to six concepts live. That does not mean five to six winners; often only one or two concepts win, while 20 to 30% of output keeps testing new ones. Over $100,000 a month: diversify who is on camera, especially if the founder fronts every ad; keep about 8 to 10 concepts and 100 or more new ads a month live; the production percentage can fall a little with scale; and build a team and system that runs without you, since that volume is too much for one person. How to apply: find your tier, count your live concepts, and close the gap before raising spend.
conditions: DTC brands on Meta deciding production budgets and concept counts at their current spend level.
fails_when: Brands in categories where one person on camera (a founder or celebrity) drives most results, or very high average order value products that need fewer, longer ads.

claim: Do not automate creative ideation with AI, which drifts to the average even with context; put AI into briefing and scripting, where Blue Sense sees the heaviest leverage.
body: Blue Sense's view on AI in creative production: every model tends to return the mean, the most typical answer. Adding brand context improves the output a lot but does not fully fix it, so ideas from AI tend to look like everyone else's. Ideation, which decides concepts, angles and the twist that makes an ad stand out, should stay with people who know the customer. Where AI pays off most is briefing and scripting, the step that turns a chosen concept into a structured script: they suggest building a reusable skill (a saved prompt and template) that outputs scripts in your house structure, such as hook, problem, promise, mechanism, objection, proof, offer, risk reversal and call to action. How to apply: keep a human list of concepts drawn from real buyer research; feed one concept at a time, with persona notes, product facts and approved claims, into a scripting prompt; then edit the draft. Track which scripts came from which concepts so the process improves.
conditions: Teams producing many scripts a month who want to use AI without making ads look generic.
fails_when: The team has no strong source of ideas, where AI suggestions may still beat a blank page; or the scripting prompt lacks real product facts and invents claims.

claim: Every ad has a fixed lifetime spend capacity: ramping it faster only fatigues it sooner, so holding or growing spend always needs a steady flow of new ads.
body: Blue Sense describes an ad's life as a curve: spend ramps up while it performs, peaks at the most it can take per day, then has to be pulled back as it fatigues. The total area under that curve, the lifetime spend the ad can absorb at an acceptable return, stays about the same however fast you push it. Scaling an account quickly does not get more out of each ad; it burns through them faster, so you need replacements sooner. The consequence for planning: spend you want to hold next month must be carried by ads that exist next month. How to apply: in Ads Manager, look at your top ads by lifetime spend and note roughly how many weeks each one held strong spend before cost per purchase rose. That gives a rough lifetime per winner. If you plan to raise budget, plan more new ads in proportion, rather than expecting existing winners to stretch. Use this with a creative volume target per spend level and a monthly count of winners lost to fatigue.
conditions: Meta accounts spending enough that individual ads fatigue within weeks or months, typically tens of thousands a month and up.
fails_when: Very small accounts where a few ads can run for many months at low spend without saturating the audience, so new ads are needed far less often.

claim: For e-commerce creative tests, change variables in this order: persona, offer, angle, then format; offer is the biggest lever but the hardest to move when you cannot change the product.
body: Blue Sense ranks what to test first by how much it changes who you reach and whether they buy. For e-commerce the order is persona, offer, angle, format. Offer is the biggest lever in theory, but in e-commerce the product is most of the offer and you mostly cannot change it, though bundles, guarantees and pricing can still move. In info, B2B and services, the order flips to offer first, because those businesses can reshape what they sell quickly. Format comes last everywhere, because format serves the concept, not the other way round. Each offer test gets its own concept and ad set, with at least 10 ads. Persona adds breadth once offer and angle work. How to apply: when planning the next month's tests, first ask which buyer types have no live concept; then whether a new bundle, guarantee or price point is ready; then new angles for proven personas; and only after that new formats. Log each test against the variable it changes so results teach the next brief.
conditions: E-commerce brands planning Meta creative tests with enough budget for several concepts at once.
fails_when: The current offer is clearly the bottleneck (poor repeat rate, weak value), where an offer change should come first even in e-commerce.
numbers: each offer test: own concept, own ad set, 10+ ads

claim: Once ads clear the quality bar nobody reliably picks winners, so prioritise volume above the bar, then concept quality, hook strength, storytelling, editing and talent, in that order.
body: Blue Sense says that when ads are good enough to be indistinguishable from winners, nobody can reliably tell which will win; some just do not work and no one knows why. That makes a hit rate above about 20% very hard to reach. The skill is knowing where the quality bar sits and then making as many ads as possible above it. Their general order of what matters: volume (assuming the bar is met), concept quality, hook strength, storytelling, editing quality, then talent on camera. Pumping out ads below the bar is junk volume that does nothing. The order changes by business: for a brand fronted by a famous figure or big influencer, talent can be first because their presence alone lifts any ad; for others, storytelling leads because their best unaware ads hold the most spend. How to apply: define your bar in writing (clear concept, structured script, on-brand, readable on mobile); reject briefs and edits below it; then judge your team on how many ads above the bar they ship.
conditions: Accounts already producing ads of reasonable quality and asking where to focus effort next.
fails_when: The bar itself is not met, where quality fixes come before volume; or a brand's results depend on one person on camera, where talent jumps to the top.
numbers: hit rates above about 20% are very hard
priority: volume, concept quality, hook strength, storytelling, editing, talent
asks: Can I predict which ads will win?
Should I make more ads or better ads?
What matters most in a Facebook ad?
What hit rate should I expect on new ads?

evidence.where: [21:43] nobody can reliably pick winners; [22:07] what matters in order

claim: Pick format after the concept by asking whether it needs teaching: colder, less aware viewers need longer ads, while product-aware viewers need only the product and the offer.
body: Blue Sense calls choosing a format first a rookie mistake; a strategy of just testing UGC is not a strategy. What makes an ad work is the script, the idea, the persona and the angle. Format is chosen to carry them. The key question is whether the concept requires teaching. If it does, you need length. Map it to the stages of awareness: the further up (unaware, problem aware), the longer the ad generally needs to be, because you are explaining a problem or a mechanism. The further down (product aware, most aware), the shorter, because the viewer already knows you and needs only the product and the offer. In info and B2B, the formats that hold most spend are long-form video sales letters that teach the mechanism, founder talking heads, screen recordings that demonstrate the mechanism and proof, advertorial funnels and podcast cutdowns; the same logic of long teaching formats for cold traffic carries into DTC. How to apply: for each new concept, write its awareness stage and whether it needs teaching, then choose length and format from that, not from what is trendy.
conditions: Planning new concepts for Meta and TikTok, especially for products needing explanation.
fails_when: Platform or placement limits force a length, such as short Stories placements, or the audience is mostly warm and short ads dominate anyway.
asks: How long should my Facebook ad be?
Should I test UGC as a strategy?
Which ad format should I use?
When do long-form video ads work?

claim: Put more variation into hooks than bodies: record three to five hooks for most bodies; Blue Sense has pulled an extra $100,000 of spend from one ad with a couple of hook swaps.
body: Blue Sense says about 80% of viewers never get past the hook, so the hook decides how many people reach the selling part. They used to favour body variations, since the body does the convincing, but about 18 months to two years ago they switched to more hook variations, as long as each hook fits the body that follows. Their reasoning: anyone who gets halfway through an ad will probably finish it and is likely to convert, so the bottleneck is how many people get through the first stretch. A hook is a promise of relevance, not a trick to stop the scroll, and it has three layers: the visual, the audio and the on-screen text. Hook testing still works under Andromeda's push for diversity. How to apply: when filming a body, record three to five different openings at the same time, since it costs little. Vary the visual and spoken line, not only the caption. Launch hook variants on bodies that have proven they convert, and track spend and cost per purchase per variant.
conditions: Video ads on Meta where a body has already shown it can convert, with creators able to film several openings in one session.
fails_when: Hooks that do not fit the body (a hook promising one thing and a body about another), or variants that only change a word of caption text and get grouped as the same ad.
numbers: about 80% never watch past the hook
3 to 5 hooks per body
extra $100,000 spend from one ad after a couple of hook swaps
approach changed about 1.5 to 2 years ago

claim: Size creative output from your revenue goal: at $3,000 new-customer revenue per ad (3x on $1,000 average spend), a $300,000 target needs 100 ads; also track how many winners churn out each month.
body: Blue Sense uses two better methods than the one-ad-per-$1,000 rule, and runs both. Method one, back-propagate from revenue. Work out the expected value of an ad: if the average ad spends about $1,000 and returns 3x on seven-day click, it brings about $3,000 in new-customer revenue. To reach $300,000 of new-customer revenue, you need about 100 ads. Method two, churn analysis. Count the winning ads at the start of the month and how many have fatigued out by the end. That gives a monthly churn rate for winners. Multiply the number of winners you need to hold spend by that churn, then divide by your hit rate to get the number of new ads to launch. For example, losing 10 winners a month at a 5% hit rate means about 200 new ads. How to apply: pull last quarter's ads, compute average spend per ad, average return and winners lost per month, and set next month's production target from both methods, using the higher. Info businesses should run the same maths on cash collected rather than revenue.
conditions: Accounts with a few months of history to compute spend per ad, return per ad, hit rate and winner churn.
fails_when: History is too short or spend too uneven for stable averages, or a big offer or season change makes past spend per ad a poor guide.
numbers: $1,000 average spend per ad at 3x gives about $3,000 per ad
$300,000 new-customer revenue target needs about 100 ads
example: 10 winners lost per month at 5% hit rate needs about 200 new ads
asks: How do I work out how many ads I need?
How do I plan creative production from my revenue target?

claim: Split new ads about 50% replicating winners, 20 to 30% iterating, and 20 to 30% net new concepts; going 80% replication left some brands with nothing when their one winner fatigued.
body: Blue Sense splits creative production into three types by leverage. About half goes to winning content replication: new versions of proven concepts with new creators, settings or formats. Twenty to thirty percent is iterative content: changes to hooks, bodies or edits of current ads. Twenty to thirty percent is net new concepts: new personas, angles or offers. Some advisers suggest 80% replication; Blue Sense thinks that overweights winners and raises risk sharply. They have turned away brands in trouble that had one winning ad, poured all their resources into copying it, spent about $3 to $5 million behind it over two years, and then had nothing ready when that concept, angle and offer fatigued. By then they were unprofitable, so they could not afford to test their way out. How to apply: tag each brief by type before production and check the monthly mix. If net new concepts drop below about 20%, add some even when current winners are strong, because the pipeline is what keeps the account alive when they fade.
conditions: Accounts producing enough ads each month to split across three types, usually dozens or more.
fails_when: A brand with very few ads per month, where every slot may need to go to the one or two proven concepts until cash allows testing.
numbers: 50% winner replication
20 to 30% iteration
20 to 30% net new concepts
cautionary case: $3 to $5 million spend on one winner over 2 years

claim: Write hooks that reposition a proven demand in a new way, between red ocean copying and blue ocean invention; once rivals copy your messaging, refresh it or you will sound like them.
body: Blue Sense advises sitting between two extremes. Copying what competitors say keeps you in a crowded red ocean where your ads blend in. Inventing a brand-new demand is risky and slow. The middle is to take a desire people already have and present it in a way no competitor is using; the same applies to formats. Their own example: in Australia so many agencies copied Blue Sense's ad scripts almost word for word that if Blue Sense went back to heavy advertising with its old messaging, it would sound like its copycats. So it would have to reposition hooks, formats and messaging into something genuinely new. Copying a script is legal, so the only defence is to keep moving. How to apply: once a quarter, read your competitors' live ads in the Meta Ad Library and list their common hooks and claims. Mark which of your own hooks now sound the same. For those, write new hooks around a different problem, mechanism or proof that the market already wants but nobody is saying.
conditions: Crowded categories where competitors watch and copy each other's ads, which covers most mature DTC niches.
fails_when: A brand is early in a quiet niche where the common message still works and few rivals advertise; novelty for its own sake can also drift away from what buyers want.
asks: Competitors are copying my ads, what do I do?
How do I make my ads stand out in a crowded niche?
Should I copy what's working for competitors?
How often should I change my ad messaging?

claim: An organic-feeling street interview that opens on a strong held belief (sunscreen is worse than the sun) qualifies the right persona in seconds, then wins them by agreeing first and reframing to the product.
body: The second ad is a beach street interview for a tallow and zinc sunscreen. The man interviewed says sunscreen is more harmful than the sun. That opening does two jobs: viewers who share the belief feel validated and keep watching, while those who disagree scroll away, which is fine because they are not the buyer. The woman then agrees with each of his points, keeping continuity, before introducing a reframe: a sunscreen made from simple ingredients. Because viewers have come to trust him, his switch to 'of course I would use that' carries them with him. Blue Sense estimates it has 20,000 to 30,000 likes and perhaps $1M in revenue, and notes it does not matter whether it was staged; what matters is that it feels like organic content, not an ad. How to apply: find a belief your best buyers already hold about the category, open by stating it bluntly through a relatable person, validate it, then present your product as the answer that fits that belief.
conditions: Categories with a strong contrarian or values-based buyer segment (clean, natural, anti-chemical) on Meta and TikTok.
fails_when: The belief is a health claim you cannot support or that breaks platform policy; or the product targets the mainstream view, where opening on a fringe belief repels most buyers.
numbers: estimated 20,000 to 30,000 likes
estimated about $1M revenue (Blue Sense guess)
asks: How do I make an ad that does not look like an ad?
Do street interview ads work?
How do I target a specific type of buyer with creative?
Is it okay to stage organic-looking ads?

claim: Blatant before and after shots tend to raise CPMs or get ads disapproved on Meta; show the comparison small in a corner and flash between the two states instead.
body: A TikTok Shop hair intolerance test ad (a woman cutting her fiance's hair to send off) includes before and after footage of her own skin and stomach. Blue Sense flags before and afters as borderline under Meta's rules: shown large and plainly they usually bring either much higher CPMs or a disapproval. This ad keeps the comparison in a small box in the top right corner and switches quickly between the two images, which they believe Meta is less likely to pick up while viewers still get the proof. The hook is also strong because it is built into the product: cutting hair live opens a curiosity gap (how can hair reveal food intolerances?), and the mood contrast between her (fixed) and him (still grumpy) keeps the story going. How to apply: if your category relies on visible results, test a small inset before and after inside a broader story rather than a full-screen split.
conditions: Health, beauty and wellness products on Meta where visible results are the main proof.
fails_when: Categories where Meta policy bans implying body results at all (weight loss, some health claims); a small inset is still a breach, so check policy before testing.
asks: Can I use before and after photos in Facebook ads?
Why are my before and after ads getting disapproved?
Do before and after images raise CPMs?
How do I show results without breaking Meta rules?

evidence.where: about [23:59] ad 7 small corner before and after

claim: Cut to a new clip about every 1.5 to 2 seconds; Blue Sense says the same winning wiper script shot as one unbroken talking head with no B-roll would not perform.
body: The wiper ad's script is good, but the pace is what lets it work on Instagram and Facebook feeds: a new shot roughly every 1.5 seconds, which makes it feel organic and easy to keep watching. The toothbrush founder ad does the same with short, sharp cuts every 1.5 to 2 seconds. Blue Sense's point is that editing is not decoration. Take the identical script, shoot it as one static shot of someone talking to camera holding the product, with no cutaways, and it would fail. So the edit pace needs to be in the brief, not left to the editor. How to apply: plan B-roll for every one to two seconds of voice-over (product close-ups, the problem happening, the person in context), and when reviewing a rough cut, scrub through and flag any shot that holds longer than about two seconds without a reason. The exception is a story-led founder ad, where they suggest holding on the speaker longer so the viewer does not feel sold to.
conditions: Short-form video ads for Meta Reels, Stories and TikTok, especially demo and problem-solution ads.
fails_when: Story or testimonial ads where trust comes from watching one person speak, or premium brand films where slower pacing is part of the positioning.
numbers: new clip every 1.5 to 2 seconds
asks: How fast should my video ad be edited?
Do talking head ads work on Facebook?
How much B-roll do I need?

claim: Do not rush the middle of a problem-solution ad: Blue Sense would add about 15 seconds (two to four sentences) explaining the unique mechanism and why current solutions fall short.
body: A dandruff shampoo ad has a strong hook (black shirts do not lie: if you see flakes, your shampoo is failing), which works as both problem agitation and a persona call-out, since only people with the problem keep watching. The call to action is fine. The weakness is the middle, which jumps from dandruff is fungal to other shampoos just scrape, ours is anti-fungal, then ingredients. Blue Sense rates it neither bad nor good and says rushing that section limits how far it can scale. Their fix is to make the ad about 15 seconds longer and spend two to four more sentences on two things: how the mechanism works and why it beats current options, and why what the viewer uses today fails them. A viewer who has tried many shampoos needs a reason to believe this one is different before the price matters. How to apply: when an ad has a good hook and CTA but stalls, look at the time spent on mechanism and on existing alternatives before changing the hook.
conditions: Problem-solution products where buyers have tried other fixes, such as personal care and supplements.
fails_when: Impulse products where the benefit is obvious and longer ads only add drop-off.
numbers: add about 15 seconds
2 to 4 extra sentences on mechanism and current solutions
asks: How long should my video ad be?
My ad has a good hook but does not convert, what should I fix?
How much should I explain how the product works?

claim: Explain the unique ingredient or mechanism before naming the product, and where honest, add an anti-sell (a warning that it works so well it needs care) to make the claim believable.
body: A Medicube volume stick ad opens with a strong persona call-out (sagging, angry-looking face, turkey neck) at problem-aware level, but introduces the product immediately. Blue Sense would reorder: explain the mechanism or ingredient first (how it works, why it is different), then reveal the product later, and they expect that version to beat the original. The same ad has a clever move worth copying: it warns viewers not to touch the stick with their fingers because the ingredient grows fat cells, joking about fat fingers. That anti-sell, a side effect from the product working too well, lends credibility to the main claim without stating it outright. The ad also borrows authority from a known category reputation (Korean skincare) and closes with a TikTok Shop style scarcity line. How to apply: in your script, move the product name after the mechanism explanation, and look for any truthful usage warning that implies strength.
conditions: Ingredient or mechanism-led products such as skincare and supplements, aimed at problem-aware audiences.
fails_when: The anti-sell would be a false or unsafe claim, or the category is regulated so that implying strong physiological effects breaks ad policy.
asks: When should I show the product in my ad?
What is an anti-sell in advertising?
How do I make a big claim more believable?
Should I lead with the ingredient or the product?

evidence.where: about [16:50] ad 5 Medicube volume stick

claim: Fashion brands should run organic-feeling video ads that rotate through many products, which widens the audience each ad can reach and keeps the ad live when items sell out.
body: Blue Sense calls this format a staple every fashion account should have: a casual, organic-looking clip with light on-screen text that flicks through a series of outfits or pieces. A single-outfit static only engages people who like that one look, which is a small slice of the audience Meta can show it to. Each extra product shown gives another viewer a reason to stop: they skip one look, then see one they would buy. That raises the share of viewers who click, sends them to a collection page to browse, and increases the chance of a multi-item order. There is an operational benefit too: when one product goes out of stock the ad does not need to be paused, because it is not built around a single item. How to apply: shoot short clips of 6 to 10 products in the same style, cut them into one fast sequence, and send the traffic to a collection rather than one product page.
conditions: Fashion and apparel brands with a range of styles and frequent stock turnover.
fails_when: Single-hero-product brands, or launches where one product needs focused education.
asks: What ads work best for fashion brands?
Should I show one product or many in my ads?
How do I stop pausing ads when items sell out?
Where should fashion ads send traffic?

evidence.where: about [18:52] fashion ad rotating through products

claim: Feature-heavy ads (temperatures, dual plates) sit low on the awareness ladder and suit middle of funnel; cold audiences need benefit-led education on why each spec matters.
body: A portable grill ad blends real footage from a market stall with a polished product clip. The hook is a bystander saying he owns a Weber but would have bought this had he seen it first, which opens a curiosity gap in the first six seconds and raises the competitor objection immediately. The middle is mostly specs: 360 degrees at the centre, 325 average across the plate, two independent grills. Blue Sense thinks that is acceptable here because buyers choose grills on the mechanism (folds better than a Weber) and heat. But it assumes product awareness. Shown to a cold viewer who does not own a barbecue, the numbers mean nothing: why do I need two plates, is 325 degrees too hot? A cold version would explain the payoffs: only light one side when cooking alone to save gas; cook steak and eggs at once without burning the eggs. So place spec-led ads in middle of funnel, and write benefit translations for top of funnel. Filming real shopper reactions at markets or stores is a cheap source of strong organic hooks.
conditions: Considered purchases with technical specs, such as outdoor, appliances and tech, on Meta.
fails_when: Audiences already deep in comparison shopping, where specs are exactly what they want to see first.
numbers: grill ad specs: 360 degrees centre, 325 average, 2 independent grills
curiosity gap opened within the first 6 seconds
asks: Should I put product specs in my Facebook ads?
Why does my spec-heavy ad not work on cold audiences?
Which ads should go top of funnel versus middle?
How do I use real customer reactions in ads?

evidence.where: about [26:30] ad 8 portable grill with market footage

claim: For cheap gadget products with a visible unique mechanism, a fast product demonstration that shows how it works within the first 2 seconds, under a bold text hook, is the format to lean into.
body: Blue Sense's first teardown is a magnetic microwave cover sold TikTok Shop style. Gadgets suit pure demonstration ads because the product's point of difference can be seen physically, so showing it working again and again does the selling. What made this one strong: a text overlay hook on screen as well as spoken ('invention of the decade'), so it works with sound off; the mechanism demonstrated inside the first two seconds; quick cuts and a fast pace; a short problem agitation explaining why the mechanism is needed at all, since many gadgets solve problems nobody has; one line answering the obvious objection (why not just leave it on top of the microwave); then extra benefits and a soft scarcity close. Because a gadget is a cheap impulse buy that solves one narrow problem, there is no need to climb the awareness ladder with heavy education, as a supplement ad must. How to apply: if your product's benefit is understood in three or four seconds of footage, script around the demo, not around a story.
conditions: Low-priced products whose benefit is obvious on camera and bought on impulse; works on Meta and TikTok feeds.
fails_when: Products whose benefit is invisible or delayed (supplements, skincare), or higher-priced items where buyers need education, proof and objection handling before they buy.
numbers: demonstrate the mechanism within the first 2 seconds
benefit should be clear within 3 to 4 seconds
asks: What kind of video ad works for a gadget product?
Do I need a story ad or just a product demo?
How fast should I show the product in my ad?
How do I write a hook for a cheap impulse product?

evidence.where: [00:41] ad 1: magnetic microwave cover demo

claim: Lead with the benefit and follow with the feature that causes it, and put every feature line through a 'so what' test, for example tying '1,000 things tested' to a competitor that tests only 200.
body: Several of the ads lose points for opening on a feature. A wiper ad names its Teflon-coated rubber before telling the viewer why they should care, and a gut test ad lists that it checks over 1,000 things, then food, drink and household exposures, with no reason the number matters. Blue Sense's rule, borrowed from supplement copywriting: say the outcome first (you will sleep far better) and then the mechanism that delivers it (because it contains magnesium). For every feature in a script, ask so what, why does it matter, why is it in the script? Then rewrite it to carry its own meaning. Their example fix: we test over 1,000 things, most competitors test about 200, and that is how this found what others missed. Now the number proves superiority instead of sitting there. Features are fine in a rapid list at the end once the benefits are landed, as a toothbrush founder ad does well.
conditions: Scripts and static copy for products whose features are not self-explanatory to a cold viewer.
fails_when: Spec-led categories where buyers shop on numbers (grills, tech), where feature-first can work for product-aware audiences lower in the funnel.
numbers: example rewrite: 1,000 things tested versus about 200 for competitors
asks: Should my ad talk about features or benefits first?
How do I make product specs more persuasive?
My ad lists features but does not convert, why?
What is the so what test in copywriting?

evidence.where: [09:54] ad 3 benefit before feature; about [24:40] ad 7 so what test

claim: Once a script and edit style work, scale by reshooting the same script with different personas on camera (mothers, first-car drivers, different cars), and always cast the persona you are selling to.
body: The wiper ad features one type of man, so it mostly resonates with viewers who look like him. Blue Sense would not rewrite it; they would reshoot it with a range of avatars and settings: a mother, a young driver with their first car, different vehicles, since the car itself changes who identifies with the ad. Each version reaches a different cluster of people while the proven script and editing carry the conversion. The flip side shows up in a skincare ad from Medicube: it uses testimonials from mothers, but the presenter is a man in his late twenties. That gap between the person on screen and the target buyer weakens it; Blue Sense would test a version with one of the mothers presenting. A toothbrush founder ad does this well by flashing a woman in her twenties, a mother in her forties or fifties, a child and others, signalling the product is for families. How to apply: list your top three to five personas and recast your best script for each before writing new scripts.
conditions: Products with several distinct buyer types; Meta accounts where a winning script is fatiguing on one audience.
fails_when: Products with a single narrow buyer, where new faces add little reach; or when recast versions are so similar that Meta treats them as the same ad.
asks: How do I scale a winning video ad?
Should the person in my ad match my customer?
Can I reuse the same script with different creators?
Our winner is fatiguing, what should we make next?

claim: Scalable ad scripts follow one old direct response order: unique hook, problem agitation, objection handling and other uses, unique mechanism and its story, social proof, then call to action and risk reversal.
body: Teardown of an earplug brand's ad shows the structure that runs through all of its ads. The hook is original (a nightclub clip with a sudden 'stop') and probably not AI-written. Then strong problem agitation (hearing damage that never heals), objection handling (current options make a $100 ticket sound like a broken radio), the unique mechanism and the story behind it (a filter that lowers volume while keeping the sound flat), social proof (DJs, engineers, audiologists, 500,000 customers), the call to action, and a risk reversal on screen. Blue Sense notes the copy shows signs of being written with AI help, such as contrast negation lines, yet it still performs, because the structure is fixed and the hook is a genuine idea. Their lesson: AI can draft well if you give it this outline and supply the hook yourself. Use the same skeleton for briefs and for checking scripts before a shoot.
conditions: Problem-solution products advertised to cold or problem-aware audiences in video ads.
fails_when: Impulse gadgets where a pure demo outperforms a full structure, or brand awareness films with no direct response goal.
numbers: ad claims 500,000 customers as social proof
asks: What is the best structure for a video ad script?
Can I use ChatGPT or Claude to write ad scripts?
In what order should an ad script go?
How do I write a direct response ad?

evidence.where: about [22:40] ad 6 earplug script structure

claim: Use AI video to dramatise the problem or the story, never to fake a product demonstration or a UGC testimonial; viewers who spot fake demos turn on the brand and believers become refunds and chargebacks.
body: Blue Sense contrasts good and bad AI use. Bad: an AI clip of an elderly woman doing spins while mowing to demonstrate a product. Beyond misrepresenting what the product does, people who notice it is AI lose trust and refuse to buy, while those fooled receive something that does not match, which drives refunds, chargebacks and no repeat purchase. They see it as a short-lived trick for dropshippers. AI UGC fails for a related reason: UGC works because of a real creator's influence and authority, which a generated face lacks, and detection repels viewers. Good: an activewear brand (Neura) shows a man overheating and wrapped in plastic to dramatise polyester; an earplug ad visualises hearing cells snapping at 110 dB against an 85 dB limit, footage that would once have been costly or impossible; a toothbrush ad visualises microplastics. Each then cuts to real footage the moment the product appears. Rule: AI as special effects for storytelling, real camera for anything the buyer will judge the product on.
conditions: Brands using AI video generation in Meta or TikTok ads.
fails_when: Clearly stylised animation or claymation ads where the whole piece is obviously illustrated, which viewers do not read as a false demo.
numbers: earplug ad: ears built for 85 dB, venue at 110 dB
asks: Should I use AI video in my ads?
Is AI UGC a good idea?
How can AI help my ad creative without hurting trust?

evidence.where: about [13:16] ads 4 and the mowing example: good and bad AI use; about [20:00] ad 6 earplugs

claim: Use zero-party survey data to find the persona, angle and offer that brought your top 20% of customers, and shift ad spend there even at a slightly worse acquisition ROAS.
body: First-party data is contact details; zero-party data is what customers tell you about themselves: what problem they bought for, what they do on weekends, what they like about the brand. Blue Sense uses it to steer paid media. Profile the top 20% of customers (who typically drive about 80% of revenue): which persona they are, which angle they came in on, which offer they bought. Then push more creative and spend toward those. Do the same for the bottom 20%, the refunders, returners and low spenders; they often came in on an angle that oversold the product. Example: a skin health supplement whose Meta team found a concept about energy that showed a 5 ROAS. Those buyers did not get the energy they expected, the packaging said skin health, so they refunded and never reordered. Without a survey, only customer support would have noticed. How to apply: add a post-purchase survey asking the reason for buying, join answers to 90 and 365 day gross profit per customer, and rank personas and angles by LTV, not by front-end ROAS.
conditions: Brands running several personas or angles on paid social, with a post-purchase survey and enough orders per angle.
fails_when: Survey response rates are too low or answers too vague to tie to cohorts; or a product genuinely serves several needs equally well.
numbers: top 20% of customers typically drive about 80% of revenue
5 ROAS on an off-target energy angle
asks: Which ad angles bring my best customers?
What questions should my post-purchase survey ask?
Why do customers from some ads refund more?
How do I use customer data to improve my ads?

evidence.where: about [57:58] zero-party data, top and bottom 20% customers, energy angle example

claim: A broad belief-challenging hook (drinking 3 L of water a day does not mean you are hydrated) can scale to big spend, while narrow persona call-out hooks cap out fast, especially in Australia.
body: Persona call-outs are popular, like asking men if they struggle to stay in the gym past 60 minutes. They may hit the target buyer, but the pool is small, so the ad runs out of people quickly, especially in a small market like Australia, and will not carry a quarter of a million dollars in spend. Blue Sense's preferred alternative, from a Hyro ad run through a newly made whitelisting page, challenges a belief almost everyone holds: drinking 3 L of water a day does not mean you are hydrated. Every viewer wonders why, so the ad scales wide. The ad then keeps attention during a bridging line by having the creator move a sponge around the table, a simple visual that pulls people into the next educational point. How to apply: list common beliefs in your category that are partly wrong, write hooks that challenge them, and keep visual movement on screen during any line that is not itself interesting. Use persona call-outs as smaller tests, not as the main scale ads.
conditions: Cold acquisition ads meant to carry large budgets, especially in smaller markets.
fails_when: Niche products where the persona is the market, or claims in the hook that are not accurate for your product.

claim: A high hook rate is not the goal; an intrigue hook that grabs everyone (like a man eating an unnamed snack) teaches Meta nothing about who buys, so hook the people the product is for.
body: The Nothin jerky ad opens with someone eating something unseen and saying how good it is. It is curious and fresh, so many people will stop. But in the early days of a new ad there is little purchase data, so Meta leans on who watches to decide who to show it to next. If vegetarians and meat lovers stop equally, the system cannot tell who to favor, and the ad spends on people who will never buy jerky. Blue Sense's rule: aim to hook the right people, not the most people. The same ad then jumps straight to the brand and lists features (no processed ingredients, grass-fed beef) without a problem, a desire or a clear buyer. How to apply: when you review a hook, ask who it filters in and who it filters out. Make sure the first two or three seconds signal the product category or the buyer's problem, and judge hooks on cost per purchase, not hook rate alone.
conditions: Cold Meta and TikTok creative, especially newly launched ads with little purchase data.
fails_when: Products with very broad appeal, where hooking almost everyone is close to hooking buyers.
asks: My ad has a great hook rate but no sales, why?

claim: Check scripts for mixed messages, such as promising energy without the crash and then saying you will be buzzing; a product name that states the outcome, like Energy and Focus, does part of the selling.
body: Blue Sense's teardown of a Zum energy gum ad found three faults that recur in many ads. It names the product at once and lists features (60 mg of caffeine, B vitamins, taurine) before giving a reason to care. It makes a benefit claim, as much caffeine as coffee without the crash, without explaining how it works, so a viewer has no reason to believe it. And it contradicts itself, ending on you will be buzzing, which clashes with the smooth, no-crash promise and leaves the viewer unsure what they are buying, and why not just have a coffee. By contrast, a competitor names its main product line for the outcome, Energy and Focus, so buyers know the benefit before any ad explains it. How to apply: read every script once only for its promise, and cut any line that conflicts with it. Explain the mechanism behind any surprising claim in plain words. Consider whether your product or variant names state the result the buyer wants.
conditions: Functional products sold through short-form video or static ads.
numbers: example: 60 mg caffeine per piece
asks: Why isn't my energy product ad converting?

claim: If a creator's best benefits only appear a minute in, move them to the front and split them into separate ads; Hyro's endurance, no cramping and faster recovery lines could be three ads.
body: Blue Sense's teardown of a weak Hyro electrolyte ad: it opens with a pitch, claims to be the best powder ever tried, shows the product in nearly every cut in the first three to four seconds, and gives no problem or reason to care. Saying the creator takes it before and after every workout means nothing to the viewer, and at a few dollars a sachet it begs the question of what changed for him. The good material is buried about a minute in: better endurance, no cramping, faster recovery. Blue Sense's fix: pull those to the front and make three ads, one per benefit. A sample reframe for a young male gym-goer: sessions shrinking from 60 minutes to 10 or 20, ruling out other causes, discovering it was hydration, finding water alone did not help, learning about electrolytes and the 500 mg sodium level, then finding this brand. How to apply: transcribe your weaker ads, mark the timestamp of each benefit, and rebuild new cuts that open on one benefit and the problem behind it.
conditions: Existing UGC footage with real benefits mentioned somewhere in the take.
fails_when: The benefits cannot be shown or felt credibly by the creator, or the footage has no usable problem or story moments to reorder.

claim: Run creator ads as partnership ads through the creator's own page for cold audiences, where the handle adds trust and data; do not pay creators to front hard-sell ads meant for warm buyers.
body: A great creator script loses some of its effect when it runs from the brand's own page, because the viewer can see they are being sold to. Haus's stronger version runs the same kind of content as a partnership ad through the creator's personal page, so it reads as a post from a person. Blue Sense also says partnership ads use the creator page's data alongside yours to find the right cold users, which is their main job. The reverse case: a Hyro electrolyte ad ran as a partnership ad but opened with a direct pitch, finished my workout and need to talk about this brand, which only works on people who already know the product. That wastes the creator fee, since warm buyers do not need an influencer's handle; the brand page would do. How to apply: put creator content with a soft, educational or story opening into partnership ads for prospecting. Keep direct-pitch scripts for retargeting on your own page.
conditions: Brands paying creators for usage rights or partnership access on Meta.
fails_when: The creator has a poor or mismatched audience, or the brand page is itself the trusted voice (a founder-led brand with a large following).
asks: Should I run UGC from my page or the creator's page?

claim: Strong VSL ads loop education and problem agitation for a minute or more before naming the product, knock down the usual remedies, then bridge from a general solution to ingredients to the product.
body: Blue Sense calls video sales letters among the best and most underused ad types. Its example, an OraCare ad about tonsil stones, runs about three minutes. Structure: 1) Educate on the cause (bacteria moving into the tonsils) and agitate the problem (sour taste, stones, avoiding close conversations), switching back and forth without offering a fix, so curiosity builds. 2) Name the usual remedies people have tried (tongue scrapers, oil pulling, charcoal, salt water gargles) and explain why each fails, which handles objections before any product appears. 3) Bridge through a general solution first (rebalance the bacteria and calm inflammation), then the specific ingredients and what each does, and only then the product as the easy way to get all of them in one tablet. 4) Close with a soft call to action. Two minutes in, the product still has not been introduced. The edit mixes real and AI UGC, animations, statics and filmed footage to stay engaging, and the same body is tested with several hooks.
conditions: Problem-solution products with an explainable cause, sold to cold audiences.
fails_when: Impulse or aesthetic products with no real mechanism to teach, or audiences already familiar with the product.
