claim: Test formats on organic first and move the ones that pop into ads early; IM8 Health turned the green-screen business breakdown format into an ad citing its own $100M ARR in 11 months.
body: Format does not make an ad good, but a new format often gives a short-lived boost before everyone copies it. Blue Sense's example: IM8 Health, David Beckham's supplement brand, ran an ad styled as a third-party green-screen breakdown of how the company reached $100M in annual revenue in 11 months. That format was everywhere on organic Instagram, yet almost no brand had used it as an ad. The angle also worked: it raised the obvious objection (it only grew because of Beckham) and answered it with studies, reviews, testimonials and other endorsers, all framed as an objective explanation, never a direct pitch, with a soft close. Using the brand's own revenue as social proof was unusual for a DTC ad. How to apply: keep a running list of formats taking off on organic in your niche and the wider feed. Try them on your own organic first; when one pops, adapt it into an ad quickly and measure it against your control.
conditions: Brands with an organic content habit and a fast creative turnaround.
fails_when: The format is already common in ads in your category, or quoting revenue or growth would read as boastful for your brand.

claim: Tie the product to a desire the buyer already has, such as looking like celebrities they admire, and push features to the end; Haus's best ads do not name the product for about 20 seconds.
body: A creator telling you how a tank top should fit raises a question for many viewers: why trust this person? Haus answers it by linking the advice to famous men the target buyer wants to look like, such as Brad Pitt or David Beckham. That turns a style tip into a desire the viewer already holds. The ad also feels like a styling video, not a sales pitch: about 20 seconds in, the product has been shown and explained but not named. Features (soft cotton, fitted cut, snaps back) only come near the end. Blue Sense calls leading with features the biggest creative mistake, because anyone can claim them; buyers care about what the product does for them and how that links to what they want. How to apply: script ads in this order: hook, the underlying desire, the benefit, proof, then features, then the call to action. Check your current top ads and note the second where the product is first named.
conditions: Cold-audience creative for products bought on look, identity or aspiration.
fails_when: Warm audiences who already know the brand, or spec-driven products where a feature is the true point of difference.
numbers: product not named until about 20 seconds in

claim: Turn each product feature into a mechanism and a felt benefit for a specific person; grass-fed beef becomes higher omega-3, which becomes no mid-morning crash and a clearer head.
body: Features like grass-fed, no processed ingredients or sugar-free are things anyone can claim, and buyers rarely care on their own. Blue Sense shows how to rebuild one into an angle. Start with the feature: grass-fed beef. Find the mechanism: grass-fed meat carries more omega-3. Link it to a pain a specific person feels: someone who eats porridge, feels sluggish and crashes mid-morning. Then the benefit: switching to grass-fed jerky gives omega-3 for brain health and no carbs to crash on, so they feel sharper. The script opens on the problem, explains why it happens, and sells the result, not the feature. The same method applies to an energy gum listing 60 mg of caffeine, B vitamins and taurine: most viewers do not know what taurine does, so explain it, or the list means nothing. How to apply: for each feature on your product page, write feature, mechanism, who feels the problem, and the benefit they get. Each row is a possible angle; test the ones with the largest audience.
conditions: Consumables and functional products where features have a real mechanism behind them.
fails_when: The claimed mechanism cannot be backed up, or health claims would breach ad policy or local advertising rules.
numbers: example: 60 mg of caffeine per piece of gum listed without explanation

claim: When a hook clearly wins, brief every creator to make their own version of it; Haus, at about $2M a month, runs its bad versus good hook on around 50 ads.
body: Haus, a men's fashion brand doing around $2M a month, found a hook that works: a creator holds up a badly fitting tank top and a well fitting one, flipping between this is bad and this is good. Blue Sense could tell it was a winner because the brand now runs some version of it on about 50 ads. Creators are asked to do their own take, with different products and settings, not a copy of the original. Why it worked: it was new (few people had seen a hook like it) and it broke the scroll pattern instantly. How to apply: when one hook clearly beats the rest on spend and cost per purchase, write it into every creator brief as a format to adapt in their own words, with your other products and their own setting. Track the variants as one concept so you can see when the hook starts to fatigue across all of them.
conditions: Brands working with several UGC creators and launching new ads weekly.
fails_when: The hook only works with one creator's personality or one product, or so many brands copy it that it no longer feels new.

claim: When an ad explains the category, do not equate your product with the generic ingredient (electrolytes like Hyro); position it as better than the cheap alternatives, or buyers just buy salt.
body: Education ads can backfire. A Hyro ad explained what electrolytes do, then said electrolytes like Hyro help you hydrate faster. That line tells viewers the product is just electrolytes, which makes it easy to buy the cheapest brand or add table salt to water. Blue Sense's fixes: first, during the education part, show the generic thing (a pile of salt) rather than the product, so the brand is not tied to the commodity. Second, add a bridge that names the alternatives and why they fall short before the product appears: some formulas lack sodium, some have too much potassium, sports drinks carry lots of sugar; then show why yours has the right balance. The same idea applies to an energy gum, which should counter both coffee and matcha and offer itself as a third option, and could use a price angle (an $8 coffee versus a $2 piece of gum). How to apply: list the cheapest ways a buyer could get the same result, and write one line per ad on why each falls short.
conditions: Products in categories where a cheap generic or home alternative exists.
fails_when: The product truly is a commodity with no point of difference, in which case compete on price, convenience or brand instead.
numbers: example price angle: $8 coffee vs $2 piece of gum

claim: Audit creator scripts against eight beats: hook, problem, mechanism, proof, objection, offer, risk reversal and CTA; Alo's try-on hauls covered only the hook, a light mechanism and proof.
body: This is Blue Sense's standard structure for video aimed at cold audiences. Alo's creator scripts look unscripted: a hook about loving a pair of leggings, a light mechanism (the fabric is smooth yet breathable), proof by wearing them in true size with good compression, sizing mentioned in passing, then nothing. There is no offer, no risk reversal and no call to action. A men's tank top ad had even less: a hook, owning five of them as proof, and a sign-off. That is fine for brand content, but it is not an ad built to hold six figures of spend on cold traffic. How to apply: lay each live creator script out in a table with the eight rows and mark which are empty. You do not need all eight. Pick one or two empty rows that suit the brand voice and fill them: why this product differs from what the creator wore before, a common objection answered, free returns, or a simple ask such as noting the drop tends to sell out. Test the edited version against the original.
conditions: Creator and UGC video ads aimed at cold audiences.
fails_when: Brand films for warm audiences, or aspirational brands where any hard sell breaks the look; avoid a returns line that encourages over-ordering.
numbers: 8 script beats

claim: Do not copy a giant brand's ad account without checking what feeds it: Alo Yoga's account harvests demand built by celebrity seeding, with 21% catalogue ads, 99.6% Shop Now and 98% landing on collection, home or product pages.
body: Alo is estimated at about $2 billion in revenue with 150 plus stores, and its Meta account looks strong on ROAS and spend, but it is not what creates the demand. Blue Sense's scrape: one ad in five is a dynamic catalogue, almost every ad uses Shop Now, nearly all traffic goes to collection pages, the homepage or product pages, and none goes to a New to Alo page the brand built for cold visitors. 15% of ads name a celebrity in the copy, such as Bella Hadid, Kylie or Gisele: the top of funnel work happens through seeding and celebrity links outside the account. Blue Sense's view is that a brand-new company running the same ads would get something like a 0.4 ROAS, because the ads are not strong on their own. The risk for Alo is that if cultural attention fades, nothing in the account can find new buyers. How to apply: before modelling a brand's ads, ask what demand engine sits outside Meta (celebrities, stores, PR, organic reach). If you have none of that, you need cold prospecting creative that opens on a person, problem or desire, and you should judge your ads on whether they work for strangers.
conditions: Using large, famous brands as creative models, especially for brands under about $50M a year without celebrity or retail demand.
fails_when: Brands with strong demand from outside paid (celebrities, retail, big organic following), where a catalogue-heavy, aspirational account can be right at scale, as Blue Sense says it is for several clients.

claim: If you have physical stores, show them in ads where people do not know about them: a store network makes buyers see an established retailer, which lifts trust and conversion across the funnel.
body: Alo has 150 plus stores but mentions none of them in its ads or main landing pages. Blue Sense's presenter, based in Australia where Alo has no stores, did not know they existed, and once he did, he saw Alo as a large retailer rather than an online brand. Blue Sense says this credibility effect works very well when it takes Australian brands into the US. How to apply: in markets where you sell online but buyers have never seen your stores, add store content to the creative mix: try-ons, new collection walk-throughs or product hauls filmed in a flagship store, with the store clearly visible. You are not asking people to visit; you are borrowing the trust that physical retail carries. It is cheap to produce, because store staff can film it during normal shifts. Also mention store count or locations on landing pages for those markets.
conditions: Brands with real physical retail (own stores or major stockists) selling online into regions without those stores.
fails_when: Pure online brands; markets where buyers already know the stores; very small store networks that could make the brand look small.

claim: In fashion, let winning ads run instead of churning the account: Alo's live ads had a median age of 5 days and none older than 24 days, which Blue Sense sees as wasting proven winners.
body: Blue Sense's scrape of Alo found 1,203 unique creative assets and 190 copy lines, with launches about every seven days in step with weekly product drops. Every ad fits one of six formats (editorial campaign panel, celebrity portrait, product grid, colourway launch, dynamic catalogue, creator UGC), with products and faces swapped in. Fashion always balances newness against getting the most out of winners, and Blue Sense says most brands lean too far towards newness. Working with 15 to 20 nine-figure fashion brands, it says doubling down on winners has always worked: if an ad holds big spend at a strong return, keep it live for as long as it performs, and if the product sells, reorder it. Alo's churn makes sense only because its account mostly shows new drops to people who already want the brand. How to apply: pause ads on performance, not on age; before cutting an old ad, check its spend and return trend; if stock can be replenished within 3 to 4 weeks, reorder winners rather than let them sell out and die.
conditions: Fashion brands using Meta as a main acquisition channel, with stock that can be replenished.
fails_when: Brands where Meta mainly shows new drops to existing fans and results depend on outside events; limited runs that cannot be restocked.

claim: In fashion, test problem-led performance scripts on the men's range first: Blue Sense sees them work better for men and knows of no $100M women's fashion brand built on problem agitation.
body: Premium women's fashion tends to sell on aspiration, and whatever a brand leans into it also pushes away the opposite style. Blue Sense has not seen problem-agitating brands selling at Alo's price points, and says it cannot name a women's fashion brand at $100 million that leans on problem-led performance ads, while it could name around six men's brands that do. Because it works with many women's fashion brands, it believes this reflects the market and not only its own view. For a mostly female brand like Alo, the men's range is a low-risk testing ground: it protects the core image, and the buyer responds better to this style. How to apply: if you sell both, run problem-led scripts (a need, a named fabric, proof) on men's products first; compare cost per purchase and new customer rate with your aspirational ads; only carry the approach to women's lines if it holds up and fits the brand.
conditions: Fashion brands selling both men's and women's lines.
fails_when: Value-priced women's brands, where problem-led ads can work; this is one agency's observation and may reflect the brands it sees.

claim: In fashion, voice-free videos that rotate several outfits and poses work well: they show fabric in motion and give viewers another option if one item does not appeal or is sold out.
body: Blue Sense transcribed 33 of Alo's 44 videos: about three quarters had only music and no voice. A typical one runs about 40 seconds, moving through four poses and three outfits. Blue Sense says this format performs very well across the fashion accounts it runs, for two reasons. First, video shows how clothes look and move better than a still image. Second, rotating products means a viewer who dislikes the first look may like the second, and if one item is out of stock the others can still sell. Product grids work for the same reasons in static form, showing several angles and products at once. How to apply: build videos and statics that feature two to four products a similar buyer would want; put your best seller early; check stock across every featured item before scaling; and run them alongside creator try-on hauls, which were the only Alo ads that make an argument for the product.
conditions: Fashion and apparel brands with several products that suit the same buyer.
fails_when: Single hero products or categories that need explaining (supplements, gadgets), where a spoken argument matters more.

claim: When the product is expensive, open the ad on a need the viewer has felt and give one named mechanism; one specific fabric claim beats five stacked adjectives.
body: The one Alo script Blue Sense rated well is a men's gym ad. It opens on needing an outfit that holds up through every set, then names the fabric (Conqueror) and says it wicks sweat and does not cling thanks to a relaxed fit. It starts from a failure the viewer has lived, then gives a reason the product solves it, which moves the ad down the awareness ladder at no extra cost. By contrast, soft, buttery, cozy, comfy and cute together say less than one line about what the fabric does. A named mechanism such as a fabric that smooths but still breathes gives the viewer a reason to believe. The gym ad still lacked an offer, objection handling, risk reversal and a CTA, and ran only 15 seconds. How to apply: rewrite hooks so they name the problem before the product; give your fabric, material or ingredient a name and one plain job; test a 30-second version with two added lines against the short cut.
conditions: Premium or higher-priced products where buyers need a reason to pay more.
fails_when: Impulse, low-priced items where a quick visual is enough; brand films where any explanation breaks the mood.

claim: As a starting fashion creative mix, Blue Sense suggests about 25% campaign shoots, 40% UGC and creator content, 20% repurposed organic and 15% statics, then shift toward what performs.
body: Teams often ask how to split creative production. Blue Sense says the right mix varies by brand and should follow performance data, but gives a rough default by volume: about 25% high-production campaign shoots; about 40% UGC and creator content, which includes founder-led and employee-made content; about 20% organic posts repurposed into ads; and about 15% statics. Some brands will drop one type entirely, others raise one. The point is that a fashion account fed only by campaign shoots, as many traditional retailers are, lacks the native, lower-polish content that converts best on Meta. How to apply: tag every ad by type in its name, and each month compare spend share and results by type. Use the default split for the next batch, then move volume toward types that win on cost per new customer, while keeping enough shoot content to protect the brand look.
conditions: Fashion brands planning monthly creative production for Meta and TikTok.
fails_when: Luxury brands whose brand rules limit low-polish content, or brands whose own data clearly favors a different mix.

claim: Ask fashion creators for a no-talking cut, put size details on screen or in the copy, and feature several products in a haul so the ad scales abroad, cuts returns and outlives single-SKU stockouts.
body: Three practical briefs from Blue Sense for fashion UGC. First, fashion UGC does not need speech, and some of their best performers had none. A version without voice is quick to shoot and avoids the accent problem that limits ads in other countries, so it can run worldwide. Ask every creator for a no-talking cut alongside the normal one. Second, add size data, such as the model's height and size worn, on screen or in the primary text, which helps people pick the right size and reduces returns. Third, show as many products as you can, often as a curated haul. A paid UGC piece featuring one product is finished the day that product sells out, and may never run again unless it is restocked. Several products keep the asset alive. Blue Sense also notes the close-up to full-body pull-back worked well at the time, but formats rotate, so keep watching organic and testing new ones.
conditions: Fashion brands commissioning creator content for paid social.
fails_when: Products that need explanation (technical features, fit systems) where speech carries the sale.

claim: At $75k to $200k a month, fashion brands need incremental attribution plus raw and returns-adjusted aMER, four to six Meta campaigns, 65 to 200 plus new ads a month, and creative volume matched to stock by SKU.
body: Blue Sense's mid-tier list. Measurement: use incremental attribution and lift studies, and track acquisition MER and returns-adjusted acquisition MER daily; study cohorts to see how repeat and return rates change and feed that into forecasts and targets. Meta: four to six campaigns, with ad sets split by concept; cap existing-customer frequency at 7 and cap catalog ads, because this is the tier where people start over-scaling DPAs. Google: Shopping can drop to about 60% to 70% of budget, and the main lever becomes size curve management, pulling products when core sizes sell out. Creative: 65 to 200 plus new ads a month, every ad mapped to a concept, and production planned with stock visibility. Ideally creative output per SKU tracks how much stock that SKU holds, with extra creative for SKUs that are not moving, which answers the problem of slow products never getting seen.

fails_when: Brands without cohort or stock data shared with the ads team; get the data in place before following the rest.

claim: Blue Sense uses AI creative heavily in other categories but not for fashion garments, because AI images drift from what the clothing really looks like and return rates go up.
body: Fashion is bought on how the garment looks, so the creative has to show it as it really is: drape, colour, texture and fit. AI generated images and video tend to change those details, even slightly. When the item that arrives does not match the ad, people send it back. That is why Blue Sense, which leans on AI tools across supplements and other categories where the ad sells a benefit, avoids it for fashion product creative. How to apply: keep the real garment, shot on real people, at the center of fashion ads. Use AI for supporting work, such as scripts, hooks, concept lists, backgrounds or editing, where it does not alter the product. If you test AI product imagery, watch return rates and reasons for that product closely, and stop if not as pictured complaints rise.
conditions: Fashion, footwear and other products bought mainly on appearance.
fails_when: Benefit-led categories like supplements where the visuals do not need to match a physical item exactly.

claim: Fashion angles come from a feature that solves something or a specific life situation; 50 products times 6 personas times 20 angles gives 6,000 concepts, or 60,000 plus ads at 10 to 20 each.
body: People assume concept testing does not fit fashion because the persona is the brand's customer, the offer is the product and the angle is just clothes. Blue Sense disagrees. Offer: usually just the product (they dislike constant discount offers). Persona: use the four to five named customer types most retailers already have in their brand document; if you lack them, survey customers about why they buy, their life stage, and whether they set trends or follow them. Angle is where the range comes from. Either show a feature that solves something, like a dress that cinches the waist, demonstrated on camera; or speak to a specific situation, like a mum who needs workwear that goes from office to home to date night without changing, told in a creator's own words. Make the ad more scalable by showing a set, such as dress plus bag. Then multiply: 50 products, 6 personas, 20 angles is 6,000 concepts, and at 10 to 20 ads each that is 60,000 to 120,000 possible ads.
conditions: Fashion and apparel brands with a range of 20 or more products and four or five named customer types.
fails_when: Very small ranges or brands without defined personas, where the matrix is much smaller; start with the persona survey.

claim: For a US launch from Australia, include lo-fi content (it beats polished in US fashion accounts), localize accents or use no-talking video, filter the site to trans-seasonal products, and target chosen states.
body: Blue Sense's US launch checklist for Australian fashion brands. Creative: lo-fi content performs better in US fashion accounts than in Australia, at least for now, so a campaign-shoot-only brand will struggle. Australian accents do worse in the US than at home; UK and Australian accents travel between those two with only a small drop. So localize voices for the US, or use statics, GIFs and no-talking UGC, which need no localization. Catalog: unless you buy a separate northern hemisphere range, filter the US site to trans-seasonal products. Shoppers land on one product, then browse the wider collection; if it is full of off-season items they bounce, and conversion rate falls. Targeting: pick specific states based on weather and demographics. A single US state can be as big as Australia's whole population, so narrowing does not limit reach and keeps the message relevant. Blue Sense also likes leading with your Australian best sellers on their own product pages, since you have no US brand yet.
conditions: Australian and southern hemisphere fashion brands launching in the US.
fails_when: Brands with a separate northern hemisphere buy and US-made creative, where filtering and accent rules matter less.

claim: Most fashion brands run about 90% aspirational and 10% pain-point creative; Blue Sense sees the best accounts closer to 30% to 40% pain-point hooks, run through partnership ads to stay on brand.
body: Fashion creative sits between pure brand aesthetic and pure direct response. Fast scalers like Haus and True Classic built on function-led performance ads. Traditional retailers only feed campaign shoots into Meta, which are not native to the platform and convert poorly. The winners sit in the middle: direct response that still looks on brand. Format does not have to set brand level; Apple could run polished UGC within its guidelines. A concrete dial is desire-based versus pain-point content. Most brands are around 90% desire and aspiration, 10% pain point. Blue Sense's best accounts lean much further, to 30% to 40% pain point. Example hooks: I never know what to wear to (an occasion), or my partner is impossible to buy for. They open on the problem, then move toward the product. How to apply: tag your live ads as desire or pain point, count the split, and brief new pain-point hooks until they are about a third of launches. Run them as partnership ads so they do not sit on the brand handle.
conditions: Fashion and apparel brands with mid-market positioning whose Meta creative is mostly campaign shoots and aspirational imagery.
fails_when: Luxury houses where any problem framing clashes with positioning, or brands already heavy on scrappy direct response that need more brand-building content instead.

claim: Use trending audio where you hold the rights (TikTok's own analysis found ads with it performed 30% to 40% better) and repurpose employee and fitting-room try-on content into ads.
body: Two cheap creative levers for fashion. Audio: Blue Sense cites a TikTok meta-analysis where ads with trending audio over them did about 30% to 40% better, because they feel like organic posts. Only use tracks you are licensed to use. Many fashion accounts use no audio hooks at all, perhaps fearing it looks off-brand, yet the best fashion ads they see are usually organic posts run as partnership ads with known influencers and a strong audio hook. Employee and fitting-room content: employee generated content means staff filming in-store or behind the scenes. Many retailers post this on TikTok but never turn it into ads. Fitting-room content, raw try-ons in a changing room, has done very well for a couple of Australian brands and helped them scale abroad. In ad library reviews, Country Road's top hook, live for 22 days, was a simple creator walkthrough of a new collection, while its few in-store staff walkthroughs stood out from a feed of shoots. How to apply: brief store staff to film try-ons and walkthroughs weekly, and test them as ads, ideally through partnership handles.
conditions: Fashion brands with stores, staff or an organic content habit to draw on.
fails_when: Music licensing is not possible for paid use in your market, or store footage cannot meet brand standards.

claim: When one angle's CAC starts rising, reposition the same SKU into a new benefit angle with its own ads and landing page before launching a new product; Grüns sells one gummy as GLP-1, energy, immunity, beauty, cognition and gut support.
body: Scaling one product on one angle always inflates acquisition cost eventually, because you exhaust the people that message reaches. Most brands respond by launching a new product, which strains the balance sheet: more inventory, a second buying cycle to manage, and the risk that a flop becomes slow C-grade stock. Grüns does something cheaper. Its gummy is essentially a multivitamin with fibre, and it sells it through many benefit lenses (GLP-1 support, energy, immunity, beauty, cognition, gut health), each with creative that agitates that problem and a landing page that matches the angle. To a cold prospect each looks like a different product for their problem. A new angle needs no product development or stock: a page and ads can be live within 24 hours. Blue Sense expects about 80% of revenue still comes from two angles. How to apply: list every benefit your ingredients or design can honestly support (supplement ingredients often have studies for several uses). Build angle-specific ads and landing pages, test them as separate concepts, and watch cost per new customer by angle. Only launch a new SKU once honest angles run out.
conditions: Products with several real benefits (supplements, multi-use consumables, versatile gear) sold mainly through paid social.
fails_when: Single-purpose products with one clear use; claims you cannot support, especially health claims under TGA or FTC rules.

claim: A brand spending $350,000 a month with only 15 live ads cut CAC about 20 to 30% after Blue Sense relaunched old winners to reach about 60 ads, then slid back when the founder refused to fund new creative.
body: The previous buyer had split the account into about 25 campaigns with bid caps and cost caps, trying to squeeze 15 ads, because media buying was the only lever left to pull. Blue Sense judged creative to be the bottleneck. With no production budget, they dug up past performers that had been switched off, reworked them slightly and relaunched them, taking the account to about 60 ads. Spend rose by about $40,000 a month, CAC fell about 20 to 30% and new customer revenue rose by roughly 28%. The founder still saw creative as a cost, signed and then backed out of production deals, and as the 60 ads fatigued the account drifted back. Blue Sense's pitch had been to move just $10,000 a month from media into production for about 40 assets (a mix of hook swaps and statics), nearly doubling live ads. A 5% efficiency gain on $350,000 is $17,500, so either cut spend for a net saving or keep spend and earn an extra $40,000 to $50,000 a month at their 3x return.

fails_when: Accounts that already have a deep, fresh creative library; relaunching old winners only buys time.

claim: A strong cold static: a tweet-style post about a problem with a wide symptom list, run from a relevant expert's own profile rather than as a tagged partnership ad, so it reads as organic.
body: Blue Sense breaks down an IM8 static: an image styled as a repost of a tweet listing signs of vitamin deficiencies (dry eyes, low energy, bad skin, bleeding gums, bruising and more) and which deficiency causes each. It runs as an ad from a doctor's own account, not tagged as a collaboration with the brand, so viewers read it as a real post until they reach the copy beneath it. Why it works: it agitates a problem for a very wide audience (almost everyone has one of the symptoms), it teaches before it sells, it borrows trust and possibly audience signal from the expert's profile, and only the primary text names the product and the offer. How to apply: find a credible expert in your category willing to have ads run from their handle, build a list-style educational image around a broad problem your product addresses, and keep the brand pitch for the copy and landing page.
conditions: Health, supplement and wellness brands that can work with a credible expert; Meta feed placements.
fails_when: Categories without a believable expert; markets where health statements are restricted; paid expert posts still need disclosure under local advertising law.

claim: Above a 7 out of 10 quality bar nobody can pick winners, so maximise volume above it; two accounts launching 2,000 ads a month on $250,000 spend stayed unprofitable because their ads fell below it.
body: Blue Sense's priority list for creative output runs: volume, then concept quality, then hook strength, editing quality, UGC talent and storytelling. Volume sits first because hit rates are limited and nobody, not even ten top creative strategists side by side, can look at five good ads and say which will become the big spender. Time spent predicting winners is wasted; time spent defining what a good ad looks like is not. So write down your bar: a clear concept (persona, angle, offer), a hook that scores on clarity and relevance, and a format that fits the awareness stage. Anything that meets it goes live; anything that does not gets fixed or dropped. Volume without the bar is junk. The two high-volume accounts the host reviewed were launching far more ads than their spend needed, yet the ads lacked the parts of a good concept, hook and format. Their problem was a missing quality standard, not a missing quantity.
conditions: Teams producing ads at scale who need a review standard.
fails_when: Very early brands with too little data to know what good looks like in their category; they should study winners first.

claim: Ads fatigue for two reasons, staleness or an audience too small; a narrow persona caps daily spend (about 1,000 to 2,000 Australian e-commerce CFOs cannot absorb $10,000 a day), so keep rotating creative to it as it churns.
body: Staleness comes from an ad reaching its lifetime spend, or from looking and sounding like the other ads in the account, so it hits the same people with the same promise and tires sooner. The second cause is pool size. Specific personas make better ads, but each persona has a spend ceiling. Blue Sense's examples: a hook calling out CFOs of $100M-plus e-commerce businesses in Australia reaches perhaps 1,000 to 2,000 people, and $10,000 a day would show each of them hundreds of ads; male gym-goers chasing a sub-4-hour marathon is bigger but still could not take $10,000 a day in Australia. The fix is to find each persona's sustainable daily spend, hold it there and keep fresh ads rotating, because many niche audiences churn (people start and finish marathon training) and refill over time. Broader personas scale further but need better creative, so widen them as you grow.
conditions: Accounts using specific persona-led ads, especially in smaller markets like Australia.
fails_when: Mass-market products where personas overlap heavily; very large markets where even narrow personas are big.
numbers: about 1,000 to 2,000 people in the CFO persona

claim: Advertorial statics (best hair growth products and the ones to avoid) only work when they click through to an education page or carry long educating copy, such as a brand-owned review site ranking its own product first.
body: The example Blue Sense shows runs from a dermatologist's page, promises a ranked list, and sends clicks to a review-style site that the brand itself owns. On that page the expert explains who they are and ranks products, and only the brand's own pick is clickable; it leads to a custom page and a quiz before checkout. The rival products listed lower show weaknesses, and some link out to Amazon affiliate links so unconvinced visitors still earn something. How to apply: if you test advertorial statics, build the matching pre-sell page first (expert intro, criteria, ranking, why your product wins, then a quiz or direct offer). A plain product page after an advertorial ad breaks the promise the ad made. Take care with compliance: the page must not hide who owns it, and comparisons and expert claims must be true and disclosed under local consumer law.
conditions: Considered purchases in crowded categories (hair growth, skincare, supplements) where buyers compare options.
fails_when: Impulse products with no comparison stage; brands unwilling to build a dedicated pre-sell page; hidden ownership can breach consumer law and Meta policy.

claim: Build each angle from a menu of parts: problem agitation, contrarian truth, persona-matched social proof, domain authority, a curiosity gap, comparison with what they tried, and a transformation.
body: An angle is the argument you make to one persona. Most brands default to listing product features, which is not an angle. Pick parts from the menu and chain them into a script. Lead with the pain and make the viewer feel heard before any solution (only possible if they already know the problem). Challenge a common belief, such as everything you know about protein timing being wrong. Show proof that matches the persona, such as studies or customer stories for their age and gender. Borrow authority from the domain: a marathon runner for a running product rather than a doctor in a lab coat for everything. Open a curiosity gap early and close it late so people keep watching. Name the other fixes they have tried and why those failed. Finish with a before and after where allowed. Meta dislikes before and after content, so it needs care to stay within policy, but it remains one of the strongest parts. You can state the whole angle in one line: persona, product, the claim and its proof.
conditions: Video and long-copy ads for products that solve a clear problem.
fails_when: Pure desire categories (some fashion) where pain is weak; before and after content breaches Meta policy in health, weight loss and some beauty claims, so check the rules first.

claim: Build retargeting creative around why people did not buy: split non-buyers into price, trust, quality and timing objections, and give each its own answer, such as cost-per-use, review counts, demos and education.
body: At a 5% site conversion rate, 95% of visitors leave without buying, each for a reason. Blue Sense's illustration splits them roughly evenly: about 20% think the price is too high, 20% do not trust the brand, 20% doubt the quality and 20% are simply not ready yet. Each group needs a different ad. Price: show the discount if there is one, anchor the value, or use cost per use (a supplement that costs half a coffee a day). Trust: customer numbers, star ratings and review counts, testimonial UGC. Quality: UGC of the product in use, demos, before and after where allowed. Not ready: stay present with education and lifestyle content. How to apply: estimate your own split from post-purchase surveys, exit surveys, reviews and support chats, then make sure your bottom of funnel ad set holds at least one ad per major objection, weighted toward the biggest one.
conditions: Brands with enough site traffic for a retargeting pool; product-aware audiences.
fails_when: Very small retargeting pools where only one or two ads get delivery; the even 20% split is illustrative, so use your own survey data.

claim: Compare what each ad costs to make with the contribution margin an average ad earns; if videos cost $500 to return $400 and images cost $50 to return $300, shift production toward images.
body: Blue Sense runs this for clients during onboarding. Steps: (1) Average revenue per ad: revenue from ads over a period divided by the number of ads launched; for most accounts it is around $2,000. (2) Turn that into contribution margin per ad by taking off cost of goods and the ad spend that served it. (3) Divide total production cost by ads made to get cost per ad. (4) Split both by format, and later by source (each creator, agency or designer). In their illustration the account averaged $350 of contribution per ad against $400 to make one, so the creative program lost money, and the split showed images at $50 to make for $300 of contribution while videos cost $500 for $400. Videos may still perform better per ad, but per dollar of production, images win. Track this monthly; it tells you which content types and suppliers to buy more of and which to drop.
conditions: Brands paying for creative production with a few months of ad history to average across.
fails_when: Very new accounts with too few ads for stable averages; long-lived ads earn their margin over months, so short windows understate them.
numbers: about $2,000 average revenue per ad for most accounts
example: $350 contribution per ad versus $400 cost per ad
images $50 cost, $300 contribution; videos $500 cost, $400 contribution

claim: Define a Meta concept as persona plus angle plus offer, with format as a weak fourth lever; a new ad only adds real diversity if at least one of the first three changes.
body: Andromeda groups ads that talk to the same person with the same message, so diversity has to come from what the ad says and to whom, not from how it looks. Change the offer (a different product, bundle or way of framing value) and a different pool responds. Change the angle (skincare sold on wrinkles versus acne) and you reach different people with the same product. Change the persona, including who appears in the ad (a 60-year-old woman versus a 20-year-old), and the audience shifts. Format (UGC, founder talking head, polished education piece, carousel, VSL) can add some new reach, because Meta learns that some people never engage with certain formats, but the same persona, angle and offer in a new format mostly reaches the same people. How to apply: set up your idea sheet and your ad naming with columns for persona, angle, offer and format, so every new ad has a clear concept and results roll up by concept.
conditions: Brands scaling on broad-targeted Meta campaigns where creative drives delivery.
fails_when: Tiny accounts with one product and budget for only a handful of ads, where getting one concept right matters more than spreading across many.

claim: For buyers aged about 50 and over on Facebook feeds, static images with long story copy and video sales letters work very well on cold traffic, because they walk the reader through every stage of awareness.
body: Older Facebook users read. A long primary text story can take someone from unaware to problem aware, solution aware, product aware and finally ready to buy within one ad, with a simple image above it. The same logic drives VSLs (video sales letters), which Blue Sense names as one of the strongest video types for older audiences in 2026. They are teaching pieces, and AI can now produce many of them end to end; some of the agency's AI VSLs hold hundreds of thousands of dollars in spend. The catch is skill: the copy must make an emotional case to one specific person, and AI help does not replace knowing how to move a reader through awareness. In the creatine runner example the host left the VSL out because that persona was too young for it. How to apply: if your buyers skew older, test at least one long-copy static and one VSL per strong angle, and invest in a good copywriter.

fails_when: Younger audiences who skim, and placements like Stories and Reels where long copy is cut off; weak copywriting makes these formats fail outright.

claim: For premium products where price is the main objection, open by stating the price outright ('this costs $120, it is our best seller, here is why'); the honesty stops cold viewers and leads into education.
body: Most ads hide the price until the end. When price is the main reason people do not buy, Blue Sense has seen the opposite work very well for one client: say up front that the product is expensive, that people buy it anyway, and promise to explain why. Cold viewers who have never heard of the brand stop because the frankness is unusual and makes them curious what could be worth that much. The body then becomes a teaching piece that earns the price: what goes into it, what cheaper options get wrong, how long it lasts. The same truth bomb can be about ingredients or the industry: an uncomfortable fact owned openly. How to apply: check reviews and post-purchase surveys; if price is the top objection and you sell above the category average, script one hook that leads with the price and an education body that justifies it, and test it against your current opener.
conditions: Premium or high average order value products where price is the main objection and the product can justify it.
fails_when: Low-priced or commodity products, where stating the price adds no tension, or products that cannot back up a premium story.

claim: Hook testing still works under Andromeda: a new hook gets its own creative ID and fresh reach; Blue Sense revived fatigued ads that had spent $50,000 to $100,000 with 50 new hooks for another $100,000 at the same efficiency.
body: A 90-second ad with a new three-second opening is the same concept, so it overlaps with the original audience, but Meta still treats it as a separate creative and finds some new people. The reason to do it anyway is cost. When filming, record the hook six ways and you have six variants for a few extra minutes. For a winner that has started to fatigue, shoot a batch of new openings (Blue Sense's batch took about an hour) and stack them on the proven body. Hook swaps also rescue ads that failed only because of a weak opening: if an ad's hook rate sits well below your account average but the hold rate after the hook is fine, replace the hook before writing the ad off. Treat hook swaps as cheap life extension, not as new concepts; you still need new personas and angles for real diversity.

claim: In top-of-funnel video, introduce the product as late as you can: move viewers from unaware to problem and solution aware first; fewer people see the product, but they buy at higher rates.
body: Teams look at retention curves, see most viewers gone by 90 seconds, and rush the product in early so more people know what is being sold. Blue Sense argues this backfires. A viewer who has not yet accepted they have the problem, or what kind of fix solves it, is not ready to hear about your brand, so an early pitch converts poorly and breaks the flow. The best cold ads, VSLs in particular, walk people through the stages: a curiosity opener, then the problem (plain tap water lacks electrolytes), then the type of solution (the right salt ratio), then the product (canned mineral water with electrolytes), and retargeting closes the now aware. One influencer testosterone ad they show reveals the product about a minute and a half in and scales well. How to apply: map your script against the awareness stages and only name the product once the solution type is clear; judge on purchases, not on how many saw the product.

claim: Keep Meta spend spread across many working ads, not one or two heroes; Blue Sense has turned away 8 to 10 brands that arrived 40% down on new customers after three ads holding $1M fatigued.
body: Every ad has a ceiling on what it can spend, and every ad fatigues in the end. Blue Sense compares two ways to spend $1,000 a day at a 4x ROAS: one ad holding it all, or three ads sharing it at the same blended ROAS. The second is far safer, because when one ad tires the other two absorb the spend at the same efficiency. How to apply: in Ads Manager, sort ads by amount spent over the last 30 days and work out what share of spend sits in your top one to three ads. If most of it does, treat creative production as urgent now, not when results drop. Keep briefing new concepts while the winners are still working. claim: Match hook type to awareness: problem-agitation hooks only reach the problem aware and stall at scale, while contrarian truths work at every awareness level on both paid and organic.
body: Blue Sense's working list of hook types, with where each fits. Problem agitation (back pain from desk work?) converts well but only for people who already know the problem, so it caps how far an ad can scale. Contrarian truth (what you were taught about protein timing is wrong) creates friction that demands an answer and works across awareness levels. Specific proof leads with a measurable result, a number and a time frame, such as losing 12 kilos in 90 days while still eating pasta. A curiosity gap opens a question only the video answers; the host says his own variants average over 45 seconds of view time on organic. Psychological confrontation talks like a friend calling you out (that drawer of products you never use). Social proof leads with a result share, such as 90% seeing results in 30 days. Price truth bombs, founder stakes and sensory openers have their own cards. Most brands can use at least seven types. Treat the list as a base, then push for novelty, because the biggest ads open with something rivals have not done.

claim: Near-copies of the same ad get bundled by Andromeda and shown to the same people, so frequency climbs, reach shrinks and ROAS falls; ask your Meta rep for your creative similarity score, where higher is worse.

If several ads say the same thing to the same person, for example one shoot with the model in slightly different poses, UGC with one line changed halfway through, or even different formats that all speak to the same buyer, Meta groups them and serves them to one pool. The signs in Ads Manager are rising frequency, falling reach and slowly falling ROAS. The fix is to launch ads that speak to different people, so each one finds its own audience and the total pool grows as spend rises. Most accounts cannot see the creative similarity score in Ads Manager yet, but a dedicated Meta rep can pull it for you; a higher number means your ads are more alike. Also avoid openers that address everyone ("hey everyone, check this out"): with no clear person in the ad, Meta has no signal for who to find.

claim: On cold campaigns no ad should run a frequency above 2 over 30 to 60 days; above that is a fatigue and diversity red flag, because purchase odds fall sharply after a second view of the identical ad.

People rarely buy on one view, so a second view of an ad can help, but a third of the same ad is mostly wasted money. Audit: open Ads Manager at the ad level, filter to cold or prospecting campaigns, set the date range to the last 30 days and then 60 days, and add the frequency column. Blue Sense says none of the accounts it runs has a cold ad above 2, and any it finds is treated as an immediate problem. If yours do, you need more ads and more different ones (new personas, angles or formats), not more budget on the same ones. claim: Pick a format only after the concept, using five questions: what is the concept, does it need education, can the value show in one frame, does it need a demo, and what awareness stage is it for?
body: Format is the last decision in concept design, not the first. Work through it in order. First define the persona, angle and offer. If the concept needs teaching (a new mechanism, a myth to bust), you probably need longer video or long copy. If the value can be said in one frame, choose a static image or carousel, which are faster and cheaper to make in volume. If the product needs a demo, you are pushed toward video unless a strong designer can show it in stills. Finally, check the stage: unaware and problem-aware viewers need a longer, teaching format, while product-aware and most-aware viewers can be closed with dynamic product ads and simple images. claim: Plan one new ad per $1,000 of monthly Meta spend, or better, divide your monthly new customer revenue target by the average revenue an ad earns: $300,000 over $3,000 per ad means 100 new ads a month.

The better method works back from targets. (1) Average spend per ad: total spend over the last year divided by ads launched; $500,000 over 500 ads is $1,000 per ad. (2) Average return per ad: multiply by your 7-day click ROAS, or use acquisition MER (new customer revenue divided by ad spend); at 3x that is $3,000 per ad. (3) Divide the monthly new customer revenue target by that figure: $300,000 needs 100 new ads. Flex the creative plan with the revenue forecast through the year. Two limits: ads take months to spend their full lifetime, so you need more volume earlier than the maths suggests, and winners and losers differ hugely, so a fuller model forecasts each separately with a time lag.

fails_when: New accounts with no history, or accounts where a few ads take nearly all spend, which makes averages misleading.

claim: Spend production time on hooks: with sound scripts, two bodies with 15 hooks will usually beat five bodies with two hooks, because about 80% of viewers never get past the hook.
body: The hook is not a trick to win a glance. It is a promise that what follows is relevant to the viewer. Since most people leave in the first seconds, the hook decides who even sees the rest, and the spread in results between hooks is usually wider than between bodies. So for the same hour of shooting and editing, make a few bodies and many hooks. The rule depends on the bodies being well scripted; if you are weak at scripts, one body may be far better than the others and the test will mislead you. Bait openers such as memes can push hook rate up but bring the wrong people and do not convert. A hook has three layers you can vary: what is on screen, what is said or heard, and the text overlay (or the primary text above the ad).

body: Three content types, ranked by leverage. Winner replication: remake proven winners with new hooks, new formats or new creators; it gives the highest return in paid and organic alike, because the same idea reaches new people each time. Iteration: fix underperformers or stretch a working concept to a near neighbour, such as a new persona or a new offer. Net new: brand new concepts, angles and formats, needed because everything fatigues and the next winners must come from somewhere. The host admits his own organic content runs 80 to 90% net new, while the 10 to 20% he repeats takes about 80% of the views. How to apply: tag every brief by type and check the monthly split. Briefing and scripting is where AI pays off: build a brand-tuned skill that walks the strategist through about 20 questions (persona, concept, offer, long or short, awareness stage) and outputs a brief or script that needs only light edits. Production also gains a lot; VSLs and static images can be about 90% AI-made. claim: When ads are not working, test angles first, then offers, then personas, and formats last; most teams do the reverse and burn months swapping UGC styles.
body: Blue Sense ranks the four concept levers by how much they move results. Angle comes first: if a persona has bought from you before, failure with that persona is almost always the message or the offer, not the person. Offer is arguably the most powerful lever, but it has little room to move: a single-product brand cannot change the product, and after roughly seven ways of packaging two or three products (bundles, gift with purchase, tiered deals, subscription) the only lever left is deep discounting, which you do not want. Persona is next, and it gives the account breadth and volume once a message works. Format is last. "UGC works" is false; the script, persona, angle and offer inside the format do the work. How to apply: when a batch fails, write new angles for proven buyer types before you change who you target or what style you shoot in. Brands with large catalogues or a new product launch can move offer and product testing higher.

claim: When hiring creators, ask for past examples and the briefs those examples were made from; the pair shows whether they need a detailed brief or can turn a rough one into something good.
body: A creator's output depends on the brief, so a portfolio alone misleads. If a creator made a great video from a thin brief, you can give them room. If their good work came from very detailed briefs, you must match that level of detail. Blue Sense's default is to write the most detailed brief it can anyway, then let the creator shoot one take on script and one in their own words; run both and keep what performs. Also hire creators native to the market you target: Australian accents in Australia and US accents in the US. The same script with a local creator does better, and while UK creators carry over fairly well to Australia, native voices still have an edge. How to apply: add two questions to your creator intake form: share two past briefs and the videos made from them, and where are you based.
conditions: Brands sourcing UGC creators or freelancers for ad content.
fails_when: Creators who cannot share client briefs for confidentiality reasons; then run a small paid test brief instead.

claim: Write personas as a person with a specific problem, not a demographic; 'busy professional' or 'women 25 to 45' gives forgettable ads, while 'consultant flying twice a week who needs one carry-on for boardrooms and bars' writes itself.
body: A persona is an archetype defined by a problem, a desire and a buying trigger. Broad personas fail because the ad cannot pick one situation, one way of talking and one kind of proof, so it ends up vague and holds little spend. A narrow one tells the scriptwriter who should be on screen, what words they use, which pain to press and what proof they need. Blue Sense's pairs: a health-conscious parent becomes a mum who has tried six supplements because her toddler refuses vegetables; one acne persona splits into women 20 to 25, women 30 to 35 (likely hormonal) and women 40 to 45, each a different problem. Fashion works the same way: a mum of young kids who needs an affordable dress that goes from work to a Friday night out. Steps: list who already buys, list each problem the product solves for them, then note how pain, language and proof differ for each. An ad for a broad persona can hold more spend if it lands, but that takes rare skill; Blue Sense advises staying narrow until you are a mid eight-figure brand.
conditions: Any brand writing Meta or TikTok ads, especially below about $20M to $50M a year in revenue.
fails_when: Large brands with proven skill at broad, unaware ads, where a wider persona can hold far more spend; a persona that is too small also caps daily spend.
numbers: stay narrow until mid eight figures in revenue

claim: A product shot on white only reaches the most-aware buyer, and about 90% of statics stop at product aware; statics can reach unaware audiences only by leaning on long primary text plus a landing page.
body: Blue Sense maps statics to Eugene Schwartz's five stages. Most aware: people who know your brand; a plain product shot on a white background reaches almost only them. Product aware: they know the product but have not bought; by their estimate this is where about 90% of statics people make sit. Solution aware: they know the problem and the kind of fix but not your product, the start of truly cold audiences, and few brands make statics here. Problem aware: they feel the problem but do not know a solution exists. Unaware: they do not know they have the problem. A static can work at the unaware stage, but one image seen for about four seconds cannot introduce a problem, a solution, your product and a reason to buy now. So the image's job becomes sending attention somewhere that can: long-form primary text, or a landing page where you can sell at length. How to apply: label each static by stage; for anything above product aware, plan the copy or the page that will do the education before designing the image.
conditions: Static ads on Meta aimed at growing beyond the existing audience.
fails_when: Retargeting or brand-aware audiences, where a clean product shot with an offer is exactly what converts.
numbers: about 90% of statics sit at product aware (Blue Sense estimate)
a static is consumed in about 4 seconds

claim: A scalable top-of-funnel static pairs a persona-matched native image with a curiosity headline, long story-led primary text and a landing page whose offer matches the ad.
body: Blue Sense's lead example targets GLP-1 users losing hair: the headline says the drug gave you your body back, then took your hair, and the image (likely AI made) shows a woman with an injection pen while hair falls in the mirror behind her. Persona and angle are instantly clear from who is shown and the problem named, but the offer is hidden, so a curiosity gap pulls the viewer into the copy. The primary text is long and personal, moving through why the hair loss happens to pumpkin seed oil as the fix. The landing page then makes an offer that matches the ad exactly (less shedding in 26 days or less). They believe an ad like this can spend hundreds of thousands. Other examples follow the same pattern: a shaving acne before and after run through what looks like a personal whitelisted page, with a custom lander for that angle; a call-out to people bloated by 3pm with a puzzling image. Good long copy also filters: a menopause story quickly loses anyone it is not for, which is the point.
conditions: Problem-solution products, especially health, beauty and wellness, with a persona who reads long copy on Facebook.
fails_when: Impulse or visual products where long copy adds nothing; health claims that need substantiation under Meta policy and consumer law.

ads like this can spend hundreds of thousands (Blue Sense estimate)

claim: A static stops the scroll in one of two ways: look native to the feed so it does not read as an ad, or be a loud pattern interrupt; being first to an untapped familiar format gives a temporary edge.
body: Blue Sense lists three jobs for a static: stop the scroll, communicate the message, drive action. Stopping the scroll comes down to two routes. Native: the image looks like organic content, so people consume it the way they consume their feed. Familiar formats help here, such as a phone notes screenshot or a text message thread, because the viewer recognises the layout before realising it is an ad. Pattern interrupt: the opposite, a clickbaity or striking image that jumps out. Copying formats that competitors or other industries already use is fine but gives little edge; inventing a familiar-feeling format that works, before others copy it, creates a short-lived arbitrage. An example from the video: the fashion brand Venroy ran a paparazzi-style celebrity photo with its logo small, which made Nathan stop to work out what he was looking at before noticing the brand. Native statics are mostly a CPG tactic; using one in fashion stands out. The job of such an ad is to start the funnel, with video retargeting doing the selling.
conditions: Meta feed placements where organic posts and ads sit side by side.
fails_when: Native styles that mislead viewers about who is speaking in ways that breach ad policy; and novelty fades once a format is widely copied.
asks: How do I make a static ad stop the scroll?

Should my ads look like organic posts?

claim: AI can help at every step of static production, but keep a human at the concepting step: language models give everyone the same concepts, while people connect ideas from other industries.
body: Blue Sense describes several real client pipelines. Some fully automate research, concepting, the build and variations with AI and keep a human only at the feedback step before launch. Others keep the build human, so a person checks the research and concept quality, with AI making variations. Another uses AI-assisted research and building but human concepting. Fully automating feedback too is possible, but Nathan doubts it and says all-AI pipelines produce slop. Where AI helps most is research: scraping large sets of reviews and comments to understand the buyer. Where humans matter most is concepting. Anyone can ask a language model for ad concepts and everyone gets near-identical answers; feeding it richer research context makes answers a little more unique, but once everyone does that the edge is gone. What models do poorly is borrow an idea from an unrelated industry and translate it into your product. Creative people make those peripheral connections, and that is where differentiation and arbitrage come from. How to apply: use AI to gather and summarise research and to build and vary, but have a person own the concept list.
conditions: Teams using AI image or language tools in creative production.
fails_when: Very small brands with no creative staff, where an AI-led pipeline with careful review is still better than no volume.
asks: Can I use AI to make my ads?

claim: Before designing any static, write down its persona, angle and offer; three new statics are only variations unless at least one of those changes, such as selling for longevity instead of weight loss.
body: A concept, in Blue Sense's creative strategy, is the persona, the angle and the offer an ad sits under, plus optionally the format (the vehicle, such as an advertorial, listicle, native static or before and after). For statics they set format aside, since copying format ideas is easy and adds little. The rule for your creative team: if they make three new statics, those are variations of one concept unless the offer, the angle or the persona differs. Offer can be a different product, or a different way of presenting the value of a single product. Angle is the reason to buy: telling people to buy for longevity rather than for weight loss is a new angle. Persona is who you are speaking to; the same message to the same people is the same ad. How to apply: add three required fields to every static brief (persona, angle, offer) and reject briefs that duplicate a live concept's three fields while claiming to be new. Count distinct concepts launched per month alongside total ads.
conditions: Teams producing statics at volume for Meta.
fails_when: Single-product brands with a narrow buyer, where only a few angles exist; new formats then carry more of the diversity.

claim: Compare creative types on expected gross profit per ad after production cost: at $1,000 revenue per ad and 10x return, a $20 static nets $880 and a $200 video $700; at 2x, $480 versus $300.
body: Blue Sense argues statics win on economics, not only on CPM. Work out, for each creative type, the average revenue an ad returns, subtract the average ad spend behind it, then subtract what it cost to produce. Their worked example: each ad returns about $1,000 in revenue. At a 10x return the spend is $100. A static costing $20 to make leaves $880; a video costing $200 leaves $700. At a more realistic 2x return the spend is $500, leaving $480 for the static and $300 for the video, so the video earns well under two thirds as much. Production speed adds to it: in the time and cost of one good 60 to 90 second video, a team can make about four statics, or three really good ones, and AI tools can push the cost of a static to around a dollar. The usual pushback is that statics only work bottom of funnel, which is true only if you make them that way. How to apply: pull average revenue, spend and production cost per ad by format from the last quarter and compare.
conditions: Brands with enough ads per format to compute reliable averages, and where both formats are used at similar funnel stages.
fails_when: Videos sit at a different funnel stage or reach audiences statics cannot; comparing per-ad returns across stages then misleads. Revenue here is not gross profit, so apply product margin before final decisions.

claim: Every static must commit to one end of a line from total clarity to a deliberate curiosity gap; ads that sit in the middle, half intriguing and half explaining, are the ones that fail.
body: At one extreme is maximum clarity: within three or four seconds the viewer knows what is sold, the angle, who it is for and the offer, so anyone who clicks is warm. At the other extreme is a deliberate curiosity gap: native statics, advertorials and listicles where the viewer cannot tell what is happening or even that it is an ad, and so clicks or reads the copy to find out. Both can work. The middle does not: a static that half teases and half explains neither intrigues nor informs. Blue Sense's example is an AG1 next generation static: a vague headline about never stopping improving, a confusing graph, and a list such as improved B vitamins and more adaptogens that most people cannot interpret. It tries to build curiosity and educate about a launch at once and does neither; Nathan notes about one like after three months. His fixes: go fully curious (blur the product, a short tease, push to click) or fully educational (explain exactly what changed and why it matters). He suspects compliance pressure keeps large funded brands in the middle, and that brand recognition props such ads up.
conditions: Static ads on Meta for any category.
fails_when: Strong brands whose logo alone carries recognition, which can partly rescue a muddled ad (Blue Sense's view of AG1).
numbers: AG1 static: about 1 like after about 3 months running (Blue Sense observation)

claim: Forecast ad volume from winner churn: with 10 winners and 20% monthly churn you must replace 2, and at a 5% hit rate (5% to 15% is normal) that means 40 new ads a month.
body: Testing as many ads as possible is the wrong goal, because each ad needs enough spend to show whether it works. Blue Sense instead works back to the volume they need, using two models. Churn model: count the winning ads live this month and how many stop working. Example: 10 winners, 2 churn out, a 20% churn rate, so you need two new winners a month. Then your hit rate: about 5% is common in large accounts, with a typical range of 5% to 15%. At 5%, finding one winner takes about 20 ads, so replacing two takes about 40 new ads a month, assuming quality matches the account's history. Average revenue per ad model: take the average spend per ad, average return and therefore average revenue per ad, plus how long ads typically run; if the month needs $1M in revenue, divide to get how many live ads you need, and so how many to launch. They use both and compare. How to apply: pull last quarter's winners, how many died each month and how many launches it took to find each new one.
conditions: Accounts with enough history to count winners and a clear definition of a winning ad.
fails_when: New accounts with no winners yet, or when ad quality changes sharply so the past hit rate no longer applies.

hit rate 5% typical, 5% to 15% range in large accounts
5% hit rate = about 20 ads per winner

claim: Make statics in this order: research, concept, build, variations, internal feedback, launch; spend about 80% of the time on research and concepting, and never start by opening Canva templates.
body: Blue Sense's production line for statics runs left to right in order of importance. Research comes first and matters most. It is also the most tedious step, which is why most teams skip it and jump to concepts; they believe they know the customer's pain points but have not done the work, so the long-form copy and landing pages they write later speak to someone they do not understand and fall flat. Concepting is next (persona, angle, offer). Then the build, which is where format choices live. Then variations, one of the least important steps, used only to squeeze more spend from a working concept. Then internal feedback and launch. Each step depends on the one before: a build is worthless without a good concept, variations without a good build, feedback without all of it. How to apply: if you are about to make a static, open a research document, not Canva. Collect reviews, survey answers, competitor ads and customer language first, concept from that, and only then move quickly through production, which should be fast.
conditions: Brands or agencies producing static ads regularly.
fails_when: Urgent offer or sale announcements where the concept is given and speed matters more than research.
numbers: about 80% of time on research and concepting

claim: Make the element the eye hits first carry the highest-awareness message (for example 'new technology' rather than 'protein powder'), and steer the eye with three levers: size, contrast and white space.
body: When someone sees an image the eye jumps to one spot, then a second, third and fourth, tracing a path through the ad. If you ignore that path, the first thing seen is often the product name, so the viewer instantly knows they are being sold protein powder and the ad works only on people already shopping for it. Blue Sense's fix is to put the most broadly appealing, highest-awareness message where the eye lands first. Instead of 'protein powder', lead with something like 'new technology'. The image then shows something that does not quite add up, such as a clear liquid being mixed (protein water), so the eye moves on for an explanation and the viewer is walked through the awareness stages towards a click. You control the path three ways. Size: the brain goes to the biggest element. Contrast: the eye goes to whatever stands out from its surroundings. White space: empty areas push the eye away and towards the elements that matter. How to apply: before launch, ask a colleague to name what they noticed first, second and third, and redesign if the product name comes first.
conditions: Static ads aimed at cold or problem-aware audiences.
fails_when: Retargeting statics for people who already know the product, where leading with the product and offer is the right first message.

claim: Map static formats to funnel stages (top: problem agitation, native, advertorial, founder statics; middle: comparisons, before and after, listicles, feature call-outs; bottom: offers, reviews, hero product), then scale a winning format by swapping one concept element.
body: Blue Sense's rough placement. Top of funnel: problem agitation statics, native statics, PR and advertorial styles, and founder statics (a photo of the founder doing something, with the founder story carried in long primary text), each either highly curious or very clear. Middle of funnel, where most teams spend their effort: comparison ads, before and afters, listicles and feature call-outs. Bottom of funnel: an offer call-out, a review, or a hero product shot. Once a format wins, do not just make tweaks of that layout. Keep the format and change one part of the concept. If problem agitation statics work for your greens powder, run the same format with the same messaging, persona and angle for your protein powder (a new offer). Or keep the offer and angle and change the persona, from women aged 30 to 40 to men. Rotating one concept element at a time is how you squeeze the most spend out of a format that works while still reaching new people.
conditions: Brands with several products or personas and at least one proven static format.
fails_when: Single-product, single-persona brands, where angles become the only lever and the format can tire.
numbers: example persona swap: women 30 to 40 to men

claim: On statics, primary text and headline deserve the same effort as the image; pair them like a YouTube thumbnail and title, where each creates a question the other half answers.
body: In a video ad most people watch rather than read, so the caption matters less. On a static, viewers are much more likely to read the headline and primary text, so treat those words as half the creative, not an afterthought. Native statics and advertorials often give almost nothing away in the image, which forces the reader into the copy; that copy is where the selling happens. Blue Sense borrows the thumbnail and title logic from YouTube: the thumbnail makes you wonder what is happening and the title adds just enough context to make you click. Their example: a headline about a miracle drug paired with an image of someone pouring a blurred powder into a drink. Neither half makes full sense alone, so the viewer either clicks through to the article behind the ad or taps to read the full primary text. You can pair image with primary text, or primary text with headline. How to apply: for each static, write the image message, headline and first line of primary text together and check each one raises a question the next resolves.
conditions: Static and carousel ads in Meta feed placements where text is shown beside the image.
fails_when: Placements that hide most text (Stories, Reels overlays), where the image must carry the message alone.

claim: Skip tiny static variations such as a background colour or a model's pose: a 1% to 2% effect cannot be measured without large split-test budgets, and Andromeda groups near-identical ads anyway.
body: Variations are worth making. Spinning up many new ads under a working concept is a high-leverage way to add volume. But a variation must be big enough to matter. Changing a red background to blue might shift performance by 1% or 2% for reasons nobody understands; detecting that would need a large budget in a controlled split test, which is a poor use of spend for a lesson you would never act on. Blue Sense's test for any swing: is it measurable, is it worth putting spend behind, and will the result change how you brief creative from now on? Telling your team to prefer blue over red fails all three; learning which offers, angles and personas win passes. Under Andromeda this has become mandatory: near-identical ads are grouped as one ad ID and shown to the same audience, so small variants add no reach. According to what Meta reps told Blue Sense, Meta built that grouping because AI image tools flooded the platform with near-duplicates and high-velocity accounts were being favoured, so it now counts lookalike ads as one.
conditions: Meta accounts making static variations, especially with AI tools.
fails_when: Very large accounts with the budget to run proper split tests on visual elements and a reason to act on small gains.
numbers: small visual changes shift performance perhaps 1% to 2%

claim: Static ads fail for three reasons: teams only make bottom-of-funnel statics, they launch variations of one concept believing they are new concepts, and they judge upper-funnel statics on last-click results without educational landing pages.
body: First, most statics sit at the bottom of the funnel. It is hard to walk someone through the stages of awareness in one square image with few words, so most teams default to retargeting-style product statics. Pushing a static higher up the awareness ladder is a skill most teams lack, not an impossibility. Second, a new design is not a new concept. Blue Sense describes a client who handed over two statics as two different concepts that were really one concept in two layouts. Reach only widens when the angle, the offer or the persona changes. Third, measurement. Top-of-funnel statics, such as advertorial or native styles with long copy, bring cheap CPMs and lots of traffic to an educational page; much of that traffic converts later through a retargeting ad that takes the credit. Judged by last click, the static looks weak even when it is feeding the whole account. How to apply: audit your current statics by awareness stage and by concept, and judge upper-funnel ones by blended results and new customer numbers rather than their own ROAS.
conditions: Meta accounts running statics alongside video and retargeting.
fails_when: Small accounts with almost no retargeting pool, where a static's own results are close to its true effect.

claim: Static image ads usually get the lowest CPMs of any creative type on Meta, beating video unless a compliance issue intervenes, and plain-looking statics have held a quarter of a million dollars in spend.
body: Blue Sense calls statics the most undervalued, highest-leverage creative type in a Meta account. Three reasons. They tend to run at the cheapest CPMs, and in their experience they nearly always beat video on that measure unless the category hits compliance limits. They are the fastest way to test a new angle, concept or offer, since a new static can be made and launched in very little time. And under Andromeda, where the creative itself steers who sees the ad, clarity matters far more than design: some of the best statics they show look so rough you would doubt they convert, yet held about $250,000 of spend. What wins is how quickly the viewer grasps the problem being agitated, the solution and who it is for. How to apply: stop spending design hours polishing layouts, and put that time into the message, the copy and the concept; judge a static first on whether a stranger understands it in a few seconds.
conditions: Meta accounts in most DTC categories; strongest where a message can be grasped visually in a few seconds.
fails_when: Categories with tight ad policy limits on images (some health and before-and-after claims), or products whose value only shows in motion.

claim: Use statics as the cheap testing ground: trial new angles, personas and offers as statics first, move winners into costlier video shoots, and split test offers on warm audiences with them.
body: Because a video costs so much more to make than a static, Blue Sense uses statics to find out what works before spending on production. A new angle, concept, persona or offer can be launched as a static; if it performs, it earns a higher-budget video shoot built around the same idea. This keeps expensive shoots pointed at ideas the market has already responded to. Statics are especially handy for offer testing. Even if a static sits in the middle or bottom of the funnel and you cannot make it work cold, you can still run head-to-head offer tests on warm audiences (for example bundle versus discount versus free gift), see which converts better, and work out which leaves more gross profit per order. That lets you keep refining the offer without reshooting anything. How to apply: before briefing a video, require a static version of the concept to have earned spend; and keep a standing warm-audience static test for offers, judged on gross profit per order rather than conversion rate alone.
conditions: Meta accounts with a warm audience large enough to read offer tests and a video budget worth protecting.
fails_when: Concepts that depend on demonstration or story, which a static cannot carry, so a failed static does not prove the idea is weak.
